In total, the number of personnel is about 300.

 

Aalto University Rotor Lab at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, in collaboration with our industrial partner Wärtsilä, is looking for a

Doctoral Researcher / Master's Thesis Worker

VIcTOR - Virtual Torque Sensing for Maritime Powertrains


Description of the project

Knowledge of the torque and torsional response of a maritime powertrain is important for emission-compliant control. Torque and torsional response are normally measured using strain gauges, dedicated torque sensors, or other instrumentation installed on the drivetrain. Torsional response can also be calculated if the external torsional forces acting on the powertrain are known, but measurements of this external forcing are rare in maritime powertrains. Instrumenting large maritime powertrains is also costly, and there is often not enough measured information available to fully determine the torsional response using conventional methods alone.

Unknown external forces and torsional response can instead be estimated using methods such as convex optimization or Kalman filtering. These torque estimation methods allow much more freedom in sensor placement and reduce the number of sensors needed to characterize the full torsional response of the powertrain.

This project aims to develop a torque estimation procedure that determines the unknown input torque and full torsional response using only encoder (speed, position) measurements together with selected available measurements from the driving internal combustion engine (e.g. cylinder pressure) or the driven electric generator (e.g. electromagnetic torque) — removing the need for an expensive, dedicated torque transducer.

Two complementary approaches will be explored. The first is convex optimization-based torque estimation, which allows constraints to be incorporated flexibly, both to keep estimated quantities physically consistent and to enforce desired structure in the results. The second is physics-informed learning, which combines available historical data with known system dynamics as a regulariser for data-driven learning — enabling nonlinear system dynamics to be learned indirectly with less training data than traditional data-driven approaches, for example to estimate the external torsional excitation from the propeller.

To ultimately remove the need for a torque flange, the estimation method must be integrated into the embedded engine control system. The work will make use of industry-standard tools such as Matlab Simulink to connect with existing control systems and support SIL/MIL simulation, and the resulting algorithm must run efficiently within the CPU constraints of an embedded system.

The project is carried out in collaboration with Wärtsilä, which provides powertrain data, operational torsional-dynamics measurements for model verification, and access to a physical maritime powertrain for validating the developed torque estimation procedure. You will be employed by the University, but your work will be conducted physically both at Aalto University campus and Wärtsilä Vaasa STH laboratory, to provide best-possible methodological support for your doctoral dissertation project.

 

Research focus

  • Defining the accuracy and operational requirements for the torque estimation algorithm
  • Building and verifying a torsional vibration model of the powertrain, based on data provided by Wärtsilä, with a final test environment in Simulink
  • Developing convex optimization-based and/or physics-informed deep learning approaches to torque estimation
  • Studying the torque estimation framework first with simulated measurements and scenarios, then verifying it against measurements from Wärtsilä's physical powertrain
  • Testing and refining the torque estimation model for implementation in an embedded environment with limited computing capacity

Skills we are looking for

Please note that these are considered assets, not strict requirements:

  • Background in mechanical engineering, control engineering, applied mathematics, electrical engineering, or a related field
  • Knowledge of torsional vibration, rotordynamics, or powertrain/drivetrain dynamics
  • Experience with state estimation or optimization methods (e.g. Kalman filtering, convex optimization)
  • Interest or experience in machine learning, particularly physics-informed or physics-constrained learning
  • Programming and modelling skills (Matlab/Simulink, Python, C or other embedded-systems languages)
  • Interest in embedded systems and control engineering, and in working with industrial measurement data

General eligibility criteria

  • Master's or Bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering, or other relevant field
  • Excellent written and oral skills in English
  • Finnish language skills are considered a benefit
  • Applicants must be able to work full-time and, for doctoral studies, meet the official eligibility requirements of the Aalto Doctoral Programme in Engineering during a trial period of 6 months: aalto.fi/en/study-options/aalto-doctoral-programme-in-engineering

What we offer

  • After graduation, doctoral researcher starting salary: 3143 €/month (gross), with possible increases based on achievements
  • Annual workload: 1612 hours

jobs.description_html:
Aalto University is a community of bold thinkers where science and art meet technology and business. We are committed to identifying and solving grand societal challenges and building an innovative future. Aalto has six schools with 16 000 students and a staff of 5200, of which more than 440 are professors. Our main campus is located in Espoo, Finland. Diversity is part of who we are, and we actively work to ensure our community’s diversity and inclusiveness. The Department of Computer Science is an internationally-oriented community and home to world-class research in modern computer science, combining research on foundations and innovative applications. With over 40 professors and more than 550 employees from 50+ countries, it is the largest department at Aalto University and the leading computer science research unit in northern Europe. Computer science research at Aalto University ranks high in several international surveys (7th in Europe and 1st in the Nordics (NTU 2023); and 88th worldwide in Times Higher Education subject ranking 2025).


We are now looking for a

Doctoral researcher

 

How can technology users judge whether a digital request is genuine when convincing messages, voices and images can be fabricated?


The research group Humans, Security and Privacy at the Computer Science Department at Aalto University is looking to hire one Doctoral Researcher in Human-Centered Security and Digital Deception (PhD student). You will be supervised by Assistant Professor Verena Distler.  


Our interdisciplinary research brings together human–computer interaction, psychology, and human-centered security to understand how people experience security and privacy online, and how they respond to digital deception, including social engineering. We combine empirical research with the design and evaluation of user-centered technologies to support critical judgment, informed decision-making, and user autonomy. Please familiarize yourself with the group’s work before applying.


Your network and team

You will work closely with your supervisor and the research group. The department also provides an international research environment and opportunities to connect with other doctoral researchers. While strong independent working skills are essential, the ability to collaborate effectively with fellow researchers is equally important.

The focus will be social engineering in everyday digital interactions. You will investigate how people assess whether requests are genuine, and how interface interventions may support them in their judgments. jobs.title: Doctoral Researcher in condensed matter physics and two-dimensional (2D) Quantum Devices
jobs.description_html:
Aalto University is where science and art meet technology and business. We shape a sustainable future by making research breakthroughs in and across our disciplines, sparking the game changers of tomorrow and creating novel solutions to major global challenges. Our community is made up of 120 nationalities, 16 000 students, 446 professors and close to 5000 other faculty and staff working on our dynamic campus in Espoo, Greater Helsinki, Finland. Diversity is part of who we are, and we actively work to ensure our community’s diversity and inclusiveness. This is why we warmly encourage qualified candidates from all backgrounds to join our community.

 

At the Department of Applied Physics, our pioneering research in physical sciences creates important industrial applications that hold great technological potential. Our research focuses on Materials physics; Quantum technology; Soft & living matter; and Advanced energy solutions. Topics extend from fundamental research to important applications. We educate future generations of research and development professionals; data specialists; technology experts; inventors; and scientists for industry and society.

 

The Atomic Scale Physics group at the Department of Applied Physics is looking for a Doctoral Researcher (PhD student) in 2D quantum devices and condensed matter physics. The research focuses on correlated electron systems, topological systems and superconductivity.

 

Gate-tunable 2D devices are at the cutting edge of condensed matter physics today. This is where many of the most exciting discoveries are being made, and the field is moving fast. You will work at the frontier of this research, combining nanofabricated devices made from 2D layered materials with low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). Our group has long experience with both the techniques and the materials.

 

Your role and goals

Your goal is to study emergent electronic phenomena in gate-tunable van der Waals materials using STM. A gate voltage lets you add or remove electrons in a device, so you can tune one sample through many different quantum phases, including exotic ones that are hard to reach in any other way. With STM, you can see these phases at the atomic scale and learn how they form and behave.


Your tasks will include:

  • Fabrication of quantum devices in cleanroom facilities, including lithography, deposition, exfoliation and transfer of 2D materials
  • Running low-temperature STM experiments on these devices
  • Collaboration with leading theoretical physicists
  • Analysis of measured data and writing scientific articles

Your experience and ambitions

Required:

  • A Master's degree in condensed matter physics or a closely related field
  • A genuine interest in experimental condensed matter physics
  • Good command of English (Finnish is not required)

A plus:

  • Experience with nanofabrication and cleanroom processing of 2D materials
  • Hands-on experience with low-temperature and ultra-high vacuum systems
  • Experience with scanning tunneling microscopy
  • Knowledge of 2D quantum materials and related physics

The selected candidate needs to apply for the study right in doctoral studies at Aalto University School of Science. Please check the student information and admission criteria at Aalto Doctoral Programme in Science | Aalto University.


What we offer

The group consists currently of 3 Academy Research Fellows, 1 Postdoctoral Researcher and 6 Doctoral Researchers. The group focuses studying physical phenomena in atomically precise materials characterized using scanning tunneling microscopy in a wide array of systems such as heterostructures of two-dimensional van der Waals materials, atomically well-defined graphene nanoribbons, and artificial lattices on surfaces.


The position of the Doctoral Researcher is initially filled for 2 years. The contract is continued for another 2 years after a successful midterm review. jobs.title: Doctoral Researcher in Physics-Enhanced Machine Learning for Floating Offshore Wind Digital Twins
jobs.description_html:
At Aalto University, curiosity moves across disciplines, roles and communities. We bring people together to ask new questions, challenge familiar thinking and turn ideas into impact.

Our work is rooted in responsibility, courage and collaboration, and in a shared commitment to shaping a more sustainable future.


The School of Engineering is inviting applications for a Doctoral Researcher in Physics-Enhanced Machine Learning for Floating Offshore Wind Digital Twins


Floating offshore wind turbines will be central to the clean-energy transition, but their behaviour at sea is difficult to predict and monitor. They move in six degrees of freedom under irregular waves and turbulent wind. The mooring lines that keep them in position are located deep underwater, where permanent sensing is costly and difficult to maintain. Operators therefore need digital twins that combine hydrodynamic knowledge with sensor data to estimate quantities that cannot be measured directly.


In this full-time, salaried Doctoral Researcher position, you will help develop the next generation of these digital twins: models that capture the wave-driven dynamics of floating turbines, update as new data arrive, detect early signs of degradation, and quantify the uncertainty of their estimates.


The position is funded by the Research Council of Finland. It is based at Aalto University's Otaniemi campus in Espoo, Finland, and starts on 28 January 2027 or as agreed.


Research environment and duties

At the Department of Energy and Mechanical Engineering, our Marine and Arctic Technology research group studies how ships and offshore structures move and are loaded in waves, wind and ice. We combine machine learning and data-driven methods with hydrodynamic theory, numerical simulation and model-scale experiments. In this role, you will help us build digital twins that track the wave-induced motions, mooring loads and structural condition of floating offshore wind turbines in real time using only a small number of sensors.


Your work will contribute to safer and more cost-effective floating wind farms, where wave loads and mooring tensions can be monitored continuously, degradation can be detected early, and maintenance can be planned before failures occur.


Your work will include:

  • Developing physics-enhanced machine-learning models that learn the coupled hydrodynamic and structural dynamics of floating wind turbines from measured data and update in real time. These methods will build on, among other approaches, Koopman operator theory and dynamic mode decomposition (DMD).
  • Embedding hydrodynamic knowledge into these models so that they remain physically consistent across sea states, including wave excitation, radiation-memory effects, slow-drift motions and mooring-line dynamics.
  • Estimating wave-induced motions and mooring loads that cannot be measured directly.
  • Detecting early mooring-system or structural degradation and distinguishing it from normal changes in waves, wind and turbine operating conditions.
  • Quantifying the uncertainty of these estimates using Bayesian filtering and probabilistic machine learning.
  • Generating and analysing data from: hydrodynamic simulations, including potential-flow methods and, where needed, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and coupled simulation tools such as OpenFAST
  • Publishing results in leading international journals and presenting them at conferences.

You will work closely with researchers in the Marine and Arctic Technology group and with our international academic collaborators.


This is an exciting time to join us. Floating offshore wind is scaling up rapidly, and industry guidance increasingly favours indirect monitoring of hard-to-access components, such as mooring lines, using sensors located elsewhere on the structure.


Our group has recently shown that digital twins learned directly from measurements can estimate unmeasured responses and loads from only a few sensors, including verification using wave-basin test data. In this role, you will take these methods a step further by embedding hydrodynamics into the learning process and moving from accurate estimation toward reliable, self-updating condition monitoring.


What you bring

To thrive in this role, you will need:

  • A Master's degree completed by the start of the position. Suitable backgrounds include naval architecture, marine or ocean engineering, offshore engineering, mechanical, civil or aerospace engineering, applied mathematics, physics, computer science, or a related field.
  • A strong foundation in linear algebra and in at least one of the following areas: hydrodynamics or fluid mechanics, structural dynamics, dynamical systems, or signal processing.
  • Good programming skills in Python or a similar language, together with a genuine interest in machine learning.
  • Curiosity, independence, and the ability to communicate clearly and work well in a team.


We also value:

  • Knowledge of marine or offshore hydrodynamics, such as wave-structure interaction, potential-flow or boundary-element methods, or computational fluid dynamics (e.g. OpenFOAM or REEF3D).
  • Experience with OpenFAST, MoorDyn or WAMIT, or similar software.
  • Experience with dynamic mode decomposition, Koopman operator methods, system identification or operational modal analysis.
  • Experience with Kalman filtering, Bayesian inference, Gaussian processes or uncertainty quantification.
  • Experience with deep learning for time series, such as Transformers or graph neural networks, using PyTorch or JAX.
  • Scientific publications or a strong Master's thesis in a related area.

Language requirements:

  • English: Excellent English-language skills are required.
  • Finnish: Finnish-language skills are not required.

We know that meaningful work is built by people with different backgrounds, experiences and perspectives. If you recognise yourself in the purpose of this role, we encourage you to apply and tell us what you would bring to our community.


What we offer

At Aalto, you can expect:

  • The opportunity to work in a growing research team at the intersection of marine hydrodynamics, machine learning and offshore structural dynamics.
  • Work with purpose in a community where research, education, creativity and services support meaningful change.
  • A multidisciplinary environment where collaboration, curiosity and new thinking are part of everyday work.
  • Extensive occupational health-care services.
  • Staff-priced sports-centre services on campus and at other UniSport locations.
  • A workplace at Aalto University's Otaniemi campus, with excellent public transport connections and a wide range of services.

If you are selected for this position, you will apply for the right to pursue doctoral studies at Aalto University School of Engineering. Doctoral studies at Aalto University typically take approximately four years. The position will initially be filled with a two-year fixed-term contract, with the possibility of extension based on progress in research and studies and on performance. We support your professional growth with varied training and development opportunities shaped around your interests and aspirations.


The expected starting salary for a Doctoral Researcher is approximately EUR 3,000 per month (gross), and it increases as the Doctoral Researcher progresses in research and studies. Work-life balance and well-being in all aspects of life are important to us at Aalto.


Curious to make a difference?

Please submit your application through our recruitment system by 28 December 2026. If you are already working at Aalto University, please apply through our internal Workday system. If you are a student or visitor at Aalto University, please apply using your personal email address.


All applications must include the following materials:

  • Cover letter / motivation letter with your contact information and preferred starting date (maximum 1 page).
  • CV including details of all academic outputs.
  • Contact details of two referees.
  • Description of your Master's thesis project (maximum 1 page).
  • Course transcripts for your Bachelor's and Master's degrees, including grades and a clear explanation of the grading scale.
  • Research statement (maximum 2 pages) answering the question below.
  • Research statement question: How could early degradation of a mooring line, such as a gradual loss of stiffness, be detected in a floating offshore wind turbine using only a few sensors on the tower and platform while wind and wave conditions keep changing?

In your statement, outline:

  • the methods you would use
  • the data you would need
  • how you would validate your approach
  • what could cause the approach to fail.

We do not expect a complete solution; we want to see how you think. You are welcome to draw on any relevant background, including hydrodynamics, structural dynamics, signal processing or machine learning.


All materials should be submitted in English as a single PDF file, compiled in the order specified above. Applications submitted by email will not be accepted. Shortlisted candidates will be invited to interviews and may be asked to complete a short technical task. Aalto University reserves the right to leave the position open, extend the application period, and consider candidates who have not applied during the application period.


For more information about the role, please contact:

  • Associate Professor Arttu Polojärvi, arttu.polojarvi(at)aalto.fi
  • Dr. Mohammad Mahdi Abaei, Academy Research Fellow, mohammad.abaei(at)aalto.fi
  • For questions related to the application process, please contact HR Advisor Anna-Maija Harju anna-maija.harju(at)Aalto.fi or hr-eng(at)aalto.fi

Aalto University builds on the legacy of three leading Finnish universities: Helsinki University of Technology, Helsinki School of Economics and the University of Art and Design Helsinki. Since 2010, we have brought science, art, technology and business together in new ways.

jobs.title: Doctoral student in computer science with focus on program transformation
jobs.department: Lund University, LTH, Department of Computer Science
jobs.description_html:
Description of the workplace

The position is within the Software Development and Environments division, part of the Department of Computer Science.  The division is exploring novel tools, languages, and methods for supporting software development, and conducts research in a variety of topics that include refactoring, program analysis, compiler construction, declarative specification languages, distributed development environments, and automatic program repair. Its research involves strong collaborations both locally within Lund University, internationally with other universities, and with industrial partners, such as ABB and Ericsson, including research driven by industrial PhD students. The division currently has twelve members, and regularly organises group activities to foster a positive working environment.

The division is actively developing the JastAdd metacompilation framework, which is the foundation for several compilers and software tools, including the division's ExtendJ extensible Java compiler and the static analysis tools IntraJ and MetaDL.

More about the Software Development and Environments group (sde.cs.lth.se/)
More about JastAdd (jastadd.cs.lth.se/web/)
More about ExtendJ (extendj.org)
More about MetaDL (github.com/lu-cs-sde/metadl)

Being a doctoral student

As a doctoral student, you are both admitted as a student and employed at Lund University.

As a doctoral student, you will learn to approach questions and challenges scientifically. In short, this means that you will be trained to think critically and analytically, to solve problems independently using the right methods, and to develop an awareness of research ethics. In addition, you will have the opportunity to work on projects, to develop your leadership and pedagogical skills. Throughout your studies, you will be guided by supervisors. Doctoral studies end with a thesis and a doctoral degree.

More about being a doctoral student at LTH on lth.se. 

Subject and project description

This research project aims to develop novel tools and techniques that enforce rigid guard-rails during software refactoring and other forms of software evolution. We assume an unreliable source of program transformations, such as a human developer or a large language model.  The guard-rail mechanism will then inspect, steer, and augment any sequence of program transformations to detect and recover from unintended behavioural change.
The position is funded by the Excellence Center at Linköping – Lund in Information Technology (ELLIIT), and it is a collaboration with the Natural Language Processing group at Linköping University, part of the division of Artificial Intelligence and Integrated Computer Systems.

More about ELLIIT (elliit.se)
More about the Division of Artificial Intelligence and Integrated Computer Systems at Linköping University (liu.se/en/organisation/liu/ida/aiics)

Work duties

You will primarily devote yourself to your doctoral programme, which includes participation in research projects as well as third cycle courses, seminars and conferences.

The work duties include:

  • Research on automatic program analysis and program transformation applied to preventing unintended behavioural change during refactoring and similar program evolution tasks. You will work towards exploring approaches that can aid real-world software evolution, and examine qualitative aspects of these approaches.
  • Applying appropriate research methods: depending on the trajectory of this research, different and possibly novel methodologies may be required to provide robust answers to the underlying research questions. You will learn, apply, and possibly support the development of suitable methods.
  • Artefact-oriented activity: You will develop software tools, algorithms, and other software components. These should be evaluated in realistic scenarios and integrated with, as well as shared within, the project team.
  • Presentation and collaboration: You will present your research findings at the annual ELLIIT workshop in southern Sweden and discuss your work at meetings with academic project partners, including personal meetings with our collaboration partners in Linköping.
  • Interaction with the industry: You will have opportunities to discuss your work and collaborate with industrial researchers, especially in Lund.
  • The duties also include participation in teaching and other departmental work (limited to a maximum of 20% of working hours).

Qualifications

To be eligible for admission and employment as a doctoral student, you must fulfil the requirements below.

Admission requirements

A person meets the general admission requirements for third-cycle courses and study programmes if the applicant:

  • has been awarded a second-cycle qualification, or

A person meets the specific admission requirements for third cycle studies in computer science if the applicant has:

  • at least 60 second-cycle credits at an advanced level with relevance for the research topic, or
  • an MSc in Engineering in Computer Science and Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Information and Communication Technology, Engineering Physics or Engineering Mathematics.

Additional requirements

In order to complete the doctoral programme in question, the following are also required:

  • Knowledge or experience in at least one of the following areas (demonstrated e.g. in the form of a university course, or through professional experiences or contributions to relevant open source projects):
    • o compiler construction, or
    • o the foundations of static program analysis.
  • good ability to work independently and to formulate and tackle research problems.
  • good written and oral communication skills.
  • good ability to cooperate.
  • very good knowledge of English, in speech and writing.
  • very good programming experience (demonstrated e.g. in the form of professional experiences, contributions to open source projects, or outstanding results in university courses).
  • persistence and the ability to plan and structure your own work
  • curiosity and willingness to learn and adopt new techniques, especially within the cross-disciplinary scope of the project

Other qualifications (advantages)

For the doctoral programme in question, it is advantageous if you can demonstrate experience or knowledge in one or more of the following subjects:

  • developing automatic program transformation tools, such as
    • o refactoring tools, or
    • o meta-programming tools.
  • software development in teams, especially in the context of:
    • o professional software engineering,
    • o open source projects, or
    • o legacy software engineering projects.
  • dynamic program analysis.
  • programming in Java.
  • functional or declarative programming (logic programming, reference attribute grammars etc.).
  • natural language processing, machine learning, and/or applying large language models, such as
    • o working with the underlying machine learning techniques, such as latent/embedding spaces, representation learning, or transformers,
    • o training or fine-tuning such models, or
    • o applying them to software development / software engineering tasks.
  • systematic evaluation of software systems and relevant statistical methods.
  • systems programming.
  • areas of discrete mathematics with relation to program analysis (lattice theory, type theory, Galois connections etc.).

jobs.title: Doctoral student in Biology (Invertebrate colour vision)
jobs.description_html:
Description of the workplace

For your doctoral research, you will be a part of the Bok lab, which uses a wide range of techniques to study the evolution and ecology of vision in diverse invertebrates. Or lab is embedded within in the Lund Vision Group, a highly collaborative cluster of eight labs, internationally recognised as one of the leading centres in comparative visual science in the world. With 35-40 academics at all education and career stages, our vision research stretches across the entire animal kingdom, from jellyfishes, insects, and crustaceans, to squids and vertebrates. Our speciality is the design and evolution of eyes, how eyes are adapted to different lifestyles and habitats, and how vision is used for navigation and for controlling behaviour. Our techniques range from optics, electrophysiology and theoretical modelling, to microscopy, molecular biology and behavioural experiments. This thriving research environment offers broad support for doctoral education and research.

Being a doctoral student

As a doctoral student, you are both admitted as a student and employed at Lund University.

As a doctoral student, you will be trained in a scientific approach. In short, you will be trained to think critically and analytically, to solve problems independently using the right methods, and to develop an awareness of research ethics. In addition, you will have the opportunity to work on projects, to develop your leadership and pedagogical skills. Throughout your studies, you will be guided by supervisors. Doctoral studies end with a thesis and a doctoral degree.

More about being a doctoral student at the Faculty of Science at naturvetenskap.se Doctoral studies | Faculty of Science

Subject and project description

Aims: Colour vision has only to date been conclusively shown to exist in two of Earth’s approximately 32 animal phyla – vertebrates and arthropods. However, there are two additional known examples where colour vision may be possible – the firefly squid, a mollusc, and the alciopid worm, an annelid. Both are midwater marine species that are night active and live in deep water, yet they have astonishing retinal specializations that may contribute to colour vision. The aims of this PhD thesis will be to discover if these marine invertebrates have convergently evolved colour vision. Further, what behaviours are controlled by colour vision, and do they use the same visual processing circuits and principles to interpret colour information as we see in arthropods and vertebrates? This project will answer these questions using molecular, neurological, electrophysiological, and behavioural techniques in the field and lab.

Project background: This project grows naturally from ongoing research in the Bok Lab and contributes directly to our overall projects regarding the evolution of complex eyes and visual capabilities in crustaceans (water fleas and mantis shrimp) cephalopods (firefly squid), and polychaetes (alciopids and fan worms). The student will benefit from mentorship from the Bok lab's existing postdoctoral researchers who have completed preliminary work for this project. Further, the project synergises well with other research in Sensory Biology and Aquatic Ecology units. The Bok lab has recently been awarded several large grants from the ERC, Swedish Research Council, and the Human Frontiers Science Program, so the PhD student will benefit from a growing and dynamic academic environment.

  • Link to the general syllabus for third-cycle studies in Biology: General syllabus

Work duties

You will primarily devote yourself to your doctoral education, which mainly consists of writing a doctoral thesis. You are expected to participate in a research project, doctoral courses, seminars and conferences. In the research project, you will use cutting edge behavioural, molecular, and neuroanatomical techniques to explore the function and evolution of possible colour receptors and their role in the visual ecology of polychaetes and cephalopods:

  1. ) Behaviour: At field stations in Italy and Japan, we will perform behavioural experiments testing the response of both species to colour and polarization stimuli. This will be based on custom light sources and projection screen setups that can vary the two light modalities independently.   
  2. ) Molecules: Alongside postdocs in the Bok Lab (Vanessa Stenvers and Alida Avola), the PhD student will use the results of single-nucleolus transcriptomic data to localize distinct photoreceptor and visual interneuron classes in the retina and optic lobe of both species. 
  3. ) Circuits: SBEM will be used to create connectomic resolution volume data for the retina and optic lobe of both species. Photoreceptor and interneuron synaptic connections and projections will be mapped to decipher the visual circuits. These data, along with the results from the molecular section will then be used to inform electrophysiology recordings to discover putative colour and polarisation opponent neurons in the optic lobe.

In addition to studies, a maximum of 20% of working time may be spent on teaching and other departmental work. You are expected to gain pedagogical experience as lab instructors for undergradate courses run by the Sensory Biology unit, and there are ample opportunities to gain experience in outreach and academic activities. You will be provided ample opportunities to present your work at local and international research conferences.

Qualifications

To be eligible for admission and employment as a doctoral student, you must fulfil the requirements below.

Admission requirements

A person meets the general admission requirements for third-cycle courses and study programmes if the applicant:

  • has been awarded a second-cycle qualification, or
  • has satisfied the requirements for courses comprising at least 240 credits of which at least 60 credits were awarded in the second cycle, or

A person meets the specific admission requirements for third cycle studies in Biology if the applicant has completed an independent work (e.g. degree project) in a relevant subject comprising at least 30 higher education credits and have good oral and written proficiency in English. The special qualification may also have been obtained through other equivalent education, which is assessed on a case-by-case basis. In order to enable interdisciplinary initiatives and significant in-depth studies in certain areas, qualifications other than the applicant's subject-specific competence in Biology may be taken into account.

Additional requirements

  • Master’s degree in biology/marine biology or substantial equivalent knowledge acquired in some other way.
  • Practical experience with animal vision behavioral experiments.
  • Experience with fieldwork-based research.
  • Good ability to work independently and to formulate and tackle research problems.
  • Good written and oral communication skills
  • Good ability to cooperate with colleagues and collaborators
  • Very good knowledge of English, spoken and written

Selection criteria

The selection of eligible applicants will be made taking into account the ability to benefit from the training based on the following criteria:

  • Knowledge and/or expereince with animal vision, sensory biology, and visual ecology, and with the requirements and methods listed above.
  • Experience in data processing, statistical computing, and scripting in Python, Matlab and R, or equivalent.
  • Demonstrate independence, collegiality and enthusaism.

jobs.description_html:
The PhD student will be based at the GIS Centre, Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lund University. The GIS Centre conducts research, education and development in Geographical Information Science (GIScience), with particular expertise in geospatial analysis, GeoAI, digital twins, and spatial data infrastructures.

The position will be part of the Centre's research activities in GeoAI and Spatial Intelligence, with a particular focus on Autonomous GIS. This emerging research direction explores how artificial intelligence, large language models and multi-agent systems can enable GIS to understand complex spatial problems, reason about geographic information, and autonomously plan and execute geospatial workflows.

The GIS Centre provides an interdisciplinary research environment where expertise in GIScience, geospatial technologies and AI meet applications in environmental analysis, urban planning, sustainability and other societal challenges. The PhD student will work closely with researchers at the Centre and have opportunities to collaborate with national and international research partners.

The Centre offers a collegial, supportive and collaborative working environment that encourages scientific curiosity, independent thinking and professional development.

Being a doctoral student

As a doctoral student, you are both admitted as a student and employed at Lund University.

As a doctoral student, you will be trained in a scientific approach. In short, you will be trained to think critically and analytically, to solve problems independently using the right methods, and to develop an awareness of research ethics. In addition, you will have the opportunity to work on projects, to develop your leadership and pedagogical skills. Throughout your studies, you will be guided by supervisors. Doctoral studies end with a thesis and a doctoral degree.


Subject and project description

The doctoral student will be admitted to third-cycle studies in Geobiosphere Science, with a specialisation in Geographical Information Science (GIScience). GIScience is an interdisciplinary research field concerned with the theories, methods and technologies for collecting, managing, analysing, modelling and communicating geographical information. The subject encompasses both fundamental methodological research and applications across environmental, societal and technological domains.

The doctoral research will focus on Autonomous GIS and Spatial Intelligence, an emerging research direction at the intersection of GIScience and artificial intelligence. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), GeoAI and multi-agent systems are creating new opportunities to transform GIS from systems that primarily execute user-defined operations into intelligent systems capable of interpreting spatial problems, reasoning about geographical information, planning and executing geospatial workflows, and evaluating their results.

Despite these advances, important scientific challenges remain. These include the ability of AI systems to understand spatial concepts and relationships, integrate geographic knowledge with computational reasoning, select and coordinate appropriate geospatial methods, and ensure the reliability, transparency and geographical validity of autonomous analyses.

The doctoral student will investigate methods and frameworks for advancing Spatial Intelligence and Autonomous GIS, potentially addressing topics such as geospatial reasoning with LLMs, multi-agent architectures, autonomous geospatial workflow planning and execution, integration of geographic knowledge and analytical tools, and evaluation of the reliability and quality of AI-generated geospatial analyses.

The research is expected to contribute new scientific knowledge and methods in GIScience while advancing the foundations of intelligent and increasingly autonomous geospatial systems. The specific research questions and methodological approaches will be further developed in collaboration with the supervisors during the doctoral studies.

Work duties

Your main responsibility will be to pursue doctoral studies and conduct independent research in Autonomous GIS and Spatial Intelligence, leading to a doctoral thesis. You will develop research questions, investigate and develop new methods, design and conduct experiments, evaluate results, and communicate your findings primarily through publications in high-quality, peer-reviewed scientific journals..

You will work closely with your supervisors and other researchers at the GIS Centre, while gradually developing your independence as a researcher. Your doctoral education will also include relevant doctoral courses, participation in research seminars, and opportunities to present and discuss your research at national and international scientific conferences. You will be encouraged to engage in research collaborations and contribute to the Centre's academic activities and research environment. International travel may be required for conferences, research visits and collaborative activities.

In addition to your doctoral studies, you may participate in teaching and other departmental duties, corresponding to a maximum of 20% of your working time. These duties may include assisting with teaching, supervising student exercises and projects, and contributing to educational activities, particularly in GIS, geospatial analysis and GeoAI. The extent and nature of these duties will be determined based on departmental needs and your qualifications and interests.

Admission requirements

A person meets the general admission requirements for third-cycle courses and study programmes if the applicant:

  • has been awarded a second-cycle qualification, or
  • has satisfied the requirements for courses comprising at least 240 credits of which at least 60 credits were awarded in the second cycle, or
  • has acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way in Sweden or abroad.

Specific admission requirements

  • To meet the specific admission requirements for third-cycle studies in Geobiosphere Science with a specialisation in Geographical Information Science, the applicant must have completed an independent degree project in a relevant subject comprising at least 30 higher education credits, or have acquired equivalent qualifications. Qualifications from other relevant disciplines may also be considered, particularly when appropriate for the interdisciplinary nature of the doctoral research.

 

Additional requirements

In order to complete the doctoral programme in question, the following qualifications and competences are also required:

  • A Master's degree in Geographical Information Science, Geoinformatics, Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, or a closely related field.
  • Good knowledge of artificial intelligence and machine learning, including an understanding of fundamental methods and principles, and familiarity with modern deep learning approaches and large language models (LLMs).
  • Experience with AI and machine learning frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, or similar technologies.
  • Strong programming skills in Python, with the ability to develop, implement, test and evaluate computational methods and algorithms.
  • Good analytical and problem-solving skills, with the ability to approach complex scientific and technical challenges systematically.
  • An interest in GIScience, geospatial analysis and spatial intelligence, with the motivation and ability to develop interdisciplinary expertise at the intersection of geographical information science and artificial intelligence.
  • Good ability to work independently and collaboratively, including the capacity to formulate research problems, take initiative and contribute constructively to an interdisciplinary research environment.
  • Good communication skills in English, both written and spoken.

 

The following qualifications will be considered advantageous:

  • Practical experience developing applications using LLMs, agentic AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), tool integration or multi-agent systems.
  • Experience with geospatial programming libraries and tools such as GeoPandas, Shapely, Rasterio, PyQGIS or ArcPy.
  • Knowledge of spatial reasoning and knowledge representation, including geographic semantics, ontologies, knowledge graphs or neuro-symbolic AI.
  • Experience in developing and evaluating computational methods and AI-based systems, including experimental design, software testing, version control, and integration of computational tools and APIs.
  • Demonstrated scientific writing skills, particularly experience preparing manuscripts or publications for peer-reviewed scientific journals.
  • Previous involvement in scientific research or publications in artificial intelligence, GIScience, GeoAI or related fields.

 

Selection criteria

The selection of eligible applicants will be made based on the above-mentioned qualifications and competences. In addition, personal qualifications will also be considered in the evaluation process including:

  • Strong scientific curiosity and creativity, with the ability to formulate original ideas and explore innovative approaches.
  • Ability to think critically, evaluate methods and results, and approach scientific challenges constructively.
  • A collegial and cooperative attitude, with a willingness to share knowledge, support colleagues and contribute positively to the research environment.

  • Reliability, responsibility and professionalism, including the ability to honour commitments and contribute constructively to shared activities.
  • Motivation and enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and GIScience.

jobs.title: PhD student in biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases
jobs.description_html:
Description of the workplace

The Biomarkers in Brain Disease research group at the Department of Experimental Medical Science investigates how disease mechanisms in the body and brain interact in Huntington’s disease. This work involves in vivo and in vitro experiments, microscopy and molecular biology methods.

The workplace and research environment are shared by five research groups, all working on neurodegenerative diseases, with approximately 25–30 people in total.

Together, they create a stimulating and international research environment in which we share research equipment and chemicals and hold joint laboratory meetings. The atmosphere is friendly and encourages a wide range of discussions. The research group is active in the European Huntington’s Disease Network and Lund University Huntington Centre.

Project description

The body’s biological clock regulates functions such as sleep, metabolism, immune function and brain activity. The central clock in the hypothalamus coordinates rhythms in the body’s cells and organs, which also have their own rhythms. Disturbances in sleep and circadian rhythms are common in neurodegenerative diseases, including Huntington’s disease (HD). Research suggests that these disturbances are not merely symptoms but may contribute to neurodegeneration.

HD is an inherited disorder that affects movement, cognition and psychiatric function. The mutated gene, which contains an expanded CAG repeat sequence, and the huntingtin protein are expressed not only in neurons but also in cells throughout the body.

Despite increasing knowledge, it remains unclear how disruptions to the body’s biological clocks affect the course of HD. It is also unknown whether modifying clock function could alter disease progression in HD.

This doctoral project will combine in vitro and in vivo studies and use methods such as RNA sequencing. The project requires a balance between experimental laboratory work and data analysis.

Tasks and responsibilities

jobs.department: Lund University, Faculty of Engineering, LTH, Department of Energy Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Description of the workplace

The doctoral student will be employed at the Department of Energy Sciences, Faculty of Engineering (LTH), Lund University, and will be part of the Division of Heat Transfer. The research environment conducts research in fluid mechanics, heat transfer and computational fluid dynamics, with particular emphasis on the numerical modelling and simulation of turbulent flows and engineering applications.

The doctoral student will work in a research environment combining fundamental research with applications of direct relevance to industry. The project will be carried out in close collaboration with Siemens Energy AB, Ericsson AB, TRATON AB and RISE. This provides an opportunity to work at the interface between fundamental research, advanced numerical methods and industrially relevant problems.

The doctoral student will have access to expertise in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), turbulence, heat transfer, numerical methods and high-performance computing. The work will involve extensive use of high-performance computing resources, including both GPU- and CPU-based computing platforms.

Being a doctoral student

As a doctoral student, you are both admitted as a student and employed at Lund University.

As a doctoral student, you will be trained in a scientific approach. In short, you will be trained to think critically and analytically, to solve problems independently using the right methods, and to develop an awareness of research ethics. In addition, you will have the opportunity to work on projects, to develop your leadership and pedagogical skills. Throughout your studies, you will be guided by supervisors. Doctoral studies end with a thesis and a doctoral degree.

More about being a doctoral student at LTH on lth.se. 

Subject and project description

Surface roughness has a significant influence on turbulent flow, wall friction and heat transfer in many engineering systems. Understanding and predicting these effects is important in a wide range of applications, including energy systems, thermal management and transport applications. Despite its practical importance, accurately predicting turbulent heat transfer over realistic rough surfaces remains challenging, particularly when the properties of the working fluid and the relative thicknesses of the momentum and thermal boundary layers vary.

The aim of this doctoral project is to develop a deeper physical understanding of the interaction between surface roughness, turbulence and heat transfer, and to translate this understanding into improved engineering models.

The research will primarily use high-fidelity numerical simulations, including Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) and Large Eddy Simulation (LES). Different CFD codes will be employed depending on the problem and required level of fidelity, including OpenFOAM, CaNS and nekRS. The simulations will make extensive use of modern high-performance computing resources based on both GPUs and CPUs.

The project will investigate how surface roughness influences turbulent flow and heat transfer for different fluids and thermal conditions. Particular attention will be given to the interaction between roughness geometry, turbulent structures, and the momentum and thermal boundary layers, including conditions in which the relative thicknesses of the thermal and momentum boundary layers differ.

The high-fidelity simulation data will be used to identify relevant physical mechanisms and scaling relations and to support the development of reduced-order and engineering models for rough-surface heat transfer, including improved models and correlations suitable for Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) simulations.

The overall objective is to establish a connection between fundamental turbulence physics, high-fidelity numerical simulations and computational models that can be applied to engineering design.

The project will be conducted in close collaboration with Siemens Energy AB, Ericsson AB, TRATON AB and RISE, providing opportunities for scientific exchange and interaction with researchers and engineers working on industrial applications of turbulent flow and heat transfer.

Work duties

You will primarily devote yourself to your doctoral studies, which include participation in research projects as well as third-cycle courses, seminars and scientific conferences.

A central part of your work will be to perform and analyse high-fidelity numerical simulations of turbulent flow and heat transfer over rough surfaces. You will use CFD and high-performance computing frameworks, which may include OpenFOAM, CaNS and nekRS, on CPU- and GPU-based systems. Applicants should already have experience with comparable simulation tools and High Performance Computing (HPC) systems; familiarity with the specific codes used in the project is an advantage.  

The work duties include:

  • Performing DNS and LES of turbulent flow and heat transfer over rough surfaces using OpenFOAM, CaNS, nekRS or comparable CFD and scientific-computing frameworks.
  • Setting up, running, validating and analysing simulations on GPU- and CPU-based high-performance computing systems.
  • Investigating the influence of surface roughness geometry and characteristics on turbulent momentum and heat transfer.
  • Investigating the effects of fluid properties and thermal conditions, including different relationships between momentum and thermal boundary-layer thicknesses.
  • Processing, analysing and visualising large datasets and identifying physical mechanisms and developing scaling relations from DNS and LES data.
  • Developing reduced-order models, correlations and improved RANS modelling approaches for turbulent heat transfer over rough surfaces.
  • Assessing and validating the developed models against high-fidelity numerical data and, where available, experimental data.
  • Collaborating with researchers at Lund University and with the project's industrial and research partners.
  • Presenting research results at project meetings, scientific conferences and international workshops.
  • Writing scientific articles for publication in international peer-reviewed journals and contributing to the doctoral thesis.

The work may involve travel within Sweden and internationally for project meetings, visits to research and industrial partners, conferences and research collaborations.

The duties may also include participation in teaching and other departmental work, however to a maximum of 20% of working hours.

Admission requirements

A person meets the general admission requirements for third-cycle courses and study programmes if the applicant:

  • has been awarded a second-cycle qualification, or
  • has satisfied the requirements for courses comprising at least 240 credits of which at least 60 credits were awarded in the second cycle, or
  • has acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way in Sweden or abroad.

Additional requirements

In order to complete the doctoral programme in question, the following are also required:

  • A Master’s degree, or equivalent qualification, in mechanical engineering, engineering physics, aerospace engineering, energy engineering, applied mathematics, computational science, or another subject relevant to the project.
  • Good knowledge of fluid mechanics, CFD, and turbulent flows, and relevant knowledge of heat transfer.
  • A substantial research project or thesis in CFD, turbulence, heat transfer, or a closely related field.
  • Demonstrated ability to independently set up, run, troubleshoot, validate and analyse numerical simulations. This should be supported by research experience, rather than coursework alone.
  • Scientific programming experience in a relevant language, such as C/C++, Fortran and Python or Matlab.
  • Practical experience running computational simulations on HPC systems.
  • Ability to plan and carry out research tasks with limited day-to-day supervision, analyse results critically and communicate findings clearly.
  • Very good knowledge of English, spoken and written.

Other qualifications

For the doctoral programme in question, the following are considered meriting:

  • Experience with DNS or LES, wall-bounded turbulence, turbulent heat transfer, surface roughness or convective heat transfer.
  • Experience with a CFD or high-fidelity simulation framework, such as OpenFOAM, CaNS, nekRS or a comparable research code.
  • Experience with parallel computing or GPU-accelerated scientific computing.
  • Knowledge of RANS, wall modelling or thermal turbulence modelling.
  • Research experience beyond the Master’s thesis, such as work as a research assistant or research engineer.
  • Experience presenting or publishing research results or collaborating with industry.

Applicants are not expected to have experience with every code used in the project. However, they should have demonstrated the ability to carry out computational research independently using a comparable CFD or scientific-computing framework. They are expected to contribute from an early stage, building on existing experience in numerical simulation and HPC.

More about terms of employment for doctoral students on Lund University’s Staffpages.

Other

The doctoral student will be expected to interact regularly with the project's academic and industrial partners. The position may therefore include visits to partner organisations and participation in project meetings, workshops and conferences in Sweden and abroad.

How to apply

Applications shall be written in English and include:

  • CV and cover letter stating why you are interested in the doctoral programme and this particular research project, and explaining how your educational background, research experience and interests relate to CFD, turbulence and heat transfer.
  • Copies of issued study certificates and/or awarded degree certificates. These must confirm that you meet the general and specific admission requirements for the doctoral programme and demonstrate that you have the subject knowledge required for the doctoral research project.

jobs.title: Doctoral student in applied nuclear physics
jobs.description_html:
The Nuclear Structure Group at the Division of Particle and Nuclear Physics at Lund University is seeking a skilled and highly motivated PhD student to work on upcycling state-of-the-art detectors used in nuclear structure studies for environmental monitoring and emergency preparedness. The Division of Particle and Nuclear Physics, which has approximately 50 employees, conducts a broad range of research in both theoretical and experimental particle and heavy-ion physics, as well as experimental nuclear physics. The Nuclear Structure Group is active in several international collaborations exploiting large-scale accelerator facilities across the globe. With the present position, however, we thrive to intensify local collaborations with the Biospheric and Anthropogenic Radioactivity group.

Being a doctoral student

As a doctoral student, you are both admitted as a student and employed at Lund University.
As a doctoral student, you will be trained in a scientific approach. In short, you will be trained to think critically and analytically, to solve problems independently using the right methods, and to develop an awareness of research ethics. In addition, you will have the opportunity to work on projects, to develop your leadership and pedagogical skills. Throughout your studies, you will be guided by supervisors. Doctoral studies end with a thesis and a doctoral degree.
More about being a doctoral student at the Science Faculty.  

Project Description

The project "From Lundium to L.U.N.D.I.U.M." (Swedish Radiation Safety Authority) will see the upcycling of various state-of-the-art components of the Lundium decay station for studies of Super Heavy Elements into L.U.N.D.I.U.M.: the Lund University Next-generation Device for Identification of Unknown radioactive sources and environmental Monitoring. L.U.N.D.I.U.M. will have unprecedented alpha-beta-gamma resolving capabilities stemming from its high granularity of detector components and contemporary multi-coincidence data acquisition systems.

The research environment constitutes an interdisciplinary community of knowledge and practice focused on data analysis and simulations of complex datasets to be used for radiation safety and emergency preparedness within the disciplines of physics, work environment, medical radiation physics, and environmental monitoring.

We are now recruiting one PhD student to be integrated into the research group and lead this development from conceptualization and optimization via Monte Carlo Geant4 simulations to realization of the device.

The PhD student will collaborate during specific phases of their doctoral education, with the Biospheric and Anthropogenic Radioactivity group for sample collection and preparation.

Work duties

You will primarily devote yourself to your doctoral programme, which includes participation in research projects as well as third cycle courses, seminars and conferences. 

The PhD project will address the need for expanding the Swedish network of environmental monitor and emergency preparedness with the development and usage of a new-generation device for nuclear forensics. The tasks include:

  • Optimize via Monte Carlo simulations the geometry and elements of the new device upcycling the existing state-of-the-art detector components for measurement of various types of environmental filter and electroplated samples.
  • Conduct and coordinate the mechanical construction of the device and develop its data acquisition system and data analysis framework.
  • Validation of the measurements using simulated contamination samples provided by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for yearly proficiency tests.
  • In close collaboration with the Biospheric and Anthropogenic Radioactivity group, develop methods to analyse radioactive aerosols from environmental samples.

At various stages of the project, close collaboration is envisaged with researchers at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, in charge of a comparable measurement station.

The research projects will be reported in the form of articles submitted for publication in scientific journals, reports to the funding organisation, and conference contributions.

The duties also include participation in teaching and other departmental work (up to a maximum of 20% of working time).

Qualifications

To be eligible for admission and employment as a doctoral student, you must fulfil the requirements below.

Specific admission requirements

A person meets the specific admission requirements for third-cycle programme in Physics, if they:

  • has at least 45 second cycle credits in physics or engineering physics or an associated field, or
  • has a second cycle (master) degree in physics or engineering physics or an associated field.

The specific entry requirement may also have been obtained through other equivalent education, which is assessed in each individual case. Finally, the student must be judged to have the potential to complete the programme.

 Additional requirements

In order to complete the doctoral programme in question, the following are also required:

  • completion of courses amounting to at least 60 credits that are directly relevant to the PhD education
  • a strong ability to work independently and the ability to formulate and address scientific problems
  • good written and oral communication skills
  • good ability to collaborate
  • very good proficiency in English, both spoken and written
  • an interest in interdisciplinary work

Other qualifications (advantages)

For the doctoral programme in question, the following are considered as other qualifications:

  • excellent laboratory skills concerning contemporary radiation detectors
  • proficiency with multi-parameter data acquisition systems
  • proficiency in modern object oriented programming
  • knowledge of environmental radioactivity or radioecology knowledge of radionuclide production in nuclear power plants and spallation sources
  • previous experience to ionizing radiation detection
  • previous experience with Monte Carlo radiation transport codes

We offer

Lund University is a public authority which means that employees get particular benefits, generous annual leave and an advantageous occupational pension scheme. It is advisable to enter information on what your unit specifically can offer as a workplace.

More information about working at Lund University on lu.se. 

About the employment

The employment is a fixed-term employment at full time, starting 1 January 2027 at the earliest. Third cycle studies consist of full-time studies for 4 years. In the case of teaching and other departmental duties, the employment is extended accordingly. Doctoral studentships are regulated in the Higher Education Ordinance (1993:100), chapter 5, 1-7 §§.

More information about terms of employment for doctoral students on Lund University’s Staffpages.

Other

Selection for admission to doctoral studies is based on the assessed ability to successfully complete the doctoral education. The assessment of this ability is primarily based on study results at the first- and second-cycle (Bachelor’s and Master’s) levels.

The following criteria will be considered:

  • Knowledge and skills relevant to the doctoral project and the field of study, as described under Work duties. These may be demonstrated through submitted documentation.
  • Assessed ability to work independently and to formulate and address scientific problems. This assessment may, for example, be based on the degree project and a discussion thereof during a potential interview.
  • Ability to communicate effectively in writing and orally.
  • Other experience relevant to doctoral studies, such as professional experience.

Consideration will also be given to good collaborative skills, initiative, independence, and personal suitability, as well as to how the applicant’s experience and competence are assessed to demonstrate the ability required to complete the doctoral education.

  • Copies of issued study certificates and/or awarded degree certificates. These must confirm that you meet the general and specific admission requirements for the doctoral programme and show that you have the subject knowledge required for the doctoral programme project.
