jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Categorification and the Local Langlands Correspondence
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Professor Shaun Stevens

The representation theory of p-adic groups has been a highly active area of research over the last fifty years, motivated by the Local Langlands Correspondence/Conjectures and its deep connections to Number Theory. To begin with, only irreducible representations with complex coefficients were considered but, more recently, representations with coefficients in other rings or fields have been studied also. Moreover, to gain a better understanding, more importance has been given to trying to match the (derived) structures of categories on the two sides of the correspondence.

On the other hand, techniques from higher representation theory give a way to study these categories: for representations of p-adic general linear groups, this leads to a 2-representation of a certain quantum group – this is an example of a categorification of this quantum group, in which we understand its elements as functors. An analogue of this result is already known for finite general linear groups, and the project will begin by making this precise in the p-adic case. It will then aim to transfer information obtained by studying this 2-representation across the local Langlands correspondence, possibly by extending it to the relevant derived categories.

The project will be co-supervised by Shaun Stevens and Vanessa Miemietz.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree in mathematics.

Start Date: 1 February 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Representations of P-adic Groups and Arithmetic
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Professor Shaun Stevens

The Local Langlands Correspondence has motivated a great deal of Number Theory and Representation Theory over the last fifty years. It connects representations of (roughly) the absolute galois group of a p-adic field to the representations of a matrix group G over the field. In the original formulation (now proved for several families of matrix groups G, including general linear groups) it considered only complex representations but, more recently, representations with coefficients in other rings or fields have been considered also. The correspondence results in a partition of the irreducible representations of G into L-packets (which are singletons for general linear groups), each of which is conjecturally characterised by an equality of local factors (L-functions and e-factors) – though a definition for such factors is only known for “generic” representations, of which there is (at least conjecturally) precisely one in each packet.

One of the difficulties in studying this is that the representations of G are (almost all) infinite-dimensional, so they are quite hard to get a handle on. One way for doing so, which has been very successful, is to restrict them to compact open subgroups K: we then look for representations of K whose presence in this restriction characterizes some property which representations of G might have; this property might be being “unramified”, ”tame”, “generic”,… Similarly, this restriction can be used to give very explicit descriptions of the representations of G, using arithmetic data. Such results also have interpretations via the Langlands correspondence, so consequences for the absolute galois group.

This project will be in the area of the local Langlands correspondence, exploring some of the problems raised above, or related questions.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree in mathematics.

Start Date: 1 February 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Machine Learning-based Control of Reacting Flow Extreme Events (AE0092)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: The development of sustainable propulsion systems, based on hydrogen or sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs), is increasing the risk of extreme events occurring in these. These are rare events where the flow in the combustor suddenly takes extreme states far, potentially with grave consequences. Examples are flashback in hydrogen or thermoacoustic instabilities triggered by the varying SAFs properties. The safe and reliable operation of these future sustainable propulsion systems thus requires the ability to anticipate their occurrence through measurable precursors and the deployment of real-time mitigation based on those precursors.

Traditional methods have generally been unable to tackle this due to the turbulent nature of the underlying flows and the complex multiscale/multiphysics nonlinear interactions at the origin of such extreme events. Recent advances in differentiable solver and machine learning offer a pathway to enable such their mitigation and control.

In this project, you will develop a framework for the control of reacting flow extreme events that combines a differentiable reacting flow solver and a machine learning-based controller. The differentiable solver will provide short-term state dependency used by machine learning-based controller to obtain an optimal mitigation control preventing the reacting flow extreme event. This will be applied across various reacting flow applications, leveraging novel reacting flow actuators such spray water injection or electrically-driven fuel droplet control.

Research Group: You will join a research group on the European project CONTEXT, at the intersection of scientific machine learning and fluid dynamics, under the supervision of Dr. Anh Khoa Doan. You will also have the opportunity to interact with experts in turbulence and machine learning across the department, such as Prof. Luca Magri. Dr. George Rigas or Dr. Andrea Novoa.

Learning opportunities: You will develop expertise in reacting flow physics, machine learning for fluids and control, and high-fidelity simulations. You will have the opportunity of using cutting-edge facilities such as Imperial College HPC facilities.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: A Lagrangian Perspective of Entrainment into Wind-turbine Wakes (AE0091)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Wind turbines clustered together for reasons relating to land availability, onwards power transmission to the grid, and maintenance scheduling amongst others. Unfortunately, wind-turbine clustering is aerodynamically disadvantageous. Each turbine produces a turbulent wake that interacts with downstream turbines to reduce the efficiency of power generation and accelerate the accumulation of fatigue damage. Improved understanding of the spreading, and propagation of wind-turbine wakes is therefore essential to design more efficient wind farms.

Wakes increase in size with distance downstream, similarly to a plume of smoke expanding as it leave a chimney. The processes by which turbulent flows expand are, collectively, known as entrainment. Wind-turbine wakes are complex flows; they involve a background that is already turbulent (due to atmospheric processes) and contain multiple coherent motions such as the blade-tip vortices. All of these features complicate our understanding entrainment into wind-turbine wakes.

You will perform cutting edge experiments to directly observe entrainment, and how the wake’s coherent motions affect these processes, in a laboratory-scale wind-turbine wake from a Lagrangian perspective (i.e. one that moves with the flow), by undertaking state-of-the-art particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) measurements. Our research group has conducted groundbreaking research in recent years on turbulent entrainment and this is the next, exciting step in the journey.

A key feature of this PhD project is that it will run in parallel to a project running at DTU (in Copenhagen) aiming to produce reduced-order models of wind-turbine wakes accounting for the coherent motions and entrainment that you will study. This project will therefore grant you the opportunity to collaborate with one of Europe’s leading research groups in wind energy as well as travel between London and Copenhagen. You will also:

  • Gain hands-on experience of PTV and running experiments in a water facility that is well optimised for entrainment measurements,
  • Work in a research group that has taken a leading role in studying turbulent entrainment,

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Structure-photodegradation-performance Relationship in Carbon Fibre-reinforced Thermosets (AE0089)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: As soon as possible

Introduction: The move towards more-sustainable transport requires lighter vehicle structures, so the high strength-to-weight and stiffness-to-weight ratios of fibre composite materials make them attractive in new applications in addition to their traditional use in aerospace. However, these composite structures are exposed to UV light, especially when used in aircraft and space applications. UV-induced photodegradation is known to damage the surface of composites through erosion and the formation of microcracks in the matrix, which can grow due to stresses on the structure. Thus, it is critical to use polymers that are highly UV-resistant for these applications, but which also possess the required mechanical and functional properties.

The objective of this project is to understand the UV degradation mechanisms of thermosetting epoxy polymers and how the structure / composition of the polymers affects their UV resistance in order to maximise their longevity and long-term performance. It is anticipated that the results arising from this PhD studentship will combine UV resistance data, and visual and chemical analysis with mechanical and fracture properties to build a map of the structure–property relationships for a given composite system. The identification of these structure–property relationships will enable the development of novel and more UV-durable formulations.

You will join the Department of Aeronautics at Imperial College London, benefiting from joint supervision by Professor Koon-Yang Lee (Aeronautics) and Professor Ambrose Taylor (Mechanical Engineering), alongside an industry research scientist from Syensqo.

You will develop specialist expertise in the analytical characterisation of composite materials, gaining hands-on experience in advanced composite manufacturing and analytical techniques in composite science and technology. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Physics of Learning in Robotic Metamaterials
jobs.description_html:
Join us!

Are you a curiosity-driven scientist with a background in physics, engineering, applied mathematics or a related discipline? Join us to lead work at intersection of metamaterials, soft matter physics, and robotics. Look at https://binyshlab.com for some of our work.

This position revolves around the physics of active mechanical metamaterials and distributed robotic systems, combining table-top experiments with theoretical modelling. The project will focus on self-learning active mechanical networks but will be tailored to your interests and expertise.

What will you do?

Nature overflows with simple organisms–from starfish to bacteria–that function without a brain. In contrast to a conventional robot, which is centrally controlled and rigid, these living materials are mechanically soft, and spread actuation, feedback and computation right across their bodies, blurring the boundary between material and machine. Living systems are unconventional robots indeed.

Our work hints that key platforms to capture such material intelligence are ‘robotic metamaterials’–mechanical networks built from many sensors and actuators that locally communicate with one another to achieve collective functionality. These active networks could enable next-generation bioinspired robots that operate without central control, withstand massive damage and adapt to ever-changing environments.

In this PhD, you will lead research into robotic metamaterials that can adapt their dynamics to an environment after deployment. You will:

  • Develop and apply decentralized learning techniques to networks of active mechanical units to sculpt their dynamics and functionality and explore fundamental physical questions on the link between network structure and functionality.
  • Capture the nonlinear dynamics of these networks using theory and numerical simulations.
  • Design and perform table-top robotic experiments that implement your learning algorithms in unpredictable environments.

Who are you?

This PhD is ideal for a curiosity-driven scientist interested in (i) the intersection between materials and machines and (ii) What robotics can teach us about physics, and vice versa. You might be a physicist interested in robotics, a mechanical engineer interested in bio-inspired materials, or a computer scientist/mathematician interested in applied nonlinear dynamics and optimization. We seek an openness to combining table-top robotic experiments with simulations and theory, and an excellent MSc/MPhys/MEng degree (or equivalent).

How to Apply

Applicants should upload information via Birmingham’s Mechanical Engineering PhD portal via the 'Apply' button above specifying the title of the PhD position, and main supervisor (Jack Binysh). We aim to have you start in Early 2027.

In your application please include:

  • A cover letter in which you describe your motivation and qualifications for the position.
  • A CV which includes the contact information of two references.
  • A transcript of your degree grades.
  • A research proposal - Here, because this is an existing project, please feel free to use the job advert as a starting point, but do include any ideas you would be most excited to work on.

Funding is currently available to cover Home UK students, i.e. covering fees and providing a stipend at UKRI rates (current stipend: £21,805 p.a.) for 42 months. Strong international candidates should look at https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/study/international/fees/scholarships, and contact Dr. Binysh if they have a viable plan for international funding.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Nonlinear waves on liquid cylinders
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Prof. Mark Blyth

Inviscid liquid jets subject to surface tension and in the absence of gravity are known to be unstable under long-wave perturbations, a phenomenon described by the classical Rayleigh–Plateau instability. However, when vorticity and swirl are included, Erhard et al. (2022) have theoretically demonstrated the existence of nonlinear travelling-wave solutions on such jets — although their detailed properties remain unexplored. In this project, we will develop new computational methods to compute and characterize these novel wave solutions, with particular emphasis on solitary waves and on analysing their stability. We will also extend the study to related configurations, such as ferrofluid jets under vorticity and swirl.

The mathematical and numerical techniques developed during this work will deepen our understanding of nonlinear wave phenomena in fluid mechanics and contribute to the broader theory of interfacial flows.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Formalising the Local Langlands Correspondence for GL₂(F) in Lean
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Christopher Birkbeck

This PhD project, based at our Norwich campus, offers a unique opportunity to work at the confluence of number theory, representation theory, and formal mathematics. You will undertake a single, ambitious research project: to begin the formalisation of the local Langlands correspondence for GL₂(F) in the Lean interactive theorem prover by leveraging AI agents. This correspondence is a cornerstone of the modern Langlands program, providing a deep and unforeseen bridge between harmonic analysis and number theory.

The primary goal of this project is to formalise the sophisticated mathematical objects required to state the main theorem. This will involve developing a computer-verified library for the two sides of the correspondence: (1) the representation theory of GL₂(F), where F is a non-Archimedean local field, including the theory of irreducible admissible representations; and (2) the intricate structure of two-dimensional Galois representations of the Weil group of F.

Once the definitions are in place, the second phase of the project will be to create a comprehensive framework to guide the formalisation of the proof itself, laying the groundwork for a long-term verification effort. This foundational work will be a landmark achievement in the digital formalisation of contemporary mathematics.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: AI-Driven fault diagnosis for wind turbine generators
jobs.description_html:
Primary supervisor - Dr Abdi Jalebi Salman

Reliability is critical to the continued expansion of wind power, particularly for offshore installations, which already contribute around 10-15% of the UK’s electricity and are central to achieving net-zero targets and ensuring the resilience of national grid infrastructure. Preventive maintenance enabled by condition monitoring systems (CMSs) plays a key role in improving turbine reliability and availability while reducing operational costs and the levelised cost of energy. However, the drivetrain, comprising the gearbox, generator, and power electronics, remains a major source of failures, accounting for roughly one third of incidents and nearly half of maintenance costs in offshore turbines. Early and accurate fault detection in this subsystem is therefore essential.

Despite widespread deployment, existing CMS solutions are predominantly based on vibration measurements from accelerometers mounted on drivetrain components, and their performance remains limited. These systems often suffer from low fault detection rates, generate false alarms that reduce energy production, or fail to identify faults sufficiently early to avoid costly repairs. Moreover, they are largely ineffective at detecting electrical faults. The lack of commercially available CMS solutions based on electrical measurements is due to inherent complexity of interpreting electrical signatures of mechanical faults in real time. This creates a clear gap and opportunity for more advanced and integrated monitoring approaches.

This project aims to address the identified gap by developing hybrid fault diagnosis methods that combine analytical approaches based on drivetrain physical properties with AI-driven data analysis techniques to enhance the accuracy and effectiveness of fault detection and classification. The work will involve analytical studies, computer simulations, and finite element (FE) analysis, alongside experimental development and validation.

Entry requirements

The minimum entry requirement is 2:1 in Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Physics.

Mode of study

jobs.description_html:
Start Date: Between 1 August 2027 and 1 July 2028

Application deadline: 23.59 on 4 January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: This PhD puts you at the forefront of structural power composites (SPCs) — a WEF Top 10 Emerging Technology of 2025 — materials that simultaneously store energy and carry load. SPC promise a step-change weight savings for electric aircraft, EVs and satellites. Transitioning from device- to component-level fabrication in a trustworthy fashion would give industry the first credible route from lab-scale to flight- or drive-relevant components, and the chance to help unveil an Electric Composites future set to shape everybody's lives.

Within EleComp, a five-year EPSRC Programme Grant spanning Imperial, Bristol and Durham, your computational focus will be building physics-informed surrogate models and process simulations within a Bayesian-optimisation loop. This loop jointly searches design and process parameters, using active learning to get maximum insight from a minimum number of costly physical builds.

You'll trace the thread from manufacturing process to defects to performance — mechanical (stiffness, damage tolerance) and electrochemical (capacity, impedance, cycle life) — across routes from partners' established hand lay-up through to more adventurous AFP and continuous-fibre 3D printing. You'll iterate continuously against mechanical/electrical testing and characterisation data: data you generate, and data partners at Bristol and Durham share, to keep your models grounded in reality. You'll start on flat and near-flat coupons, where you can iterate fast. Then you'll push into genuinely uncharted territory: curved and ultimately cylindrical geometry. You'll ask the question nobody has yet answered — where do flat-trained models hold, where do they break, and how little curved data do you actually need to adapt them? You'll finish with a validated, geometry-transferable design-to-manufacture pipeline that's never existed before.

If you want a PhD at the genuine cutting edge of where machine learning, composites manufacturing and energy storage intersect, this is it. You'll be supervised by Dr Ajit Panesar and Prof. Emile Greenhalgh, working alongside the SPC and IDEA lab teams and, more widely, with leading academics (at Chalmers and KTH besides the core EleComp team) and industrial partners — helping to shape the Electric Composites future of tomorrow.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Sustainable Aviation Fuel Thermochemical Modelling ENG422
jobs.description_html:
Location: UK Other

Applications are invited to undertake a PhD programme, in partnership with Airbus, to address key challenges in ensuring adoption of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) by understanding the thermophysical and thermochemical behaviour across conditions typical of fuel systems. This research will remove barriers to the adoption of SAF, both for current and future fuels.

Project overview

The research programme will use a mixture of computational, analytical, and machine learning approaches to model the heat transfer to fuels and their physical and chemical behaviour including changes in chemistry and physical properties. The interaction between fuel chemistry and physical behaviour will be investigated. If appropriate, experimental analysis to provide validation data will be acquired as part of the PhD, although where possible validation data will be taken from industrial and openly available literature. You will gain experience in computational, analytical, and experimental approaches across mechanical and chemical engineering applied in an aerospace industry context.

You will be based in the Mechanical and Aerospace Systems research group (previously known as the Gas Turbine and Transmissions research centre) within the Faculty of Engineering and will be part of a supportive team of 50 researchers, technicians, support staff, and academics. The group has a dynamic research culture with a programme of seminars, writing, and social events with a research office hub providing a quiet working environment with social and meeting spaces.

You would be expected to spend part of the PhD period based in Bristol at the Airbus site and will receive supervision support and training from both the university and Airbus. This research will support the path to net zero flights and there may be opportunities to become involved in practical aspects of fuel system design and testing during the PhD.

Candidate requirements 

We are looking for an enthusiastic and self-motivated person with a rigorous approach to research.

  • You should have or be expected to gain a high 2:1, preferably a 1st class honours degree in chemical, mechanical or aerospace engineering or a chemistry or computer science related degree
  • A good knowledge and/or experience in heat transfer is essential, as is the ability to work well in a team

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Characterising the Molecular Pathology of POLG-related Liver Disease in Alpers-Huttenlocher Syndrome
jobs.description_html:
Award summary

This PhD project is focussed on investigating the mechanisms underpinning liver dysfunction in childhood POLG-related mitochondrial disease, also known as Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome.

The award covers 100% of home (UK) tuition fees and an annual stipend of approximately £21,805 per year (UKRI Rates).

Overview

POLG-related mitochondrial disease is the most common inherited mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance disorder and is caused by pathogenic variants in the POLG gene, resulting in mtDNA depletion. Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is a childhood form of POLG disease that predominantly affects the central nervous system and liver, with patients developing epilepsy, hepatic dysfunction, or both. Acute liver failure is a particularly severe manifestation that most commonly affects infants and is associated with high mortality. Despite the clinical significance of hepatic involvement, the mechanisms underlying liver vulnerability in POLG disease remain poorly understood, and there are currently no disease-modifying therapies that prevent or treat liver failure.

To investigate the mechanisms underpinning POLG-related liver dysfunction in Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome, the molecular pathology of donated post-mortem liver tissue from children and adults with POLG disease will be characterised using quantitative untargeted proteomics and immunohistochemical techniques. Using POLG patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), hepatic organoids will be generated to investigate disease mechanisms and establish a platform for therapeutic screening.

The awardee will join the internationally recognised Newcastle Mitochondrial Research Group and will be affiliated with the Translational and Clinical Research Institute at Newcastle University and the School of Medicine at the University of St Andrews. The studentship will be based at Newcastle University with the opportunity to do a research placement at the University of St Andrews.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Enhancing the Otago Exercise Programme to Preserve Bone Health in Women with Osteopenia or Osteoporosis
jobs.description_html:
Project:

Exercise can preserve bone mineral density, but high-impact or heavy-load programmes may be unsuitable or unappealing for women with osteopenia or osteoporosis, particularly where weakness, impaired balance or fear of falling are also present. This PhD will develop a more accessible alternative by enhancing the established, home-based Otago Exercise Programme. Exercise bands will provide resistance throughout each movement, while high-speed contractions will aim to increase rate of force development and skeletal loading.

The PhD candidate will complete four linked studies: an evidence review; a laboratory electromyography comparison of traditional and banded Otago exercises; a feasibility and repeatability study in adults aged over 55 years; and a 12-month clinical study comparing usual NHS care, banded Otago and high-speed banded Otago in postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis. Bone mineral density, measured by DEXA and blood based bio-markers, will be the primary outcome, supported by measures of strength, balance, falls, fear of falling and body composition.

The PhD candidate will gain experience in exercise prescription, surface electromyography, DEXA, clinical research, patient and public involvement, and mixed research methods while working with the University of Hull, Osprey charity and the local NHS Trust.

Applicants should hold at least a 2:1 honours degree, or equivalent, in sport and exercise science, strength and conditioning, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, biomechanics, human movement science or a closely related subject. A relevant taught MSc or Masters by Research is highly desirable. Applicants should demonstrate an interest in exercise for clinical or older populations, strong communication and organisational skills, and the ability to work sensitively with participants and clinical partners. jobs.title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail: Understanding rainfall-induced slope failure risk
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/

The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance efficiency, safety and sustainability.

Network Rail manage the UK's rail assets including many embankments and cuttings and possess a large amount of data from a variety of sources on their condition and performance. Failures of these slopes have a substantial impact on the rail network in terms of both safety and economic losses from speed restrictions and an understanding of the factors influencing the risk of failure is hence critical to focus remediation work on key locations within the network.

The project will aim to understand from available databases and modelling what processes and conditions drive the hotspots of failures seen around the rail network. These factors may include local geology and hydrogeologic conditions both from natural topology and the performance of drainage systems. As many of these failures are driven by periods of high rainfall, the effects of climate change on changing risks to the network will also be investigated. The project will use Network Rail data to identify common factors amongst clusters of slope failures and will then use Centrifuge and Finite Element modelling to investigate why these factors are critical and the influence of future climate changes on risk. This understanding will then allow machine learning or AI models to be used to identify risk hotspots within the network and to focus remediation efforts on these locations.

jobs.title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail: Low-carbon cements for low-risk rail infrastructure applications
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/

The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance efficiency, safety and sustainability.

The extensive use of cement and concrete by Network Rail across its UK rail infrastructure combined with the high emissions associated with their manufacture, are fuelling opportunities for lower carbon alternatives. Cement-based binders are widely deployed in lower strength and/or lower risk applications in conventional rail infrastructure including ancillary applications and low-risk exposure classes. These could include concrete for walkways and kerbs, blocks and pavers, drainage channels and cable troughs, signal and fence bases, some platform components and concrete fill; and mortars and grouts for slope and subgrade stabilisation, erosion control, repairs and surface treatments.

These assets have varying manufacturing, design and performance criteria. Current standards, e.g. BS EN 197 and FLEX 350 already include a range of binary and ternary low carbon cements and alternative binders, while other low compositions are not yet covered. Poor workability, limited durability data and lack of a clear acceptance route are barriers to uptake. Lower risk assets enable tailored binders, including those using recycled railway, and other secondary materials, to be assessed.

A subset will be investigated based on initial mapping of cementitious binders and applications, and design and performance requirements. The project will combine advanced material characterisation and mix design development, early age performance and modelling, sensor technology and accelerated and long-term mechanical and durability testing. The aim is to deliver the performance and whole-life carbon evidence needed for uptake on the rail network.

jobs.title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail: Infrastructure system management in a changing climate
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/

The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance efficiency, safety and sustainability.

Climate change and shifting patterns of extreme weather are impacting risk profiles of transport assets, requiring re-evaluation of investment strategies to maintain reliable services. This research will investigate how environmental and operational thresholds for key rail assets can be scientifically defined, quantified and integrated into long-term climate adaptation planning. The main aim of the study is to develop methods to identify tipping points arising from climatic stressors such as extreme heat, high-intensity rainfall, soil moisture variation, and compound weather events. This will require an interdisciplinary systems approach and data analysis to explore historical asset/network performance. The insight will then be used as a starting point for evaluating future performance. 

This project is not about advancing fundamental physics or engineering models of a specific asset type, but rather, understanding how the data available via Network Rail can be modelled to support identification of thresholds or tipping points for the railway infrastructure system. It is envisaged that the project will evaluate how threshold-based insights can enhance the timing, prioritisation and appraisal of adaptation options within existing decision frameworks used by Network Rail and national transport bodies.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Microbiomes for Sustainable, Low-Input Agriculture
jobs.description_html:
Primary supervisor - Dr Myriam Charpentier

Can we harness beneficial soil microorganisms to grow productive crops with less fertiliser?

Modern agriculture relies heavily on nitrogen and phosphorus fertilisers, but their intensive use has significant economic and environmental costs. Plants naturally interact with diverse soil microorganisms such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi that can improve nutrient acquisition, soil function and resilience. Understanding how crops recruit and interact with these beneficial microorganisms could therefore provide new opportunities for more sustainable agriculture.

Building on recent discoveries from our laboratory, the student will investigate how wheat genetics can be exploited to enhance beneficial interactions between crop roots, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and additional soil microbiome, and whether these tripartite interactions can improve crop performance under reduced-fertiliser conditions.

You will combine field experimentation, crop phenotyping, plant-microbe biology and microbiome approaches to investigate how wheat genotype and nutrient management influence beneficial microbial associations. You will assess crop performance and nutrient-use efficiency, characterise fungal and bacterial communities associated with roots, and identify microbial functions linked to improved crop performance under reduced-input conditions.

Based at the John Innes Centre, you will work within a collaborative research environment bringing together expertise in plant-microbe interactions, wheat genetics, crop physiology, field experimentation, microbiome science and microbial genomics across JIC, NIAB and the Earlham Institute.

This interdisciplinary PhD is ideal for a student interested in plant science, microbiology, crop genetics, bioinformatics or sustainable agriculture who wants to translate fundamental biological discoveries into approaches for reducing agricultural inputs while maintaining crop productivity.

This studentship offers the opportunity to undertake a 4-year PhD research project whilst enhancing professional development and research skills through a comprehensive training programme provided by the UKRI-BBSRC Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership (NRPDTP). You will join a vibrant community of world-leading researchers.

Our partners value diverse and inclusive work environments that are positive and supportive. jobs.title: AstraZeneca funded Non-clinical PhD Studentship (Fixed Term) in Improved 2A peptides for co-translational separation of a polyprotein
jobs.description_html:
Applications are invited for a 4-year PhD studentship starting on 1 October 2027 and based in the Department of Pathology, University of Cambridge, and the AstraZeneca Discovery Centre at Cambridge. The student will be working on a collaborative project jointly supervised by Prof. Andrew Firth at the University of Cambridge and Dr Giovanni Ciotta at AstraZeneca and will have the opportunity to work across the two sites. The project focuses on manipulating peptide-bond skipping sequences to aid protein engineering.

2A peptides mediate co-translational separation of a polyprotein via a mechanism known as "ribosome skipping" or "StopGo". These ~20 amino acid peptides adopt an unusual conformation within the translating ribosome that prevents peptide bond formation at a specific site but instead promotes release of the nascent peptide followed by continuation of translation. These sequences have proved to be exceptionally useful in biotechnology because they allow the introduction of all components of a pathway or multi-subunit complex in a single step, with stable stoichiometric co-expression from a single promoter. However, 2A peptides have some caveats - including ribosome drop-off, ribosome pausing/stalling, and some amount of separation failure - which constrain their functional utility. We have identified new classes of 2A sequences, some of which have improved properties compared to traditional 2A peptides. This PhD project will contribute to our work investigating these new 2A sequences and optimising them for biotechnological applications.

The UCam team has expertise in molecular biology including ribosome profiling, ribosome structure and function, cell biology, cryo-electron microscopy, and bioinformatics. The AZ team has expertise in cell therapy, CRISPR/Cas9 technologies, and viral vectors. The PhD project will focus on molecular biology techniques but there will also be opportunity for bioinformatic skill development and there may be scope to obtain structural biology experience. At the AstraZeneca site, the student will focus on implementing optimised sequences in specific biotechnological applications, e.g. in cell therapy.

For full details and application process please click the 'Apply' button above.

jobs.title: Doctoral Fellowships in Maternity Disparities
jobs.description_html:
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Inequalities Challenge: Maternity Disparities Consortium (MDC) is proud to announce its doctoral fellowships competition. We are seeking the next generation of researchers to help us tackle persistent inequalities in maternity. 

The MDC brings together a UK wide collaboration of universities, NHS trusts, councils, charities, and industry partners. You can find information about our consortium members here. Our goal is to improve outcomes for women and babies before, during, and after pregnancy through inclusive, evidence-based research.

Capacity Development 

The MDC capacity development programme aims to build the next generation of maternity disparities research leaders, strengthen the workforce to deliver and sustain impact across the UK.

The Consortium focuses on growing long-term research capacity and expertise, especially within underrepresented disciplines, professions and underserved communities; inspiring and supporting the next generation of researchers with the right skills mix to work across clinical, practice and research sectors.  

The Opportunity 

We are offering up to 8 funded salaried doctorates across a range of potential projects at universities across our Consortium. We are specifically looking to grow research capacity among underrepresented disciplines such as midwives, health visitors, neonatal nurses, social care practitioners and community pharmacists.  

  • Start: June 2027 
  • Duration: Up to 3 years (Full-Time) or 4 years at 0.8WTE (Part-Time) dependent on project, please see individual project pages. 

Funding:  

  • Full salary, including national insurance and superannuation, based on your current full time equivalent (fte) salary, up to a salary of £68,000fte (100% direct costs only). 
  • Active clinician or practitioner applicants, or applicants that are registered practitioners employed in a local authority setting, can claim up to 20% clinical or practice time within the award 
  • Full PhD tuition fees, at UK home rate 
  • £5,000 contribution towards research, travel, training and consumables. 

Who is a MDC doctoral fellowship for? 

To be eligible for this scheme you should be an active clinician or practitioner or a registered practitioner based in a local authority setting. Applicants must hold a substantive contract in a clinical / local authority practice role. 

For this award, we define ‘active clinicians or practitioners’ as people who hold a contract of employment in the UK who are either: 

  • Registered UK health, public health or social care professionals  
  • Doctors or dentists registered with the General Dental Council or General Medical Council 
  • Health and care professionals (HCPs) (which includes nurses, midwives, allied health professionals, regulated clinical and practitioner psychologists, pharmacists, and healthcare scientists) registered with one of the national regulatory bodies, including the: 
    • Nursing and Midwifery Council 
    • Health and Care Professions Council 
    • General Dental Council 
    • General Medical Council 
    • General Optical Council 
    • General Osteopathic Council 
    • General Chiropractic Council 
    • General Pharmaceutical Council 
    • Pharmaceutical Society of Northern Ireland 

Fixed term contracts of employment of any duration are acceptable but honorary contracts or bank work are not.  

We define ‘registered practitioners based in local authority settings’ as people who are:  

  • Registered UK health, public health or social care professionals, registered with a national body including:  
  • Social Work England, Northern Ireland Social Care Council, Scottish Social Services Council, Social Care Wales 
  • UK Public Health Register 
  • Health and Care Professions Council 
  • Nursing and Midwifery Council 

And hold a contract of employment in the UK with either a: 

  • local authority  
  • provider of local authority commissioned services, or a 
  • non-profit organisation, such as a charity that provides services on behalf of a local authority, or that otherwise supports a local authority in meeting its objectives 
  • fixed term contracts of employment of any duration are acceptable but honorary contracts or bank work are not 
  • non-profit organisation, which provide services on behalf of a local authority, or that otherwise supports a local authority, do not need to be commissioned or funded by that local authority, but the support does need to be co-designed with, or at the very least acknowledged and signposted by, the local authority or authorities in question 

We welcome applications from individuals passionate about maternal health equity and particularly from areas that are underrepresented in maternity disparities research. We are committed to building a supportive, inclusive, and caring research community. We particularly encourage applications from: 

  • People from underrepresented ethnic backgrounds. 
  • People with disabilities, neurodivergent conditions, and long-term health requirements 
  • Candidates of all genders, ages, and beliefs. 

Each project has a supervisor, theme lead and capacity development lead listed on the project page. We encourage you to contact them to ensure the project is a right fit for you. 

Frequently asked questions 

I am a registered practitioner, but I currently work in higher education and do not have active employment in practice. Am I eligible?

This scheme is specifically for active clinicians, practitioners, or registered practitioners based in a local authority setting. Applicants must hold a substantive contract in a clinical / local authority practice role. 

Doctoral Fellowships in Maternity Disparities

Accessibility & Support 

We want you to perform at your best. You may contact individual supervisors when asking for more details about the projects and your suitability for the project. General enquiries about the recruitment process and MDC, including if you require any reasonable adjustments for the application process or the interview (such as alternative formats, extra time, or specific technological needs), please contact nihr.mdc.capacitydevelopment@newcastle.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship Archaeobotany of Zambezi Valley
jobs.description_html:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in April 2027 under the co-supervision of Dr Alexander Weide and Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones as part of the ZAMBEZI project. This PhD studentship is funded as part of an ERC Advanced Grant project. 

Zambezian Entanglements in the South-Central African Iron Age (ZAMBEZI) is a 5-year project based on fieldwork in Zambia and Zimbabwe. The project centres on renewed excavations at the site of Ingombe Ilede, Zambia, and exploration of the broader region, including further sites in Zambia and northern Zimbabwe. As such, ZAMBEZI will be generating new data for some key sites through which the archaeology of this region is known and offers the opportunity to rethink second-millennium lifeways and connections in this place. The project is a collaboration with the National Museum of Zambia. 

We are looking for a highly motivated applicant to join the project. The selected applicant will be jointly co-supervised by the PI of the project, Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones, and Dr Alexander Weide, with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers depending on training needs. 

The successful applicant's research will focus on plant use, agricultural practice and landscape change, using data from flotation of material from excavations at Ingombe Ilede and neighbouring sites.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship Zooarchaeology Later Pastoralism
jobs.description_html:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in October 2027 under the co-supervision of Professor Paul Lane and Dr Lizzie Wright, as part of the Landscape Historical Ecology and Archaeology of Ancient Pastoral Societies in Kenya (LHEAAPS) project. This PhD studentship is funded by a UKRI Frontier Research Grant.

The LHEAAPS project aims to investigate the origins and evolution of Pastoral Iron Age societies in north-central Kenya through integrated analysis of patterns of human and livestock mobility, dietary practices, exchange networks, and responses to periods of known drought and increased rainfall over the last c. 1800 years. Through the innovative use of diverse bioarchaeological, archaeological and zooarchaeological approaches, the PhD project is intended to contribute to the reconstruction of diets, animal economies and herd management strategies (including seasonal and longer-term mobility of livestock) via combined zooarchaeology and isotopic analyses. The study will contribute to wider syntheses and analyses aimed at demonstrating the value of understanding these pastoralist pasts as paths for planning more sustainable futures for the region’s contemporary pastoralist societies. In doing so, the project aspires to respond to calls to build long-term sustainability and resilience into social-ecological systems in sub-Saharan Africa through provision of deep histories of human-environment interactions and holistic approaches to the reconstruction of past and present human responses to climate-induced socioecological vulnerability.

We are looking for a highly motivated student to join the project. The selected student will be jointly co-supervised by the PI of the project (Professor Paul Lane, University of Cambridge) and Dr Lizzie Wright (Assistant Professor in Zooarchaeology), with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers depending on training needs.

The successful applicant’s research will focus on reconstruction of the animal economies and herd management strategies associated with Pastoral Iron Age sites across north-central Kenya, assessing changes and continuities over time in terms of dietary breadth, mobility strategies and related factors. In order to do this a combination of zooarchaeological (analysis of species composition, body part representation, mortality, pathological and metric data), and isotopic analyses will be employed.

Candidates must meet the requirement for a PhD application in archaeology (https://www.graduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/directory/hsarpdarc/requirements), and have (or expect to obtain by July 2027) an MA, MSc or MPhil degree in archaeology, archaeological science or a cognate discipline, with evidence of a sound grounding in and specialist knowledge of zooarchaeology. Ideally, applicants will have knowledge of East African Holocene archaeology and/or on the archaeology of pastoralist economies, and practical field experience in researching the archaeology of pastoralism.

For further details and how to apply please click the 'Apply' button above.

For informal enquiries, please contact Professor Paul Lane and Dr Lizzie Wright via email: pjl29@cam.ac.uk and eew39@cam.ac.uk

Sustainable aviation fuel thermochemical modelling

Applications are invited to undertake a PhD programme, in partnership with Airbus, to address key challenges in ensuring adoption of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) by understanding the thermophysical and thermochemical behaviour across conditions typical of fuel systems. This research will remove barriers to the adoption of SAF, both for current and future fuels. 

Project overview

The research programme will use a mixture of computational, analytical, and machine learning approaches to model the heat transfer to fuels and their physical and chemical behaviour including changes in chemistry and physical properties. The interaction between fuel chemistry and physical behaviour will be investigated. If appropriate, experimental analysis to provide validation data will be acquired as part of the PhD, although where possible validation data will be taken from industrial and openly available literature. You will gain experience in computational, analytical, and experimental approaches across mechanical and chemical engineering applied in an aerospace industry context.

You will be based in the Mechanical and Aerospace Systems research group (previously known as the Gas Turbine and Transmissions research centre) within the Faculty of Engineering and will be part of a supportive team of 50 researchers, technicians, support staff, and academics. The group has a dynamic research culture with a programme of seminars, writing, and social events with a research office hub providing a quiet working environment with social and meeting spaces.

You would be expected to spend part of the PhD period based in Bristol at the Airbus site and will receive supervision support and training from both the university and Airbus. This research will support the path to net zero flights and there may be opportunities to become involved in practical aspects of fuel system design and testing during the PhD.

Candidate requirements 

We are looking for an enthusiastic and self-motivated person with a rigorous approach to research.

  • You should have or be expected to gain a high 2:1, preferably a 1st class honours degree in chemical, mechanical or aerospace engineering or a chemistry or computer science related degree
  • A good knowledge and/or experience in heat transfer is essential, as is the ability to work well in a team
  • Prior experience in the areas of computational fluid dynamics, chemistry, machine learning, or computational heat transfer will be an advantage.

Eligibility and funding

Due to funding restrictions this studentship is only available to UK (home fees) citizens.

The PhD studentship will cover fees and tax-free stipend of £24,000 p.a. for four years. 

How to apply

Closing date: 5 January 2027

Applications with a CV, cover letter and academic transcripts should be emailed to Hadrian Moran via the 'Apply' button above (E: hadrian.moran@nottingham.ac.uk) 

Suitable applicants will be interviewed, and if successful invited to make a formal application. 

Informal enquiries may be emailed to Professor Carol Eastwick - carol.eastwick@nottingham.ac.uk

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in the Landscape Archaeology of East African Montane Systems
jobs.description_html:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in October 2027 under the co-supervision of Professor Paul Lane and Dr Stefania Merlo, as part of the AFRI-CAN project. This PhD studentship is funded by ERC Synergy grant No. 101224449.

The AFRI-CAN project (– Lead PI Professor Rob Marchant, University of York) explores the interlinked interactions of human systems and mountain ecosystems understood as mountain socioecological systems by combining state-of-the-art modelling, interdisciplinary insights and valuation assessments to co-produce pathways for sustainable mountain futures. Focussed on six contrasting East African mountain settings, the AFRI-CAN project aims to investigate how communities interact with nature, how ecosystems evolve, and which pathways could support sustainable and resilient mountain futures.

We are looking for a highly motivated applicant to join the project and contribute to Work Package 1. The selected applicant will be co-supervised by Professor Paul Lane and Dr Stefania Merlo with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers that are part of the AFRI-CAN project, in particular Dr Daryl Stump, at the University of York.

The successful applicant’s research will focus on developing detailed historical land-use and land cover map of landscape change across the mountain study sites over the past 6,000 years through the integration of archaeobotanical, faunal and material culture data and historical maps with a particular focus on forestry and forest management. The doctoral student will play a central role in collating and assessing existing historical and archaeological records from the MAEASaM (Mapping Africa’s Endangered Archaeological Sites and Monuments) project and other data sets (e.g. the Pandora repositories), as well as conducting supplementary targeted archaeological fieldwork relating to land use activities across the target study sites and synthesising detailed archaeobotanical, faunal and material culture data relevant to the sites. This will include analysing historical maps, aerial photographs and remote sensing and integrated historical data across the study sites to develop finer-resolution maps of land-use and landcover for the past 150 years.

Applicants must meet the requirement for a PhD in Archaeology (see details here: https://www.postgraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/directory/aaarpdarc), have (or expect to obtain by July 2027) an MA, MSc or MPhil degree in a relevant discipline and possess the following additional skills:

  • Expertise in landscape archaeology, historical geography or landscape history preferably in an African context (Essential)
  • Familiarity or experience in the using databases and geospatial analysis and mapping (Essential)
  • Experience with using historical maps and remote sensing imagery to identify archaeological sites (Essential) and create Land Use Land Cover maps (Desirable)
  • Experience with synthesising archaeological and historical datasets (Desirable)
  • Experience in conducting archaeological field surveys (Desirable), ideally in an African setting

For further details and how to apply please click the 'Apply' button above.

For further information and informal enquiries, please contact via email either Professor Paul Lane (pjl29@cam.ac.uk) and/or Dr Stefania Merlo (sm399@cam.ac.uk)

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Digital Twins for waste reduction in Industry 5.0
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Mohsin Raza

Reducing industrial waste is a key challenge in achieving sustainable manufacturing and advancing the vision of Industry 5.0. Manufacturing processes can generate significant waste through material inefficiencies, defective products, equipment failures, excessive energy consumption, and suboptimal production planning. Digital twins, integrated with artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and advanced data analytics, offer opportunities to monitor manufacturing operations, identify sources of waste, and support proactive, data-driven interventions.

This PhD project will investigate the development of intelligent digital twin frameworks to predict, monitor, and reduce waste in manufacturing processes. The research will explore how near real-time data from industrial sensors, machinery, and production systems can be integrated into digital twins to identify 2inefficiencies, detect anomalies and predict product defects, to optimise the use of raw materials and reduce waste. AI and machine learning techniques will be investigated to support waste prediction androot-cause analysis.

The project will explore simulation-based approaches that enable manufacturers to evaluate alternative production scenarios and assess their potential impact on waste generation before implementing changes in real-world environments. Relevant sustainability indicators may be incorporated to measure improvements in material utilisation and overall waste reduction. The research will further investigate key metrics to understand waste patterns and make informed operational decisions.

The successful candidate will contribute to innovative research addressing industrial waste and environmental sustainability. The project aims to develop intelligent digital twin solutions that help manufacturers minimise waste, improve resource efficiency, in line with Industry 5.0. The project will offer opportunities to develop innovative digital twin solutions, publish research in leading academic venues, and explore practical applications.

The standard minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Dynamics driving photoswitchable molecules using laser spectroscopy
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. James Bull

A PhD position is available in laser spectroscopy at the University of East Anglia, supervised by Assoc. Prof. James Bull and supported by an EPSRC grant. The project will investigate the excited- and ground-state dynamics of molecular photoswitches, which undergo light-driven structural changes with applications in photomolecular motors, smart materials, and photopharmacology.

The research will examine how molecular structure and environment control photoisomerisation, excited-state relaxation and photochemical efficiency. These dynamics ultimately define light-driven molecular function. Experiments will be conducted in both the gas phase and condensed phase, combining photoisomerisation action (PISA) spectroscopy, time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy, with condensed-phase ultrafast spectroscopies. Comparing the dynamics in isolated (gas phase) molecules with those in solution will reveal how solvent polarity, hydrogen bonding and viscosity influence excited-state lifetimes, relaxation pathways, branching ratios and photoisomerisation quantum yields.

The project will use custom-built vacuum instrumentation and advanced ultrafast laser systems to characterise molecular isomers, probe short-lived intermediates and uncover the mechanisms underlying photoswitching. Many of the experimental capabilities in our laboratory are unique worldwide, providing opportunities to study reactive species and photochemical processes that are difficult to access using conventional techniques. The ultimate aim is to establish structure-dynamics relationships that guide the rational design of more efficient and functional molecular photoswitches.

The successful candidate will receive comprehensive training in laser spectroscopy, ultrafast experimental techniques, vacuum instrumentation and data analysis, working alongside experienced rearchers.

Further details are available at http://www.eigenket.org/(opens in a new window). Queries and further discussion on the project is welcome.

A 2:1 or 1st Bachelor's degree in Chemistry or Physics.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Historical genomics of the declining red squirrel in Britain
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Anders Bergström

The red squirrel in Britain is one of the most iconic examples of a declining population. It has suffered greatly since the introduction of the invasive grey squirrel in the late 1800s, but even before then it was struggling due to hunting and deforestation. However, already since the late 1700s, people have tried to counter the decline by bringing in new red squirrels from continental Europe. How all these past processes have affected the genetic make-up, fitness and ancestry of British squirrels is poorly understood.

This project will study the rollercoaster history of the red squirrel in Britain using historical DNA. By tracing the genetics of the red squirrel over the past few hundred years, the project has two goals:

1) To provide general insights into the genetics of population decline and rescue, broadly applicable across organisms.

2) To reconstruct the specific history of the widely cherished red squirrel, to potentially help future efforts to conserve it.

The project will use historical DNA techniques to sequence genomes from squirrels in museum collections, to directly analyse how genetic diversity, inbreeding and genetic load has changed over time, and evaluate the effects that the many translocations had on populations. The project will also address how much native British squirrel ancestry persists today, to test whether the many introductions has led to a complete loss of native ancestry (‘genetic swamping’).

The student will receive broad training in molecular biology, historical DNA, genomics, bioinformatics and population genetics. The student will take part in journal clubs and departmental seminars, present their work at conferences, and develop skills in critical thinking and science communication.

The ideal candidate will have a background in a biological science (e.g. genetics, molecular biology, zoology, evolution, ancient DNA), and have strong interests in genomics, wet-lab work, data analysis, and evolution.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 Bachelor's degree in Biology, Genetics, Zoology, Ecology, Biochemistry, or Archaeology.

Mode of Study

Start Date

1 October 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Quantum-Resilient Security for Safety-Critical Vehicular Systems
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Hassan Malik

The rapid growth of connected and autonomous vehicular systems is transforming modern transport infrastructure. However, advances in quantum computing are expected to undermine the security of current cryptographic methods. This creates a pressing need for robust and future-proof security solutions for safety-critical, real-time vehicular communication systems.

This PhD project aims to develop quantum-resilient security approaches for connected vehicular systems. The research will investigate the suitability of post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) techniques for dynamic and resource-constrained vehicular communication infrastructures operating within emerging 6G-enabled networks. A key focus will be on understanding the trade-offs between security strength, computational overhead, and communication latency in time-sensitive environments.

The project will combine system modelling, simulation, and algorithmic implementation to evaluate PQC schemes under realistic vehicular conditions. Beyond performance analysis, the research will explore adaptive and lightweight strategies to enable efficient key management and secure communication in highly dynamic settings. It will also investigate optimisation techniques for resource-constrained platforms and identify practical design principles for integrating quantum-resilient security into deployable vehicular systems.

The expected outcomes include novel approaches and frameworks for deploying efficient, low-latency, and scalable security mechanisms tailored to vehicular applications. The research will support the secure operation of autonomous transport systems and strengthen the resilience of vehicular communication networks.

The broader societal impact lies in improving the safety, reliability, and trustworthiness of connected transport systems. By enhancing the resilience of vehicular communication, the project contributes to safer mobility and reduced vulnerability to cyber threats.

The student will gain interdisciplinary expertise in cybersecurity, networked systems, and applied cryptography, with opportunities for collaboration with academic and industry partners.

Entry Requirements

A minimum of a 2:1 honour degree (or international equivalent) in a relevant discipline. Candidates should have a strong background in programming and/or networking. Prior knowledge of cybersecurity or cryptography is desirable but not essential.

Mode of Study

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The long, the short and the sticky: finding the mass of natural polymers by NMR
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Matthew Wallace(opens in a new window)

Polymers extracted from natural sources are ubiquitous in modern life, from texturing agents in foods to cell encapsulants in biomedicine. In addition to the structure and sequence of the monomers, the molecular mass i.e. chain length of polymers is crucial in determining their performance in these applications. However, mass determination of natural polymers is extremely difficult due to the tendency of the chains to self-associate and form gels, even at low concentrations. Common techniques such as size-exclusion chromatography assume polymer molecules behave as non-associating spheres. However, aggregation can severely distort measurements and irreversibly contaminate expensive equipment. Our inability to determine polymer molecular mass severely hinders our ability to use natural polymers for targeted applications, where extraction and processing steps must be carefully designed to obtain the correct mass fractions and properties.

In this project, you will develop and apply advanced nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) methods to determine the chain length and aggregation state of a range of natural polymers, including those extracted from seaweed by our industrial partner. Through advanced experimental and pulse sequence design, in collaboration with Dr Rob Evans (UoManchester), you will develop first-of-their-kind models linking the Brownian motion of polymers with their macroscopic diffusion along concentration gradients at high dilution. You will thus create a unique toolset for the self-consistent determination of the overall mass distribution that could be extended to other aggregation-prone macromolecular systems such as synthetic nanoparticles for cancer therapy. Your work will provide a turning point in our ability to characterise macromolecular sizes by NMR, overcoming critical limitations of chromatographic approaches and current NMR methods that consider Brownian motion (self-diffusion) alone.

Training: You will develop a diverse and highly competitive skillset spanning NMR spectroscopy, mathematical modelling, data analysis and complementary analytical techniques including dynamic light scattering and chromatography.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 Bachelor's degree in Chemistry, Pharmacy, Pharmacology, Physics, or a related discipline.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Clean and safe: Developing antimicrobial formulations for food preservation and hygiene
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Yan Fen Lee(opens in a new window)

Foodborne pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes can be present in up to 12% of raw fish, posing serious food safety risks, including listeriosis, which can be life-threatening if left untreated. Listeria is particularly difficult to control because it can grow at refrigeration temperatures and form biofilms that persist on equipment and surfaces in food processing plants, protecting it from desiccation, heat, and standard cleaning and disinfection agents.

This exciting PhD project aims to design and optimize a commercial product to reduce microbial contamination in the seafood industry. Supervised by Dr Yan Fen Lee (UEA) and Dr Matthew Gilmour (Quadram Institute), you will use natural, food-safe ingredients to formulate a multipurpose antimicrobial disinfectant for use within seafood processing plants to control Listeria and other microbes. You will also incorporate the disinfectant into ice blocks/flakes to control microbial growth during shipping and storage. The project will make a significant real-world contribution towards minimising seafood spoilage, food safety risks and expensive wastage, and supporting a more sustainable and resilient seafood industry.

You will have opportunities to train and work in different research laboratories at UEA and the Quadram Institute, and will gain practical experience and highly transferable skills in areas such as microbiology, formulation science, antimicrobial resistance, and genome sequencing. There will also be opportunities to gain experience in the commercial aspects of research translation at Norwich Research Park. Training in scientific writing, communication, and career development will be supported through local and international conferences, seminars, group research discussions, and institutional training programmes.

Motivated, self-starting candidates with a background in (micro)biology, applied chemistry or a related discipline are welcome to contact Dr Yan Fen Lee (yan-fen.lee@uea.ac.uk) for more information.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Modelling and Mitigating the Impacts of Climate Change in Historic Buildings
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Jack Panter

The southern/eastern UK climate is showing a rapid and significant increase in the prevalence, duration, and severity of hot, dry weather. One surprising impact is on our historic houses and cultural heritage: in the National Trust’s portfolio (a key example being Blickling Estate, Norfolk), interior temperatures

are placing significant heat-stress on staff and visitors, leading to site closures, and low humidity is degrading their collections. In response, Blickling Estate aims to become a pioneer in experimentally analysing and computationally modelling the climate impact on internal temperature and humidity, and developing new cooling and humidification interventions. A large research gap is ripe for exploring: while modelling buildings in urban environments is experiencing significant research interest, similar modelling in a historical context is almost wholly unexplored. Thus, this is a unique challenge at the intersection of engineering, climate science, culture, and health.

You will join UEA’s Thermofluids Laboratory, and use state-of-the-art experimental and computational techniques to understand, model, and propose solutions to the heat and humidity challenges at Blickling Estate. This project will also involve time on-site at Blickling gathering experimental data and testing solutions. The project has the following aims:

  • Develop the first thermo-fluid digital twin of Blickling Hall to model how the local geography and climate, air flows, materials, and building layout influence internal temperatures and humidity; explain which factors impact internal conditions; and predict response to future weather/climate events.
  • In collaboration with Blickling Estate, develop and explore a range of interventions aimed at cooling the building and maintaining appropriate humidity.
  • Perform laboratory and on-site experimental testing of trial interventions, supported by the thermo-fluid model, to ultimately understand and explain efficacy.

Ultimately, the successful outcomes of this project will likely lead to national impact on the future of UK buildings heritage in the face of climate change.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree in Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Physics, Applied Physics, Applied Mathematics, Computer Science, Chemistry, or Environmental Science.

Mode of Study

Start Date

1 October 2027

jobs.title: PhD in Mathematics and Applications
jobs.description_html:
Call for Applications

The PhD Program in Mathematics and Applications at Bocconi University is a four-year program taught in English. The program builds on the Department of Decision Sciences’ internationally recognized faculty, vibrant research environment, and Bocconi University’s mission to foster interdisciplinary innovation. The Department has a strong tradition in both pure and applied mathematics, with several faculty members holding prestigious ERC grants.

For the PhD in Mathematics and Applications, the PhD School offers 4 fellowships fully funded by Tech Europe Foundation (TEF).

Fellowships amount to € 27,000 gross per year for four years. Students with fellowship are exempt from the payment of tuition fees for the duration of the four-year program

Curriculum and timeline

The first year provides rigorous core training at the heart of Mathematical Analysis—bringing students quickly to the research frontier and enabling them to launch a substantive research agenda—and is complemented by electives that may cover other areas of mathematics or, depending on their interests, economics, finance, statistics, or machine learning. The second year completes this preparation, offering a view toward applications and providing advanced, research-oriented courses, also taught by visiting professors. The program is structured accordingly: research begins in the first year and develops progressively thereafter. Years three and four are devoted fully to research and thesis writing, with opportunities for international research visits and exchanges.

In addition to a strong core in cutting-edge Mathematical Analysis, the program offers distinctive opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration in economics, finance, decision theory, and computer science, in line with Bocconi’s tradition in the social sciences.

Faculty and visiting scholars

The faculty includes internationally acknowledged researchers in Mathematical Analysis, Applied and Computational Mathematics, Decision Theory, and Mathematical Finance. The program also benefits from authoritative visiting professors who deliver short monographic courses on frontier topics.

Careers

The PhD in Mathematics and Applications is designed for highly motivated students aiming for first-rate research careers in academia, research institutes, and quantitative roles in industry and finance, as well as strategy consulting, operation research, optimization, and AI/ML labs.

Admission profile

We welcome applications from highly qualified and motivated candidates with an MSc degree in pure or applied Mathematics, as well as from candidates in Computer Science, Physics, Economics, Data Science, Engineering, or related areas, provided they have a solid background in mathematics.

Student support

The PhD School’s tutors and Career Service are available to support candidates during the application process and students throughout their studies.

QUALIFICATIONS:

Applications can be submitted by candidates of any citizenship who:

  • have completed or are completing their graduate studies and
  • have at least a “proven” B2 (CEFR) level of competence in English
