jobs.description_html:
Call for Applications

Bocconi University offers a 4-year full-time PhD program in Economics and Finance designed for highly qualified and motivated students wishing to acquire world-class research skills.

The program is multidisciplinary, featuring three curricula (i.e. tracks) – Economics, Finance, and Accounting – linked by a common core. Students are able to choose from a wide range of electives.

First year core courses develop a broad set of theoretical and empirical skills relevant to advanced research in the chosen curriculum. The second year offers advanced core courses in the field of specialization within the chosen curriculum, and a wide range of electives. In the second year students also start working on their first research paper. The third and fourth years are largely dedicated to thesis research work, but students are expected to attend the regular research workshop series presented by internationally renowned speakers.

Students have opportunities to enhance their development and network through short visits to other leading overseas universities. International exchanges are promoted within the framework of the European Doctoral Group in Economics (http://www.edge- page.net).

Bocconi faculty publish regularly in leading international journals and are active members of the international academic community. Our PhD program lays the foundations for successful international academic careers. We place great emphasis on preparing students for the international academic job market. However, the research skills and competences developed during the program also open up career opportunities in central banks, governments, international organizations, investment banks and asset management companies. The tutors and career service of the PhD School are always available to assist candidates.

Recent academic job market placements include Harvard University (Kennedy School of Government), London School of Economics and Political Science, London Business School, University College London, Queen Mary University London, Toulouse School of Economics, ESSEC International Business School, University of Alicante, Bolzano University, Stockholm University (Institute for International Economic Studies (IIES)), and Imperial College Business School Placements in international institutions include IMF, World Bank, OECD, Bank of England, Bank of France, Bank of Portugal, Bank of Italy, and National Bank of New Zealand.

QUALIFICATIONS: 

Applications are welcomed from candidates with educational backgrounds in economics, finance, and accounting, but also other quantitative disciplines, e.g., engineering, statistics, and data analytics. 

Applications can be submitted by candidates of any citizenship who:

  • have completed or are completing their graduate studies and
  • have at least a “proven” B2 (CEFR) level of competence in English 

The PhD School offers a maximum of 17 places with a fellowship for the PhD in Economics and Finance. Fellowships amount to € 27,000 gross per year for four years. Students with fellowship are exempt from the payment of tuition fees for the duration of the four-year program.  

The PhD School also offers 3 places with payment of tuition fees which amount to € 15,000 for years 1 and 2 and € 5,000 for years 3 and 4.  

Students may also work part-time as research assistants and teaching assistants on a remunerated basis, within limits set by national and internal regulations. 

APPLICATION PROCEDURE: 

To apply for our PhD program, only our online application procedure may be used.

Applications are due by 18 January 2027. 

The assessment of the applicant is based on:

  • Personal curriculum: full CV (mandatory)
  • Academic records: transcript of exams and certification of undergraduate and graduate degrees awarded and final grade (if any); if the graduate program has not been completed, an enrollment document with the full study plan, the exams taken and the grades achieved (mandatory)
  • International Graduate Admission Tests scores: Graduate Record Examination (GRE) or Graduate Management Admission Test (GMAT) – (optional but highly recommended)

  • Reference letters: up to three reference letters uploaded by referees appointed in the online application procedure (optional but strongly encouraged) 

A minimum of 60 total points out of 100 is required to be eligible for admission to the program. 

Please consult our website for complete details of our application procedure. Click the Apply button above to access.

jobs.title: PhD in Legal Studies
jobs.description_html:
Call for Applications 

Bocconi University invites applicants for 8 fully funded PhD positions within the Legal Studies doctoral program. Fellowships amount to € 27,000 gross per year for three years. Students with fellowship are exempt from the payment of tuition fees for the duration of the three-year program. 

The International and European Law curriculum seeks to foster world-class research on any topic within the two broad subject areas of international law and European law. Potential fields of interest include, but are not limited to, general public international law, international trade law, international investment law, international cultural heritage law, international criminal law, private international law, European economic law, European trade law, European internal market law, European external relations law, European Citizenship, comparative and European constitutional law, EU governance, EU fundamental rights, and European social law, privacy and media law. Interested students will become part of  the Bocconi European Studies Lab (BLEST - https://www.blest.unibocconi.eu/ ), a center for interdisciplinary research in the field of European matters, and might co-operate with the Institute for European Policy Making (IEP, https://iep.unibocconi.eu/).  

The Business and Social Law curriculum aims to promote excellence in study of business law with an approach combining an interdisciplinary perspective, an international orientation and the analysis of the specific fields of the law covered by the program (e.g. corporation, securities, competition, commercial contracts, bankruptcy, IPRs, labor law, white collar crime). The study of law and economics and social sciences complements the study of business law. 

Bocconi University is part of CIVICA, the European University of Social Sciences (civica.eu), a network of 10 European universities (Science Po, European University Institute, Hertie School, London School of Economics and Political Science, Stockholm School of Economics, Central European University, and SNSPA School of Governance, National University of Political Studies and Public Administration, SGH Warsaw School of Economics). Beside the courses offered by the Bocconi PhD in Legal Studies Program, students can choose from a rich portfolio of courses offered by our partners. PhD students are encouraged to take part in exchanges and activities (including targeted summer and winter schools) within the CIVICA network. Furthermore, Bocconi has several exchange programs with partners outside the CIVICA network. 

During their second and third years, students are expected to actively engage in department life, with opportunities to serve as Teaching Assistants where available. 

Students are encouraged to network with PhD students from other departments and universities and with speakers at our guest seminar series and other events. 

The program aims to create a vibrant community of young researchers fully integrated into the life of the Department and in this way to contribute to forming the next generation of research leaders. Successful applicants will spend the first part of the program at Bocconi following a set of tailored courses on legal and interdisciplinary research methodologies and specialized seminars on selected topics. Students are subsequently encouraged to spend a period abroad as visiting researchers at foreign universities, taking full advantage of the opportunities offered by the CIVICA network and by the other partner institutions in international research centers or international organizations. Bocconi University provides financial support to all PhD students for research stays abroad during their second or third year. 

QUALIFICATIONS: 

  • Applications can be submitted by candidates of any citizenship who have completed or are completing their graduate studies and have at least a “proven” B2 (CEFR) level of competence in English. 

For the PhD in Legal Studies, the PhD School offers:

  • a maximum of 8 places with a fellowship (4 for the curriculum in International and European Law, 4 for the curriculum in Business and Social Law);
  • a maximum of 2 places with payment of tuition fees (1 for the curriculum in International and European Law, 1 for the curriculum in Business and Social Law). 

Tuition fees for students without a fellowship or tuition waiver amount to € 15,000 for year 1 and € 5,000 for year 2 and 3. 

For more detailed information, please see the full official call published on the webpage here. 

For more detailed information about our program, please visit the website here. 

APPLICATION PROCEDURE: 

To apply for our PhD program our online application procedure must be used. The deadline for applications is 18 January 2027.

Applicants shall select on the on-line application the curriculum they opt for. 

The selection process consists of two stages: an initial evaluation of applicant qualifications, followed by an interview for shortlisted candidates. 

The first step assessment is based on a candidate’s: 

  1. Personal curriculum (mandatory): full CV;
  2. Research proposal (mandatory): detailed description of research proposal (max 1200 words, references excluded) coherent with one of the curricular disciplinary fields;
  3. Reference letters: up to three reference letters uploaded by referees appointed in the online application procedure (not mandatory but highly recommended);
  4. Academic records (mandatory): transcript of exams and certification of undergraduate and graduate degrees awarded and final grade (if any); if the graduate program has not been completed, an enrollment document with the full study plan, the exams taken and the grades achieved;
  5. Statement of purpose (mandatory): short description (max 1200 words) of candidate’s motivation for enrollment in a Bocconi PhD program and of his/her professional goals;
  6. Other relevant documents (maximum five): e.g. thesis’ abstract, publications, other programs attended, etc. 

The Admission Board will interview (online) candidates who have obtained at least 70 points out of 100 in the assessment of qualifications.

The second-phase assessment is based on the online interview, whose maximum score is 30 points.

A candidate will be eligible for admission if they have obtained at least 70 points out of 100 in the qualifications assessment and at least 20 points out of 30 in the interview.

jobs.description_html:
Call for Applications

The PhD in Statistics and Machine Learning at Bocconi University is a rigorous, internationally oriented four-year doctoral program taught in English, the working language of Bocconi's international research community. It provides in-depth training in modern Statistics and Machine Learning, with strong foundations in probability and an emphasis on integrating theory, statistical modeling, and computation. 

The program features two years of structured coursework, following the model of leading US PhD programs. The first year provides rigorous foundational training in Statistics, Probability, and Machine Learning, and concludes with the Summer School in Advanced Statistics and Probability. The second year offers specialized, research-oriented courses focusing on advanced topics and recent developments in the field. Alongside this coursework, students begin working on original research problems, develop their research interests, and identify an advisor. The third and fourth years are devoted to original research and the completion of the doctoral dissertation, with close faculty supervision. 

The faculty includes internationally renowned researchers with strong publication records in leading academic outlets. Their expertise spans Bayesian statistics, machine learning, nonparametric and high-dimensional inference, computational methods and algorithms, and applied probability. Students also have opportunities to interact with distinguished visiting professors, attend Statistics seminars and seminars organized by the Bocconi Institute for Data Science and Analytics (BIDSA), participate in international conferences, and spend research periods abroad. 

The program's overarching objective is to train researchers capable of making original contributions at the highest international level. It prepares students for research careers in academia as well as in industry and public organizations. The program builds on Bocconi's longstanding tradition in Statistics, dating back to the University's foundation, and is a natural evolution of its PhD in Statistics, established in 2001. Graduates of the PhD in Statistics have secured positions worldwide at leading universities and research institutions, as well as in major public and private organizations.

jobs.title: Four year fully funded Graduate Teaching Fellowships for Accounting and Finance PhD students
jobs.description_html:
Hours: full time

Closes: 27 November 2026

Are you planning to start an Accounting and Finance PhD in October 2027? Don’t miss the opportunity to apply for one of the University of Liverpool Management School’s 4-year Graduate Teaching Fellowships (GTF).

Receiving one of our GTF gives you the funds to launch your academic career, while you gain valuable teaching training and experience to become a rounded scholar:

  • £21,805 annual maintenance grant* (for four years)
  • Full coverage of PhD programme fees (for four years)
  • HE teacher training and practice.

This means that as well as pursuing your PhD research, you’ll also be involved in a fixed number of teaching hours during your time with us.

In year one, alongside your specific PhD research modules, you’ll complete a short teacher training programme by the University of Liverpool.

As well as gaining a formal HE teaching qualification, you’ll learn key pedagogical skills for the academic job market, primarily through shadowing mentored classroom involvement.

During the remainder of your PhD, you’ll have the opportunity to put your research skills into practice while completing your doctoral research thesis.

*Stipend amount of £21,805 for 2026/27 is for guidance purposes only and subject to change.

Who is this for?

These studentships are open to full-time PhD students worldwide.

You’ll need a UK master’s degree, or international equivalent, in accounting and finance or a related discipline, preferably at merit or above, plus demonstrable quantitative and programming skills.

How to apply

Before formally applying, you must express your interest in a GTF position by completing this form before Friday 27 November 2026 at 5pm (UK time), an submit a strong research proposal in areas including, but not limited to:

  • Asset pricing and investment
    • Empirical asset pricing and performance evaluation
    • Investment technology, ethics and strategy
    • Equity and other asset classes
    • Financial econometrics and machine learning.
  • Corporate finance and accounting
    • Corporate governance and shareholder value
    • Corporate finance, networks and insider trading
    • Market-based accounting research and corporate transparency
    • Sustainability, corporate social responsibility (CSR) and environmental, social and governance (ESG).
  • International financial markets and the macroeconomy
    • Sovereign debt and international monetary policy
    • Time series analysis of macro and financial indicators
    • Impact of social media on financial markets.
  • Financial technology (FinTech)
    • Payment technologies and the future of money
    • Explainable artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services
    • Integration of FinTech and big data in financial markets and sustainable finance.

You’ll also need to submit:

  • A personal statement
  • A copy of your highest degree transcript
  • A curriculum vitae (CV).

If you’re a suitable candidate, we’ll contact you directly and invite you to submit a formal application. Please, be aware that applicants who skip the steps above will not be considered for a GTF position.

You're welcome to suggest potential supervisors in your application, although this is not compulsory. If you would like to do so, please check our list of Accounting and Finance experts to review their research areas and visit their individual profiles.

We'll take into consideration your suggested supervisors when we review your application, but please bear in mind that we'll make the final decision after assessing who the best match for your intended research project is.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Fatigue Failure of Target Graphite
jobs.description_html:
Research Studentship in Graphite Composite Materials for High-Power Neutrino Targets

Project title: Fatigue Failure of Target Graphite

3.5-year DPhil studentship 

Project title: Fatigue Failure of Target Graphite

Supervisors: Prof Dong (Lilly) Liu (Oxford), Dr Kavin Ammigan (Fermilab)

The Department of Engineering Science at the University of Oxford invites applications for a fully funded D.Phil. project investigating fatigue failure and degradation mechanisms in graphite materials used as proton-beam targets for next-generation neutrino facilities. The project is supported by Oxford and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) and is closely linked to international neutrino programmes including DUNE. The research will develop new fatigue-testing methodologies for target graphite, investigate crack initiation and propagation under cyclic loading, and characterise the relationships between microstructure, thermal properties, irradiation damage and mechanical performance. Experimental work will involve advanced characterisation techniques including X-ray tomography, FIB-SEM tomography, Raman spectroscopy, thermal conductivity measurements, high-temperature mechanical testing, ion irradiation, and synchrotron experiments at Diamond Light Source. This project will work closely with Dr. Chris Densham's group at Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) to support targets design.

Eligibility

This studentship is funded jointly by the Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory and is open to all students. The award covers Home tuition fees and a full stipend.

Award Value

Course fees are covered at the Home rate. The stipend (tax-free maintenance grant) is c. £21,805 for the first year, and at least this amount for a further two and a half years.

Candidate Requirements

Prospective candidates will be judged according to how well they meet the following criteria:

  • A first-class or strong upper second-class degree (or equivalent) in Engineering, Materials Science, Physics, Mechanical Engineering, Nuclear Engineering or a closely related discipline.
  • Strong interest in materials behaviour under extreme environments and experimental research.
  • Excellent written and spoken English communication skills.
  • Ability to work effectively within an international multidisciplinary collaboration.

The following skills are desirable but not essential:

  • Experience in mechanical testing, fracture mechanics or fatigue analysis.
  • Experience with materials characterisation techniques.
  • Data analysis and scientific programming (e.g. Python, MATLAB). 
  • Interest in particle accelerator, nuclear or energy applications.

Application Procedure

Informal enquiries are encouraged and should be addressed to Prof Dong (Lilly) Liu (dong.liu@eng.ox.ac.uk).

Candidates must submit a graduate application and satisfy the University of Oxford admission requirements for the DPhil in Engineering Science.

Please quote 27ENGMM_DL in all correspondence and in your graduate application.

Application deadline: Noon on 2 December 2026 (subject to University admissions deadlines).

Start date: October 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Distributed Machine Learning over Mobile Networks
jobs.description_html:
This is a project focused on how AI will provide a seamless service to mobile users of tomorrow. It is expected the student will have a background in AI with a curiosity on wireless networking.

Machine learning that occurs over a distributed network is attractive to reduce latency, ensure data and compute is sovereignly hosted, and utilise available edge computation resources. There are many challenges when the demand is spatially and temporally mobile, and when the inference is computationally heavy. This PhD studentship will advance the research in AI on Radio Access Networks (AI-on-RAN) by exploring how to optimise distributed and mobile inference of large language models by adapting how tokens, memory, and network bandwidth is used in real time.

The outcomes are expected to shape how future AI algorithms are designed, as well as how future computation and communication resources are invested in 6G telecommunication networks.

There is both university-based and wider FTH ecosystem training with other PhD students from other universities across UK. The experience gained is not only cross-disciplinary (AI and telecoms), but also there will be exposure to different stakeholders beyond these including defence, government, and infrastructure.

Supervisor

1st Supervisor: Prof. Weisi Guo

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: SCALE-Decode: Unlocking Growth Workflows in UK SMEs
jobs.description_html:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) underpin UK employment and innovation, yet many struggle to turn early success into sustainable growth. Rising demand can expose informal routines, disconnected systems, founder dependence and employee overload. Managers may see delayed delivery or lost sales without understanding how constraints travel across the firm. Research and policy treat issues separately, while generic AI lacks context. SCALE-Decode examines how responsible AI can reveal growth workflows, diagnose bottlenecks, and build an AI system to support managerial actions.

Work Package 1 (months 1-12) will map and explain SME scale-up workflows. Manager and employee interviews, walkthroughs, task diaries, process documents and privacy-preserving event logs, where suitable, will be integrated through qualitative analysis, Business Process Model and Notation and process mining. Cross-case comparison will distinguish symptoms, including delay and rework, from underlying causes such as centralised approvals, capability gaps and poor information transfer. Stakeholder validation will refine three deliverables: a Scale-up Workflow Framework, anonymised maps and a bottleneck taxonomy. Together, they will help firms and advisers trace local constraints across an organisation and strengthen workflow-centred scaling theory through credible evidence.

Work Package 2 (months 10-24) will build SCALE-Decode, a secure AI system to help SMEs scale by reconstructing workflows, diagnosing scaling bottlenecks and generating feasible action plans. A knowledge graph will connect activities, dependencies, organisational conditions, evidence and interventions. Four AI components will gather information, produce editable maps, diagnose constraints, and generate and critique actions. Each recommendation will identify its evidence, prerequisites, expected benefit, cost, effort, risk and uncertainty. Managers will correct maps and approve recommendations. Technical, adversarial, usability and unseen-case testing will assess fidelity, traceability, feasibility and unsupported claims. Deliverables comprise a validated prototype, documentation and responsible-use guidance.

Work Package 3 (months 22-36) will evaluate feasibility, usefulness and implementation in SMEs. A longitudinal field study will compare AI-assisted diagnosis with existing approaches and track workflow understanding, decision quality, action completion and selected operational indicators. Usage records, surveys and interviews will show why recommendations Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award are accepted, adapted or rejected and whether outcomes vary with workflow maturity, digital readiness or owner-manager dependence. Case studies will examine employee capability and wellbeing, recognising that gains must not depend on work intensification. Deliverables will include an evaluation dataset, comparative findings and implementation evidence, establishing where SCALE-Decode adds value, where human expertise remains essential and which conditions support responsible adoption.

Work Package 4 (months 36-42) will integrate findings and translate them for research and practice. Outputs will include academic papers, reusable workflow passports, sector templates, checklists, an adviser toolkit, policy brief and public-engagement materials. Practitioner workshops will refine resources and inform future development. This package will convert evidence into usable guidance for SMEs, advisers, growth hubs, policymakers and technology providers.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Fermi surfaces in metallised 2D materials
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor:  Dr C R S Haines 

To realise the potential applications of 2D magnetic materials we must be able to manipulate both their magnetic and electronic properties. You will add electrons to a family of semiconducting 2D magnetic systems thereby tuning them into the metallic phase. You will then use measurements of the electronic properties to definitively characterise the nature of this metallic phase – crucial understanding for future application that has so far proved impossible to determine. This metallic state may well be novel due to strong electron correlations - in fact preliminary data strongly suggests this is the case. The nature of the magnetism in this metallic state remains an open question. There is evidence that this metallic state gives way to superconductivity at low temperatures. So far studies have focussed on accessing these states at extreme pressures. By using intercalation of alkali metals, you will access these states at ambient pressure (or low applied pressure) allowing definitive characterization and then exploitation of them. Understanding the metallic state is crucial for understanding the magnetism and superconductivity reported in these compounds. Furthermore, it will allow us to determine the way in which the Mott insulator state is destroyed and what kind of metallic state it gives way to when confined to two dimensions – a phenomenon which is widespread.

jobs.title: PhD Studnetship: Nonlinear Internal Waves Under Ice
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Internal waves occur in many stratified oceans, including ice-covered regions of the Arctic and Antarctic. This project will investigate the interaction between large solitary internal waves and sea ice, considering both continuous ice sheets and broken ice. Different models for the ice will be used. The waves can deform and displace the ice, while the presence and motion of the ice can, in turn, significantly modify the propagation and structure of the waves. Understanding this two-way interaction is important for improving our knowledge of wave–ice processes in polar regions. The project will combine applied mathematics, nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), and numerical modelling. Mathematical models capturing the key physical processes and nonlinear PDEs describing the coupled wave–ice system will be derived analytically. Numerical simulations will then be used to investigate the resulting wave dynamics and compared with fields data and experimental observations (see Carr et al. 2019).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Composite Phase Change Materials for Off-Grid Thermal Energy Storage
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Energy poverty remains a major challenge in rural regions of developing countries, where access to reliable grid electricity, heating and domestic hot water is limited. Thermal energy storage (TES) offers a promising approach for capturing waste heat and surplus thermal energy from off-grid solar, biomass sources, and processes. Phase change materials (PCMs) are central to this strategy due to their high energy density and isothermal transition. However, PCMs suffer from low thermal conductivity and phase separation during cycling, which limits their practical deployment. Recent developments in composite PCMs (CPCM), e.g. incorporation of conductive fillers, encapsulation, and form-stable matrices, have led to significant improvements in thermal performance and durability. These innovations open up new possibilities for designing TES systems tailored to off-grid rural applications like water heating, space heating, and cooking.

Aim

This project aims to design, develop, and evaluate CPCMs integrated into compact TES systems to deliver off-grid households heating and domestic hot water. A prototype unit will be conceptualised and optimised for off-grid rural applications.

Objectives

Formulate CPCM with enhanced thermal conductivity, shape stability, cyclability.

Evaluate CPCM thermal properties under real-life cycling.

Identify efficient manufacturing procedures for TES CPCM module.

Design, build and test a CPCM TES module.

The project will benefit from a possible co-tutelle with Dr Bennett (UTS Sydney), subject to institutional approval, and co-supervision with UEA Thermofluids research partners including HSLU CC Thermal Energy Storage and University of Birmingham.

CPCMs will be developed using PCM combined with shape-stabilisers and enhanced with thermally conductive additives. Materials will be characterised for melting point, latent heat, thermal conductivity, stability. A TES module will be modelled in ANSYS to simulate heat transfer under intermittent solar heating. A prototype system will be designed, fabricated and tested in a laboratory environment simulating charging and thermal demands typical of rural homes.

Entry requirements

The standard minimum entry requirement is 2:1 in Mechanical Engineering, Energy Engineering, Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Chemistry, Chemical Physics, Material Science.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: 2-Representation Theory and Applications to Representation Theory and Number Theory
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
In the last 20 years, categorification has started to play an important role in representation theory. For example, categorifications of algebras such as quantum groups and Hecke algebras have led to proofs or counterexamples of major conjectures, such as proofs of Broué’s abelian defect group conjecture for symmetric groups and the Kazhdan—Lusztig conjectures for all Coxeter types, as well as counterexamples to James’ conjecture and Lusztig’s conjecture.

This success has led to a desire to understand the categorified structures by studying their representation theory. Where in classical representation theory an algebra acts on vector spaces by linear transformations, in the categorified version a 2-category (categorifying the algebra) acts on categories (categorifying the vector space) by functors. Since functors have morphisms between them (so-called natural transformations), we obtain an extra layer of data that gives additional information about the algebra we originally wanted to study. On the other hand, the natural transformations often form algebras that we are already interested in and we obtain categorical actions on their representation categories.

The most important examples include:

1) categorifications of quantum groups, where applications are obtained by analysing the action of these categorified quantum groups on suitable (derived) categories of representation of p-adic general linear groups with the aim to translate this information through the local Langlands correspondence to obtain new information on questions in number theory.

2) categorifications of Hecke algebras via Soergel bimodules, which have very interesting and only partially understood 2-representation theory in their own right, as well as applications to the representation theory of algebraic groups through studying the categorification of the anti-spherical module.

This PhD project will study some of these examples, for which it will also be necessary to develop the abstract theory further.

Entry requirements

The standard minimum entry requirement is 2:1 in Mechanical Engineering, Energy Engineering, Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Chemistry, Chemical Physics, Material Science.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Nonlinear waves in axisymmetric geometries
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
The classical water wave problem provides a foundational framework for modelling gravity waves on liquid surfaces—from ocean swells to river flows. Incorporating additional physical mechanisms such as capillarity (surface tension), electrical forces, and shear fields reveals extraordinarily rich physical phenomena and complex wave dynamics. While traditional models focus on waves over flat base states, this research will tackle water-wave dynamics in non-flat geometries. Axisymmetric systems (such as waves on the surface of a liquid jet) provide a fertile ground for exploring and understanding novel wave propagation phenomena in regimes where the underlying no-wave state is inherently unstable.

In this project, you will address fundamental open challenges in fluid dynamical wave propagation on non-flat geometries. This will include, for example, studying conjugate flow solutions, solitary waves, and stabilization mechanisms. The project will involve the use of cutting-edge applied mathematics and modelling techniques, including numerical computation and asymptotic analysis. The student will develop a highly-valued skillset, developing expertise across theoretical mechanics, nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), computational modelling, and nonlinear mathematical methods.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Passive Phase Change Thermal Control for Perovskite Solar Cells in Space
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Mohammad Arqam 

Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are an emerging photovoltaic technology with exceptional power‑to‑weight ratios, making them ideal for small satellites and deep‑space missions where size, weight and power (SWaP) are critical. However, their extreme sensitivity to thermal cycling in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), where temperatures range from -150 °C to +150 °C, causes rapid degradation and limits lifespan. Existing spacecraft employ conventional thermal strategies, including passive measures such as multi‑layer insulation (MLI), coatings and radiators, as well as active systems like pumped fluid loops and thermoelectric coolers. While effective for large satellites, these are too rigid, heavy or power‑intensive for CubeSats, and none are tailored to PSC vulnerabilities. 

This project asks whether a passive phase‑change material (PCM) can close that gap. By absorbing and releasing latent heat across its melt transition, a PCM could hold cell temperature within a safe operating window (below ~60 °C) without power, pumps or moving parts. PCMs already buffer spacecraft electronics, but have never been co‑designed with a photovoltaic cell, and their transient behaviour in vacuum, where buoyancy‑driven melt convection is absent and heat transfer becomes conduction‑limited, remains uncharacterised. 

You will develop the underpinning heat‑transfer science. In UEA’s Thermofluids and Solar Energy laboratories you will build and validate transient models of PSC‑PCM stacks, formulate high‑conductivity PCM composites with PCM Products Ltd, and apply machine‑learning surrogate optimisation to trade thermal buffering against mass. Prototypes, using perovskite cells from the University of Surrey, will be characterised in UEA’s vacuum and climatic chambers under simulated solar load, with flight‑representative thermal‑vacuum qualification accessed through Space East’s industry network (SSTL, SuperSharp Space). 

You will graduate with rare expertise spanning thermofluids, energy materials and space systems, and a strong record of journal publications.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Human Referenced Colour Processing
jobs.description_html:
We live in an era where machine learning (ML) based systems can solve a wide variety of image-based problems. However, the architectures deployed are not biologically plausible and the training required to use them can be orders of magnitude more complex than that available to human vision. Further, there are still visual competences where we as human observers outperform even the most complex networks. One such competence is dynamic range compression (related to tone mapping) where an initial image has its dynamic range reduced. In dynamic range compression (DRC) a large 10,000:1 signal range e.g. images of scenes where there is strong sunlight and deep shadows - is compressed by two orders of magnitude to 100:1. The human vision systems and ML-based algorithms attempt to compress the dynamic range so that the bit-depth compressed image `looks good. DRC is a key component in all photographic processing pipelines.

In this project we will investigate the similarities and divergences between architectures for solving the dynamic range compression in human and machines. Our aim is to design an architecture that is consistent with human vision but where modern machine learning techniques might be deployed to optimise performance. Our work will build on Land and McCanns seminal Retinex theory [1], its interpretation in the context of known brain physiology [2] and its modern re-engineering as an effective numerical algorithm [3]. We will also investigate why the current non-human-vision-referenced ML algorithms produce poor results [4]. The research will take place in the Colour & Imaging Lab at the University of East Anglia.

[1] Land EH, McCann JJ. J Opt Soc Am. 1971;61(1):111.

[2] Hurlbert A. J Opt Soc Am A. 1986;3(10):16841693.

[3] Karami A, Finlayson G. London Imaging Meeting. 2024;5(1):1721.

[4] Karami A, Finlayson GD. AIC 2025. 2025; 143-148.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Integrating Migration Dynamics into Biodiversity Forecasts
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Marius Somveille 

Seasonal migration is a distinctive and ecologically important features of many animals. Yet migration also poses a profound challenge for conservation. The tools most commonly used to predict biodiversity responses to global change fail to capture the dynamic nature of these seasonal movements, leaving a major gap in our ability to forecast and manage migratory species effectively. 

Species Distribution Models (SDMs) are central to biodiversity forecasting. They use statistical associations between species’ observed occurrences and environmental variables to estimate where suitable habitats exist under current and future climate conditions. While powerful, SDMs are inherently static: they describe where suitable conditions occur but not how individuals move between them. For migratory species, this limitation is fundamental. 

This PhD project aims to fill that gap by integrating spatial population genomics with ecological niche modelling to predict how migratory connectivity responds to global change.  

You will integrate seasonal migration into an existing framework developed in the lab of co-supervisor Manica, which integrates SDM outputs with demographic processes (i.e., dispersal, colonisation, growth) and genetic evolution. Leveraging large movement and genomic datasets for birds, you will use this framework to (i) understand how global change has shaped migratory connectivity and (ii) forecast how migration is likely to change under future climate and land-use scenarios. 

The resulting forecasts will reveal where and when migratory connectivity may break down, providing direct guidance for conservation planning. The tools developed throughout the PhD could later be applied to other migratory taxa (e.g. mammals, fish). 

Training 

You will be part of a supportive and dynamic research environment at UEA and work closely with collaborators in Cambridge. You will receive hands-on training in spatial analysis, ecological modelling and genomics, while developing conceptual understanding and critical thinking in movement ecology and conservation. You will also build strong transferable and interdisciplinary research skills.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: New pharmacological tools for targeting P2X receptors in cancer
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy, and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
About the Project

Primary Supervisor - Dr Leanne Stokes

There is a growing literature documenting the exploitation of ion channels by cancer cells. P2X receptors are ligand-gated ion channels (P2X1-7) activated by the extracellular signalling molecule ATP. Concentrations of ATP are known to be high within tumour microenvironments potentially driving cellular adaptations and exploiting downstream signalling associated with P2X receptors. This project will undertake two main lines of investigation; i) to characterise the expression of important P2X receptors and their variants within cancer cells under different conditions, and ii) to determine the benefit of blocking various P2X receptors (either individually or through dual antagonism) to cancer cell growth and survival.

Aberrant splicing events are common within cancer and novel splice isoforms have the potential to be neo-antigens (e.g. targets for immunotherapy or markers for diagnostic/prognostic purposes). At least 18 splice variants of P2X7 have been described but very little is known about their expression levels and functionality. Nothing is known about P2X4 variants as yet. We will explore RNAseq data from public databases and together with quantitative PCR data, we will assemble this information. Our recent work has discovered compounds that can act as dual antagonists of P2X7 and P2X4 receptors and we will compare their efficacy to individual blockade of either P2X7 or P2X4.

The aims of the project are to 1) characterise splice variant expression of P2X7 and P2X4 receptors across a range of cancer cell lines and conditions, 2) generate P2X7 and P2X4-null cancer cells using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to further understand how these ion channels contribute to cancer cell biology, and 3) testing of dual antagonists of P2X7/P2X4 in in vitro cancer cell survival and growth assays. Skills developed: cell culture, molecular biology, gene editing and pharmacology plus transferable skills. This project would suit a graduate from Biomedical Science or Pharmacology.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Next-Generation Brushless Doubly Fed Generators: Electromagnetic Design and Optimisation
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Malihe Heidary 

Brushless Doubly Fed Machines (BDFMs) offer a promising solution for offshore wind energy applications due to their brushless operation, reduced maintenance requirements, and ability to operate with partially rated power converters. However, their wider adoption is limited by challenges such as relatively low torque density, complex electromagnetic interactions, and undesirable harmonic effects. 

This PhD project aims to develop advanced mathematical and electromagnetic modelling approaches to support the design and optimisation of high-performance BDFMs for offshore wind energy applications. 

A key focus will be the development of an accurate and computationally efficient analytical or Magnetic Equivalent Circuit (MEC) model capable of representing the complex magnetic interactions between the stator windings and rotor. Particular attention will be given to capturing the effects of rotor geometry, winding configurations, magnetic harmonics, and potentially magnetic saturation on machine performance. 

The developed model will be validated against Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and used to investigate the influence of key design parameters on electromagnetic torque, torque ripple, and power factor. Building on these findings, optimisation techniques will be applied to identify improved machine configurations, aiming to enhance torque density and overall electromagnetic performance. 

The project will contribute to the development of efficient modelling and design tools for next-generation BDFMs, supporting their potential application in reliable and cost-effective offshore wind energy systems.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Making drugs out of sunlight and “thin air”
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Michael Stephenson 

Could you uncover a hidden pathway to medicinally important plant molecules? 

Plants are extraordinary chemists, producing a diversity of complex molecules, many with valuable medicinal properties. But how they make some of these compounds remains a mystery. 

Join us at the University of East Anglia (UEA) to solve a puzzle in plant natural product biosynthesis: how are sesquiterpene coumarins, a rare and medicinally promising class of natural products, formed? 

This project will investigate a new hypothesis: that plants produce these compounds using an unexpected family of enzymes, related to the oxidosqualene cyclases involved in triterpene biosynthesis. Success will reveal an unknown biosynthetic mechanism and change our understanding of how these molecules evolved. 

Working at the interface of organic chemistry, synthetic biology and bioinformatics, you will search for and characterise these enzymes, investigate their evolutionary origins, and explore their potential to produce valuable natural products sustainably. 

You will use a plant-based expression platform, enabling you to investigate enzyme function, engineer biosynthetic pathways and produce compounds with potential pharmaceutical applications. 

Why should you apply? 

This project offers the opportunity to make a discovery while developing expertise across several advancing areas of chemical and biological research. 

Based in UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology, you will work with an interdisciplinary supervisory team with strong links to the wider Norwich Research Park, including the John Innes Centre. 

You will gain hands-on experience in techniques spanning bioinformatics, computational chemistry, molecular and synthetic biology, enzyme engineering, natural product chemistry and structural elucidation. From identifying candidate genes and engineering enzymes to isolating and characterising complex molecules, you'll develop a versatile skill set at the interface of chemistry and biology. 

If you're excited by molecular discovery, curious about how nature creates complex chemistry, and keen to develop new approaches to producing medicinally valuable compounds, apply now.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Reliable and Generalisable Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
jobs.description_html:
About the Project

Primary Supervisor - Dr Farhana Ferdousi Liza

Emerging techniques in model editing, also discussed in the literature as knowledge editing and memory editing, offer promising approaches for correcting erroneous or harmful information, incorporating specialised knowledge, and improving the usability, security, and accountability of large language models (LLMs). The overall aim of this PhD project is to develop and evaluate methods for reliable, localised, and generalisable knowledge updating in large language models. Using accessible open-weight language models suited to available computational resources, including NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada 48GB GPUs and UEA high-performance computing (HPC) facilities, you will adapt established editing methods, such as ROME and MEMIT, and compare them with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), external memory mechanisms, and conventional fine-tuning. Experiments will investigate how models can incorporate new information or knowledge, correct inaccurate information, and remove outdated or unwanted information while minimising unintended changes to existing capabilities. Evaluation will use established factual model-editing benchmarks, such as CounterFact and zsRE, supplemented where appropriate by a domain-specific dataset. Performance will be assessed in terms of editing efficacy (whether the target knowledge is successfully updated), generalisation (whether updates remain effective across paraphrases and related queries), locality (whether unrelated knowledge and capabilities are preserved), and retention (whether updates persist following subsequent edits or conflicting information). Further evaluations will examine factual consistency, general reasoning, and robustness to adversarial prompts. Where feasible, the project will also investigate knowledge provenance and update traceability to support accountability. Comparative experiments will establish the strengths, limitations, and trade-offs of different knowledge-updating approaches. You will also have the opportunity to deploy selected models in embodied AI systems or social robots, such as Furhat, and conduct human-AI interaction experiments to investigate how knowledge updates affect responses, consistency, and behaviour during real-time interactions. The project will contribute practical methods and empirical evidence for developing reliable, trustworthy, and accountable LLMs for knowledge-intensive applications.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Machine Learning-Guided Engineering of Next-Generation Cancer Therapeutics
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy, and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Amit Sachdeva

Monoclonal antibodies have transformed the treatment of cancer by selectively recognising tumour-associated receptors and triggering cellular responses that lead to cancer cell death. Despite their clinical success, conventional full-length antibodies often show limited effectiveness against solid tumours because their large molecular size restricts deep penetration into tumour tissue. Overcoming this challenge represents a major opportunity in the development of next generation cancer therapeutics.

This interdisciplinary PhD project aims to develop small, highly effective antibody fragments capable of penetrating solid tumours more efficiently than conventional antibodies. The student will employ state-of-the-art machine learning approaches to design novel antibody fragments. These computationally engineered molecules will then be expressed in Escherichia coli. The project will involve cloning, expression and purification of engineered antibody fragments, followed by detailed biochemical and biophysical characterisation. Their binding affinity to the target will be evaluated on cancer cell lines, using our previously developed methods. Furthermore, the most promising candidates will be equipped with non-canonical amino acids through synthetic biology approaches, enabling the introduction of new chemical functionalities to improve targeting, and therapeutic performance.

Working at the interface of chemistry, biology, and artificial intelligence, the successful candidate will gain extensive training in cutting-edge methodologies including machine learning-guided protein design, molecular cloning, recombinant protein expression, protein purification, cell-based assays, gel electrophoresis, Western blotting and chemical protein modification techniques. The project offers a unique opportunity to contribute to the development of next-generation biologic medicines while acquiring a highly sought-after multidisciplinary skillset spanning chemical biology, synthetic biology, biotechnology, and cancer research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Self-Supervised Learning for Sparse and Heterogeneous Spatio-Temporal Data

About the Project

Primary Supervisor - Professor Beatriz de la Iglesia

Can AI Learn When Data Are Scarce?

Artificial Intelligence is transforming our ability to understand and predict complex systems. But what happens when the data we need most are scarce, incomplete or irregularly collected? Can AI algorithms learn from the vast amounts of unlabelled information available and make reliable predictions with very few observations?

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Geometric and combinatorial inverse monoid theory
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
This PhD project is in the area of combinatorial algebra which is the study of algebraic objects like groups, and more generally monoids, defined in terms of a generating set, and a set of defining relations holding among those generators. For groups this topic is part of geometric group theory where ideas from geometry, topology, combinatorics and theoretical computer science (e.g. automata and formal language theory) are used to study infinite groups.

The main objects of study in this PhD project are a generalisation of groups called inverse monoids. While groups are an algebraic abstraction of permutations, and semigroups of arbitrary mappings, inverse monoids correspond 2to partial bijections and provide a framework for studying partial symmetries. Combinatorial and geometric inverse monoid theory is a much newer area of research than the corresponding theory for groups, and the main aim of this PhD project will be to build new theory and apply it to prove results about finitely presented inverse monoids.

In this project building on results of Gray, Silva and Szakács (2022), you will establish results that relate the geometry of Cayley graphs of inverse monoids to the algorithmic and algebraic properties of the monoid. You will also develop

new tools for the analysis of Schutzenberger graphs of inverse monoids and apply them to construct families of finitely presented inverse monoids with interesting and unexpected properties. In addition, developing ideas from Gray and Kambites (2025), you will investigate the relationship between properties of finitely presented inverse monoids and properties of groups associated with them and, building on work of Mangioni and Tesolin (2026), you will study the action of inverse monoids on directed metric spaces (and related ordered spaces) and prove results that relate properties of the inverse monoid to those of the space and the action.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Photon correlations and information dynamics in atomic ensembles and molecules
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Quantum optics provides powerful methods for determining and quantifying the quantum-mechanical nature of systems and processes, providing fundamental tools for the rapidly developing quantum technologies. Quantum-optical measurements become especially intriguing in systems such as atomic ensembles, or in molecules for processes whose quantum nature remains unclear. These open quantum systems can range from Markovian (“no memory”) to non-Markovian, where information is exchanged between system and environment. The relationships between light emission, quantum coherence, and non-Markovianity therefore become important both for fundamental physics and for eventual practical applications.

In this PhD project, we will develop the theory for interrogating systems ranging from atomic ensembles to molecules. Cooperative effects are known to enhance quantum behaviour in atomic arrays [1]. We ask how the quantum dynamics changes when such systems are placed in optical cavities [2]. We have previously shown that photon correlations can reveal information about the vibrational (phonon) dynamics of a molecule’s interactions with its environment [3]. We will extend this to, e.g., complex molecules, ultimately seeking to identify photonic signatures of non-Markovianity. For sufficiently Markovian systems, the photon-photon correlations can be computed using the quantum regression theorem together with a Lindblad equation for atomic ensembles or a HEOM model of a molecular system. For non-Markovian systems one must proceed with care but methods for computing correlation functions beyond the quantum regression theorem have been proposed [4]. An ultimate goal will be to develop these to allow accurate predictions of photon-correlation signatures where non-Markovianity can be a resource for quantum-information science.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The stability of superconducting neutron stars
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Neutron stars host the strongest known magnetic fields in the Universe, which appear to remain essentially stable and unchanged over decades. Simple models of neutron-star magnetic fields, however, all appear to suffer instabilities that rearrange and dissipate the field over mere seconds - and so these models are not representative of the real star.

A key stabilising ingredient is likely to be the fact that the star's core forms a superconductor - the only known setting in astrophysics for this phenomenon. More specifically, the neutron-star core contains a superconducting proton fluid that coexists with superfluid neutrons, and a (normal) electron fluid, and potentially other particle species too. The theory of superconductivity is well developed, but for the context encountered in labs on Earth: superconducting electrons in solid materials. This needs to be adapted carefully to be applicable to neutron stars.

This project entails studying the stability of magnetic fields in superconducting neutron stars. Initially, suitable steady-state background configurations will need to be created by solving the equilibrium equations for the model, followed by a perturbative analysis of the system to look for unstable modes. This will be done through two different approaches: one based on adapting the equations of magnetohydrodynamics, and another based on the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equations for a superconductor. Through this we will answer the question: does superconductivity stabilise neutron-star magnetic fields, or is a different mechanism required? With a reliable model for the magnetic field, we will then be able to calculate the expected gravitational-wave emission from magnetised neutron stars, and so determine whether this signal will be detectable in the near future.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Model Theory of Complex Powers
jobs.description_html:
About the Project

Primary Supervisor - Dr Jonathan Kirby

The field of complex numbers is in many ways the most elegant and important example of a mathematical structure in model theory. It has been the prototype for many developments in model theory, starting with strong minimality, as well as providing some of the most important applications where model-theoretic tools are applied to algebraic geometry.

After the field operations of addition and multiplication, raising to a fixed power is the most basic and universal operation in mathematics. However, the model theory of the complex field with fixed (irrational) powers is only just starting to be understood, following on from seminal work of Zilber which showed that when we restrict to a sufficiently generic power we get a superstable first-order theory. More recent work of Gallinaro and Kirby shows that the complex field with all complex powers is quasiminimal – the definable subsets are countable or co-countable – so in particular the real field is not definable.

This project will investigate both the algebra of these powered fields and the model theory, aiming to give a description of all the definable sets, and of their geometry. This geometry is intermediate between the algebraic geometry of algebraic varieties (which deals with polynomial equations only) and analytic geometry (which allows more general analytic functions).

Applicants should have some knowledge of mathematical logic or Galois theory or algebraic geometry. Knowledge of model theory would be an advantage, but is not essential. They are advised to contact Dr Kirby directly to discuss their application.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Alternative splicing regulation by snRNA modifications
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Alper Akay

How do snRNA modifications regulate RNA splicing? Our RNA (epi)genetics laboratory addresses this broad question using the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans as an animal model.  

RNA is at the centre of many gene regulatory processes. There are currently more than 150 distinct chemical modifications on RNA, and a greater number of proteins are required for their synthesis and recognition. Recent discoveries have shown that RNA modifications can be dynamically regulated, and they have been implicated in embryonic development, longevity, neurological diseases and cancers in humans and in animal models.  

The PhD project will focus on how spliceosomal snRNA modifications regulate RNA splicing. Our lab has shown that snRNA methylation can affect splice site choice during pre-mRNA splicing (1). The project will use molecular biology, genetics and RNA sequencing to investigate how gene-specific splice site choice influences transcript isoform expression in C. elegans and human cells. 

The project will be based in Dr Akay’s group and carried out in collaboration with the groups of Dr Wilfried Haerty and Dr James Smith. We offer a multidisciplinary and supportive research environment. The student will receive extensive support to learn a range of techniques and will interact with national and international laboratories working on RNA modifications. The student will attend conferences, seminars and cross-laboratory events. The student will receive internal and external mentorship and career development support. Our RNA (epi)genetics laboratory is funded by a prestigious UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship and provides generous resources and instrumentation. This project is particularly suitable for students interested in RNA biology, biochemistry and RNA sequencing analysis.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: New Dimensions in Ultrafast Spectroscopy with Structured Light
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Kayn Forbes

Ultrafast spectroscopy allows us to follow some of the fastest processes in nature, capturing the motion of energy, electrons and molecular excitations on femtosecond timescales. In this sense, it offers a route towards making “molecular movies”: watching how a system responds immediately after absorbing light and following its evolution in real time. Understanding these processes is important across areas such as solar-energy conversion, photocatalysis, optoelectronics and emerging quantum materials, where performance is often controlled by ultrafast energy flow and relaxation. 

At the same time, modern photonics allows light itself to be sculpted in increasingly sophisticated ways. Beyond colour and polarisation, we can control its spatial phase, intensity, angular momentum and three-dimensional structure. This PhD will bring these two areas together by developing time-resolved spectroscopy with structured light. 

The central aim is to determine whether specially designed ultrafast beams can reveal information about molecular and material dynamics that conventional spectroscopy cannot access. The project will begin with pump–probe spectroscopy, where one laser pulse excites a system and a second pulse tracks how it evolves, before extending these ideas towards multidimensional techniques such as 2D electronic spectroscopy. 

The student will combine analytical theory with computational modelling to predict new structured-light signatures in ultrafast measurements. Particular emphasis will be placed on identifying experimentally observable effects and understanding what new information they provide about excited-state dynamics. 

A key part of the project will be close collaboration with experimental groups, allowing theoretical predictions to guide measurements and, where possible, be tested directly in realistic molecular and material systems. 

No prior experience of ultrafast or 2D spectroscopy is required; the necessary techniques will be developed during the PhD.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Curvature, Topology and Nonlinear Excitations in Quantum Fluids
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Davide Proment

This PhD will explore an emerging frontier in quantum-fluid physics: the interplay between geometry, topology and nonlinear dynamics in superfluid helium films and ultracold Bose–Einstein condensates confined to curved two-dimensional surfaces. 

Recent advances are making it possible to create quantum fluids on spherical shells and other unusual geometries. Our recent work has revealed striking new physics on a sphere: rotating vortex dipoles can continuously transform into vortex-free Jones–Roberts solitary waves, which subsequently hybridize with collective modes associated with the spherical geometry [1]. You will build on these results to investigate how curvature and topology reshape vortices, solitons, sound, instabilities and quantum turbulence. 

Using analytical theory and large-scale numerical simulations of nonlinear quantum-fluid models, you will study systems ranging from spheres and tori to more general curved surfaces. How does topology constrain vortex configurations? Can curvature stabilise entirely new solitary waves? How does rotation generate vortices and turbulence on closed surfaces? What signatures could be observed experimentally? 

The project offers considerable freedom to pursue directions matching your interests, including connections to finite-temperature physics, many-body effects and quantum sensing. 

You will join an international research programme led by Dr Davide Proment at the University of East Anglia (UEA), with opportunities for research visits and close collaboration with theorists at the University of São Carlos (Brazil) and Universidad Rey Juan Carlos (Madrid), and experimentalists at Lancaster University and CNR-INO/LENS in Florence. 

Davide Proment is a theoretical and computational physicist working on quantum fluids, nonlinear waves, vortices and turbulence. You will join his international network of collaborators at UEA in Norwich, a vibrant city close to the Norfolk countryside and coast. For further information, contact d.proment@uea.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: AI-Driven Condition Monitoring System for Offshore Wind Generators
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Salman Abdi Jalebi

Reliability is essential to the continued expansion of wind power, particularly offshore, which contributes around 10–15% of UK electricity generation and plays a key role in achieving net-zero targets. Condition monitoring systems (CMSs) improve turbine reliability and availability by enabling preventive maintenance, reducing operational costs and the levelised cost of energy. However, drivetrain components, including gearboxes, generators and power electronics, remain major sources of failure, accounting for approximately one-third of incidents and nearly half of offshore turbine maintenance costs. 

Existing CMS solutions predominantly rely on vibration measurements using accelerometers mounted on drivetrain components. Their effectiveness is limited by missed or delayed fault detection, false alarms and poor sensitivity to electrical faults. Despite their potential, electrical measurement-based CMS solutions remain commercially underdeveloped, largely due to the complexity of interpreting electrical signatures associated with mechanical and electrical faults in real time. 

This project aims to address these limitations by developing advanced hybrid fault diagnosis methods that integrate physics-based analytical models of drivetrain behaviour with AI-driven data analysis techniques. The objective is to improve fault detection accuracy, early fault identification and fault classification while reducing false alarms. 

The research will combine analytical investigations, numerical simulations, finite element (FE) modelling and experimental development and validation. The anticipated outcome is a more reliable and effective condition monitoring approach for offshore wind generators, supporting predictive maintenance, reducing downtime and maintenance costs, and improving the long-term operational performance of offshore wind energy systems.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Development of Lossy Mode Resonance Optical Fibre Sensors for Energy Applications
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Keith M. Alcock

Through your insights and innovation, you will help shape the future of optical sensing for energy applications. The race is on to develop sensors that enable smarter, safer, and efficient energy systems. One technology to achieve this is Lossy Mode Resonance (LMR), which occurs when light guided in an optical fibre couples to a lossy mode in a suitably engineered thin-film coating, generating a characteristic attenuation band in the transmission spectrum. Changes in the properties of the coating or its surrounding environment shift the resonance wavelength, enabling highly sensitive measurements. LMR sensors can therefore monitor temperature, chemical species, humidity, and other parameters relevant to energy technologies. Recent demonstrations include temperature monitoring in lithium-ion batteries, illustrating their potential for energy storage. 

The project will examine how changes in fibre geometry, thin-film composition, and fabrication technique influence LMR sensor performance in energy environments. It will also address the miniaturisation of established sensor designs, supporting integration into compact energy-monitoring systems. 

Your research will allow you to: 

  •  Explore sensor geometries to understand their influence on sensitivity and robustness. 

  •  Investigate thin-film materials, including metal oxides, conducting polymers, and hybrid coatings, for optical, chemical, and thermal stability in energy-system environments. 

  •  Develop manufacturing methods, including spin and dip-assisted layer-by-layer coatings, for reproducible and scalable fabrication. 

  •  Miniaturise current LMR sensor prototypes for integration into energy systems such as battery packs, and solar panels. 

You will join a growing international team at the University of East Anglia (UEA) and the Institute of Carbochemistry (ICB) in Spain, developing and applying LMR optical fibre sensors. You will have the opportunity to undertake a research stay at ICB, gaining hands-on experience with complementary expertise and facilities. Training in advanced analytical and experimental techniques at both institutions will support you in developing new approaches for optical fibre sensors for energy applications.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Stabilised Gold Nanoclusters for Intracellular Catalysis
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Sophie Thomas

The ability to perform selective chemical reactions inside living cells offers exciting opportunities for chemical biology, biotechnology, and medicine. This PhD project will explore the design, synthesis, and biological application of atomically precise gold nanoclusters stabilised by N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) ligands for use as intracellular catalysts. 

NHC ligands form exceptionally strong bonds to gold and provide a versatile platform for tuning nanocluster stability, solubility, and catalytic activity. The successful candidate will develop water-soluble NHC ligands and use them to prepare well-defined gold nanoclusters with controlled sizes and surface properties. The project will investigate how ligand structure influences nanocluster formation, stability, catalytic performance, cellular uptake, and behaviour in complex biological environments.

Emphasis will be placed on exploiting these nanoclusters as catalysts for abiotic reactions within living cells, including the activation of fluorogenic probes and therapeutic prodrugs. The modular nature of NHC ligands will also enable the incorporation of targeting functionalities, such as antibodies, peptides, carbohydrates, or other biomolecule-recognition motifs, allowing future generations of nanoclusters to be directed towards specific cell types, intracellular compartments, or disease-associated biomarkers. Understanding how catalyst design affects intracellular reactivity will provide fundamental insights into the emerging field of bioorthogonal catalysis. 

This highly interdisciplinary project combines synthetic inorganic and organometallic chemistry, nanomaterials science, spectroscopy, and cell biology. Training will include the synthesis of NHC ligands and gold nanoclusters, characterisation by NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, UV-Vis and fluorescence spectroscopies and electron microscopies, together with cell culture, fluorescence imaging and biological evaluation. 

The project is suitable for ambitious applicants with a background in chemistry, pharmaceutical sciences, materials science, or a related discipline, who are looking to work at the chemistry-biology interface. Experience in synthetic chemistry is desirable but not essential. The outcomes may lead to new catalytic nanomedicines and chemical tools capable of controlling molecular processes directly within living systems.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Intelligent Coordination of Aerial and Ground Vehicles for Future Urban Mobility
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Xu Zhang

Urban mobility is undergoing rapid transformation through advances in autonomous aerial systems, electric vehicles (EVs), artificial intelligence, and connected transport technologies. While drones offer flexibility and rapid access to locations that may be difficult or inefficient to reach by road, ground vehicles provide greater carrying capacity, endurance, and access to established transport and energy infrastructure. Coordinating these complementary capabilities creates new opportunities for more efficient, sustainable, and responsive urban mobility systems. 

This PhD project will investigate intelligent coordination between autonomous aerial systems and ground vehicles, particularly EVs, for future urban mobility applications. Rather than operating aerial and ground vehicles independently, the research will explore how they can cooperate in activities such as urban logistics, sensing, infrastructure monitoring, and other emerging city services. Key challenges include deciding how tasks should be allocated across heterogeneous vehicles, when and where vehicles should interact, and how routing, scheduling, charging and energy use can be jointly managed under dynamic urban conditions.

The project will develop optimisation and intelligent decision-making approaches for coordinating air–ground mobility systems in real time. Depending on the research direction, this may involve mathematical optimisation, scheduling algorithms, simulation, machine learning, or multi-agent decision-making. Particular attention will be given to dynamic demands, limited vehicle energy, heterogeneous operational capabilities, and the scalability of coordination across multiple vehicles. 

Ultimately, the research aims to advance integrated air–ground mobility from independently operated vehicles towards intelligent, cooperative systems capable of supporting efficient and sustainable urban services.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Legal Geographies of Vehicle Dwelling
jobs.description_html:
Applications are invited for a funded PhD studentship with the Manchester Law School at Manchester Metropolitan University. This socio-legal research project will explore the everyday legalities and mobilities of vehicular dwelling.   

Vehicular dwelling sits uneasily within legal and spatial categories designed around fixed forms of residence. As people increasingly live, travel and work from vehicles, they move through legal and jurisdictional spaces, encountering a range of legal processes: parking and traffic regulation; insurance; social care; health; employment; education; planning and waste management, each overlaid by a longstanding legal tension around the public/private divide. Drawing on legal geography and mobilities scholarship, this project understands vehicular dwelling as a form of everyday mobility through which law, movement and dwelling are continually negotiated. 

Exploring ‘van life’ as a specific form of vehicular dwelling, this project expands on the aspirational and/or touristified framing of this way of life to scrutinise inequities, immobility and systemic legal inadequacies faced by vehicle dwellers. 

Objectives

This project aims to examine how mobile forms of dwelling are governed and regulated.

Research Objectives: 

  • To map the plural legal and regulatory frameworks encountered through vehicular dwelling. 
  • To understand vehicle dwellers' everyday experiences of these legal and regulatory frameworks and how they shape mobility practices. 
  • To understand what these encounters reveal about the normative assumptions underpinning law and its privileging of fixed forms of dwelling. 

Funding

This studentship is open to home and international applicants. Home and international tuition fees will be covered for the duration of the 3-year award.  

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. These payments are set at a level determined by the UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27. 

Candidate requirements

  • A postgraduate degree (or equivalent) in the subject of law or a field demonstrably relevant to the area of research inquiry (together with a first-class or upper second class undergraduate degree in a related subject). 
  • Excellent written and oral communication skills in English. 
  • Enthusiasm for multidisciplinary research and innovative methodologies.
