jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Board Approaches to Workforce Engagement, Employee-Perceived Effectiveness, and Sustainable Corporate Efficiency in UK Firms
jobs.description_html:
This project intends to examine how workforce engagement mechanisms recommended by the UK Corporate Governance Code relate to sustainable corporate efficiency through employees perceived effectiveness. The Code recommends that boards engage with their workforce through one or more of three mechanisms: a workforce director, workforce advisory panel, or designated non-executive director. These provisions reflect the Financial Reporting Councils view that effective workforce engagement can contribute to long-term sustainable growth.

However, given the UKs long-standing shareholder-primacy model and differences in how these mechanisms enable employees to communicate with boards and influence strategic and monitoring decisions, whether they shape employees perceived effectiveness and, in turn, sustainable corporate efficiency remains under-explored.

The project intends to address this gap by combining primary survey data on employees perceived effectiveness with secondary firm-level data on engagement mechanisms and sustainable corporate efficiency.

Objectives

The project aims to examine how workforce engagement mechanisms recommended by the UK Corporate Governance Code relate to sustainable corporate efficiency and whether employees perceived effectiveness of engagement explains this relationship.

The objectives are to:

  • Assess whether employees perceived effectiveness of workforce engagement differs across the Code-recommended mechanisms.
  • Examine the association between different workforce engagement mechanisms and sustainable corporate efficiency.
  • Investigate whether employees perceived effectiveness of workforce engagement mediates the relationship between the engagement mechanism adopted and sustainable corporate efficiency.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - From Fan to Father: Exploring the Role of Football Fan Communities in Supporting New Fatherhood
jobs.description_html:
We are pleased to announce the opportunity for a funded PhD project within the Faculty of Business and Law. The project will explore the role of football fan communities in supporting new fathers as they start their fatherhood journey. While many men aspire to greater involvement in childcare, they often feel excluded from traditional parenting support, which is frequently oriented towards mothers. The project will explore whether football fan communities, which provide strong social bonds and a sense of belonging for many men, can act as sources of support during early fatherhood.   

While scholarship has explored how parenthood impacts sports fandom, this has often prioritised the voice of mothers. This project will use qualitative research methods to explore the transformative potential of sports fan communities to support new fathers in their parenting roles and practices. The project has potential to make a significant impact, informing practice within sports clubs and governing bodies. 

Objectives

The project will explore the role of football fan communities as sites of social support during the transition to first-time fatherhood. Specifically, the project is organised around three interrelated strands of inquiry: identity transformation, social support, and masculinity and belonging.

  • To explore how first-time fathers negotiate and reconstruct their identities as both football fans and parents during the transition to fatherhood.
  • To identify what forms of support (e.g., emotional, informational and practical) football fan communities provide to first-time fathers, and how these forms of support are experienced by fathers themselves.
  • To explore how football fan communities shape, reinforce or challenge understandings of masculinity and fatherhood during the transition to first-time parenthood. 

Funding

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Digital State Capitalism in International Business: Geopolitics, Digital Sovereignty and Techno-Nationalism
jobs.description_html:
This PhD explores how dynamic geopolitical rivalry expressed through digitalisation strategies and techno-nationalism changes the relationship between states and international businesses. It examines how governments seek technological independence and how businesses respond to new opportunities, restrictions and pressures. 

You will compare countries with different political-economic systems to investigate emerging forms of ‘digital state capitalism’, or how states shape digital markets to pursue economic, security and political goals. Your findings will help businesses and policymakers understand the consequences of digitalisation strategies for international trade, innovation and business decision-making. 

Through comparative case studies, policy analysis and business and media data, you will develop skills in research design, critical analysis and communicating complex findings. You will draw on university databases and digital resources, supported by supervisors specialising in international business and state–business relations. 

Objectives

The study asks: 

  • How are geopolitical rivalries transforming how states use digital technologies to influence international business? 
  • How do states use regulatory, financial, infrastructural and organisational mechanisms to pursue different digitalisation strategies that seek to increase their technological autonomy? 
  • How do these mechanisms and resulting forms of digital state capitalism vary across different political-economic systems? 
  • How do MNEs respond to these interventions, and what are the consequences of their internationalisation strategies? 
  • What are the consequences and outcomes for international trade, investment, and innovation?

Funding

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (Re)claiming and (Re)shaping Place: The Economics and Geography of Women’s Football Stadiums
jobs.description_html:
We are excited to announce the opportunity to apply for a funded PhD project within the Manchester Metropolitan University’s Faculty of Business and Law. The project will examine how stadium infrastructure arrangements contribute to the development of women’s football and the places in which the game is experienced. Using comparative case studies and mixed methods, the research will explore how stadiums influence supporter attachment, identity and legitimacy, and how these processes relate to attendance and economic outcomes.

The project offers an opportunity to contribute to the rapidly expanding field of women’s football research while engaging with leading research communities in sport policy, place management and applied sports economics.

Objectives

The project has four main objectives:

  • To develop a conceptual framework explaining how stadium infrastructure contributes to placemaking in women’s football.
  • To examine how different infrastructure arrangements shape attachment, identity, and legitimacy.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Operationalising Artificial Intelligence in Elite Sport Organisations: Readiness, Governance and Integration Pathways
jobs.description_html:
This PhD tests a new explanation: readiness for AI depends not only on money, staff and data, but on an organisation's relationships with technology suppliers, regulators and peers. Working across football, cricket and basketball, including women's professional sport, you will investigate how organisations move from experimenting with AI to embedding it, and help create a practical diagnostic tool for the sector.

You will gain advanced skills in case study research, interviewing and social network analysis while working with decision makers in sport, and you will be encouraged to shape the research design.

You will design and lead a comparative multiple case study of how clubs adopt and govern technology. The fieldwork combines semi-structured interviews with senior decision makers and social network analysis of the relationships between clubs, technology providers, leagues and governing bodies. You will receive training in case study design, qualitative interviewing and analysis, and network methods, including data collection, measurement and modelling. The research will examine whether current governance arrangements for technology reduce or widen resource and performance inequalities between clubs, and the results will feed directly into policy discussions with partners in the sport.

Objectives

  • Explore how data quality and interoperability, undermined by conflicting standards across vendors, leagues and governing bodies, constrain AI deployment.
  • Explore and understand what organisational and technical factors shape integration of AI systems with legacy and outsourced infrastructures, and the trade-offs imposed.
  • Explore how ESOs reconcile short-term operational gains with long-term capability building, and how technical debt accumulates through AI procurement.
  • Analyse how governance, regulation and position within the technology ecosystem shape unequal organisational capacity to operationalise AI.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How Hematopoietic Transcription Factors and Epigenetic Coregulators Shape Gene Regulatory Networks in Immune Cell Development
jobs.description_html:
This is a 4-year PhD studentship to join the group of Dr Tianyi Zhang in the Department of Cancer and Genomics Sciences at the University of Birmingham. This is a competition funded PhD through the Midlands Integrative Biosciences Training Partnership and is open to UK, EU, and International students.

Project
Transcription factors (TFs) and epigenetic coregulators cooperate to drive gene expression programmes that control cellular development. Ikaros is a hematopoietic TF that plays an essential role in the development of B cell and T cells, white blood cells that are crucial for healthy immune function. Ikaros also acts as a tumour suppressor that is highly mutated in progenitor B and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Previous proteomic and functional biochemical studies from the lab have mapped key Ikaros partners, including the NuRD chromatin remodeller and HDAC complex, factors involved in the formation of repressive heterochromatin, SWI/SNF chromatin remodellers, and HAT coactivators. Several of these novel TF-coregulator molecular interfaces have been elucidated, while others remain to be identified. Moreover, mechanisms of how TFs such Ikaros direct the epigenetic activity of different coregulators to genomic targets with spatial-temporal precision during cellular differentiation remains poorly understood.

The aim of this PhD programme is to 1) uncover the molecular interfaces that mediate these key interactions 2) dissect how Ikaros partners with epigenetic coregulators to shape the chromatin landscape and gene regulatory networks 3) determine the impact of different Ikaros mutants in immune cell development in an vivo zebrafish model. This research project will reveal the molecular workings of a key driver of immune cell development, and in later years explore how other TFs cooperate with Ikaros or utilise similar mechanisms to exert their gene-regulatory functions.

Jointly supervised by Dr. Tianyi Zhang and Dr. Rui Monteiro, this project will provide comprehensive training in biochemistry, molecular biology, proteomics, genomics, and the use of cellular, cancer, and zebrafish model systems. The PhD student will be embedded in a broader research programme supported by Wellcome Trust funding.

Applicants should have a first-class or upper second-class honours undergraduate degree, a Master’s degree and/or relevant research experience in areas including biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics and bioinformatics. Proven research track record appropriate to career stage, strong analytical ability, communication skills and enthusiasm for collaborative research is essential. We are committed to building a diverse and inclusive research community, and welcome applications from talented candidates from all backgrounds regardless of age, disability, ethnicity, gender identity, religion, sexual orientation, or socioeconomic background.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship|: Polymergeddon Rise of the Osmotic Pressure
jobs.description_html:
Polymers are everywhere, and they're built to last. Their strength and chemical stability make them incredibly useful, but also frustratingly difficult to destroy. Here in the Fielden group (www.fieldengroup.net), we think it's time they were held accountable. We're exploiting their own chemical properties to engineer their downfall.

We use organic supramolecular chemistry to create a molecular tug-of-war that controls how molecules move between materials. By pulling monomer units out of polymers, we will break them down one unit at a time.

Controlling the equilibrium between monomers and polymers will create dynamic, shape-shifting materials that can adapt, transform and even dismantle themselves on demand. This opens up exciting possibilities, from developing more sustainable, responsive plastics to creating new methods for molecular barcoding and anti-counterfeiting.

The project

This PhD project will subject polymer nanoparticles to osmotic pressure, our method of choice for initiating Polymergeddon. By designing reaction systems in which monomers can diffuse away from their parent polymers, you will investigate how to dismantle polymers into their constituent building blocks.

Using state-of-the-art polymerisation methods, you will explore reversible depolymerisation under a range of conditions, with different reaction media and catalysts, including emulsions and nanoparticles. You will synthesise and characterise polymers, then investigate how to trigger their disassembly by coupling depolymerisation with other chemical reactions or changes in phase behaviour. Finally, you will use these discoveries to develop dynamic materials in which monomers can be exchanged between different polymers, opening up new ways to control their composition and properties.

Training and mentoring

We are looking for curious, enthusiastic researchers who are keen to experiment, think differently and shape their own projects as new discoveries emerge. This project offers plenty of scope to explore unexpected ideas, develop new chemical approaches and take the research in exciting new directions. It would suit motivated students with backgrounds in supramolecular, polymer or synthetic organic chemistry who want to push the boundaries of what molecules and materials can do.

You will gain broad experience in organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, nanoscale characterisation, NMR and electron microscopy. You’ll also have opportunities to collaborate with other research groups to gain expertise in SAXS, SANS and microscopy, attend conferences, and shape the direction of your own project.

You will receive close mentoring in project design, writing, and presentation skills. Thanks to more than £3 million in support from the EPRSC, an ERC Starting Grant and a Royal Society Dorothy Hodgkin Fellowship, there is additional enhanced funding for training and travel. You will be well prepared for a career across all areas of science and technology.

Application process

Interested candidates should contact Steve by email in the first instance with a copy of their CV and a covering letter outlining their research interests. Applicants should have obtained a strong Master's degree in chemistry or a related discipline. There is no closing date but please apply as soon as possible since the position will be filled as soon as the right candidate is found.

The School of Chemistry is keen to achieve a gender and diversity balance across the School and welcome applicants from all backgrounds.

Due to funding restrictions, non self-funded applicants not eligible for UK home fee status will only be considered in exceptional circumstances. Self-funded students are always welcome to contact Steve to discuss their situation further.

jobs.title: PhD Studentships in Applied Mathematics for Formulated Products
jobs.description_html:
Two fully-funded 3.5-year PhD studentships (covering UK home student fees and an annual stipend of £21,805) is available in Applied Mathematics for Formulated Products. The PhD will be under the supervision of Professor Rosemary Dyson, in the School of Mathematics (in the College of Engineering and Physical Sciences), and interface with the SUM4Products Network.

Background

The formulated product sector influences many aspects of everyday life- the sector is responsible for producing food and drink, personal-care products, cosmetics, washing and cleaning products, and medicines. Due to the wide scope of the formulations sector, it contributes a staggering £142bn (GVA) to the UK economy each year.

There is a growing shift in the sector towards the rapid development of smarter, greener, and more personalised products. This includes:

  • Developing high-quality, nutritious, and sustainable foods that reduce fat and sugar use without compromising the flavour and texture profiles demanded by consumers.
  • The rapid formulation of medicines, therapeutics, and foods to provide cost-effective and personalised products to different age/health groups
  • Reformulation of existing products to incorporate new ingredients in response to regulatory changes or shortages, or to avoid degradation due to time in storage.

Despite their variety, companies across the sector face shared challenges in processing, engineering and performance. Mathematics is the key to unlocking innovation and addressing these complexities. They all require new, predictive models that can link the processing and microstructure of formulated products to their final function and performance.

What you will do

Your degree programme will be the Applied Mathematics PhD. You will conduct mathematical modelling of formulated products, working with experimental data provided by industry partners. Examples of projects include examining fluid dynamics of thermal change, modelling taste release of chocolate, modelling sustainable beverage emulsions.

You will be part of a team working on diverse collaborative research opportunities with industry partners. Your final PhD project will likely have a cross-cutting theme, which will have multiple industry uses and applications. There may be a possibility of conducting a research internship with one of our industry partners.

You will have play a key role in researching new interdisciplinary methods for mathematical modelling in the formulation sector. You will gain experience working directly with industry on real-life challenges and made connections which will shape your future career.

Who we are looking for:

  • Candidates should have a first-class master’s level degree (or equivalent) in Mathematics, Chemical Engineering, or related discipline at the time of taking up the position
  • Candidates should be able to learn new mathematical approaches and be experimental in their approach.
  • Candidates will be expected to represent the University with industry and academic partners and should demonstrate experience in working collaboratively in a range of team contexts
  • Prior exposure and knowledge about mathematical modelling and continuum mechanics in applied contexts would be an advantage
  • Eligibility for the studentship is limited to UK / Home students or Overseas students who have secured other sources of funding to cover the difference in fees.

We strongly encourage an informal conversation with Professor Rosemary Dyson prior to submitting a formal application. Please send a covering email to r.j.dyson@bham.ac.uk (copying in sum4products@contacts.bham.ac.uk), including a short summary of your research interests and suitability for the position and a CV, to arrange a conversation. We recommend getting in touch as soon as possible to discuss your interests.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Metagenomic insights into respiratory microbiome dynamics across the disease severity spectrum
jobs.description_html:
Respiratory infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality, however, important gaps remain in our understanding of their aetiology, early risk stratification, and the role of microbial communities in disease.

This project will apply advanced computational methods to analyse large-scale metagenomic sequencing data from patients across the respiratory disease severity spectrum, ranging from adults presenting with respiratory symptoms in A&E to patients with severe pneumonia in intensive care. The project aims to define how the respiratory microbiome changes with disease severity.

Initial work will focus on microbial profiling and genome reconstruction to characterise bacterial, viral, and fungal communities. Particular attention will be given to the virome, including bacteriophages and anelloviruses, as potential indicators of microbial imbalance and disease progression. The project will investigate interactions between microbes, with a focus on phage–bacteria dynamics, and define ecological states associated with stable and disrupted communities. Machine learning models will then be developed to integrate bacterial, viral, and ecological microbiome features for improved pathogen detection, severity classification, and early identification of patients at risk of deterioration. The project will deliver both fundamental insights into respiratory microbial ecology and practical computational tools with potential clinical application.

The aims of this project include:

• To characterise the respiratory microbiome across a spectrum of disease severity and antibiotics exposure, using metagenomic sequencing data.
• To investigate interactions between bacteria, viruses including bacteriophages, and other microbes, and define ecological states of infection.
• To develop and validate predictive models for pathogen detection, disease severity classification, and risk of clinical deterioration.
• To assess the role of the virome as a complementary source of diagnostic and prognostic information.

This project requires a computational/bioinformatics background and will provide exposure to clinical and public health research. It offers opportunities to collaborate with clinicians and microbiologists, supporting the development of both technical and translational skills.

Supervisors: Professor Nick Loman, Dr Meera Chand and Dr Sofia Morfopoulou.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Designing synthetic proteins for sustainable control of fungal plant diseases
jobs.description_html:
Fungal pathogens are expert manipulators of their plant hosts, which they achieve through secreting effector proteins which disable host defences. However, sometimes effectors are recognised by plant immune receptors to trigger rapid defence responses. Effectors are therefore both an asset for the pathogen, and a weakness, as they can potentially activate host immunity.

We want to take cutting-edge advances in AI-based protein biology to design synthetic proteins that can help plants fend off fungal pathogens. These synthetic proteins will either (1) directly bind to fungal effectors to stop them working, or (2) be incorporated into immune receptors to confer a new recognition ability to the host plant. We recently identified a number of immune-suppressing effectors from the wheat pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici which we will use as targets in this project.

The student will learn computational protein design pipelines (eg. RFdiffusion, BindCraft) and produce both effectors and synthetic proteins in heterologous expression systems (bacterial, yeast, insect). Pairwise interactions will be tested in vitro by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) or microscale thermophoresis (MST) in collaboration with the lab of Prof. Andy Lovering. Protein interactions in plants will be tested using Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana. We anticipate that the highest affinity interactions will be both detectable by ITC/MST and modify effector phenotypes in plants. This project will be an important proof-of-concept that AI-designed synthetic proteins can interact with pathogen effectors and either suppress their activity, or allow us to build new immune receptors to bolster plant defence.

For informal enquiries, please contact Dr Graeme Kettles at g.j.kettles@bham.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The hidden immune system of fungi uncovering the roles of NLR genes
jobs.description_html:
NLR genes play important roles as the sensors/receptors of non-self molecules and in activation of immune responses. The role of NLRs in immunity has been thoroughly described for plants and animals, but how they contribute to the fungal immune system is unknown. Fungal NLR genes also show hugely increased diversity of N- and C-terminal domains in comparison to their plant and animal counterparts, suggesting that fungal NLRs may have interesting and unique functions not previously described. Our goal is to understand how NLR genes contribute to the cryptic fungal immune system.

To achieve this, we will use the genetically tractable model fungus Zymoseptoria tritici. This wheat pathogen has a complement of 20 NLRs, a comparatively small number compared to other ascomycete fungi. This makes it an appealing system to study how this gene family contributes to diverse processes such as fungal-bacterial interactions, self-incompatibility and host plant interactions.

This project will provide training in diverse techniques related to molecular and cellular biology, bioinformatics and protein biochemistry. A key activity will be the generation of fungal gene knockout strains for subsequent characterisation. In addition, high-throughput screens of microbial collections will be used to identify antagonistic interactions between specific fungal or bacterial species. RNAseq profiling of the fungal transcriptome during interactions with other microbes will be used to identify gene networks important for a coordinated immune response. Confocal fluorescence microscopy will be employed for direct visualisation of microbe-microbe interactions using labelled reporter strains. Finally, proximity labelling techniques such as TurboID will be used to identify key protein-protein interactions during fungal immune responses.

For informal enquiries, please contact Dr Graeme Kettles at g.j.kettles@bham.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Biomimetic Foldamers as a New Class of Sustainable Catalysts
jobs.description_html:
Foldamers are synthetic oligomers that adopt stable conformations bio-inspired (e.g., helices) but their solid forms have recently been shown to have functional applications in materials science, supramolecular chemistry and biological chemistry. Foldamers possess excellent bio- and environmental-compatibility and, due to their modular system design, have highly tuneable molecular properties. Importantly, we have shown that the compressibility and molecular dipole of foldamers can be readily and widely tuned. Hence, given their bio- and environmental-compatibility and highly tuneable nature, this makes biomimetic foldamers ideal candidates in the search for new sustainable catalysts.

Objective: This project will establish foldamers as a new class of bio- and environmentally-compatible sustainable catalysts, which are highly tuneable for use in green synthesis of functional organic molecules.

Methodology: The project requires a combination of organic chemistry synthesis and advanced analytical study including computational analysis to generate the novel foldamers and to assess their performance as sustainable catalysts. This work will be carried out under the supervision of Drs. Pike and Michalchuk in the Department of Chemistry.

The project will be supervised by Dr Sarah Pike and Dr Adam Michalchuk.

Candidates should check their eligibility on the Midlands Integrative Biosciences Training Partnership CDT website (https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/cross_fac/mibtp) before applying.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Understanding Intrinsically Disordered Protein-Protein Interactions Using Peptidomimetics
jobs.description_html:
Understanding and modulating protein-protein interactions (PPIs) is a key objective in understanding both healthy and disease processes,[1] and, for providing leads to develop new treatments for diseases of unmet medical need.[2] This project will develop methods to target the interactions of intrinsically disordered regions engaged in PPIs.

The β-strand is the second most abundant secondary structure (20-30%) and bioinformatics analyses have established that ~16% of PPIs have an interfacial β-strand.[3] The student will systematically explore backbone amide modification across a series of peptidomimetics designed to inhibit β-strand-mediated PPIs, specifically by: (a) biasing the conformational ensemble towards one that excludes unproductive low energy conformers; and, (b) increasing the rate of target binding. They will use N-alkylation[4] (which is already known to enhance cell-uptake and suppress proteolysis),[5] alongside amides→thioamide substitution. High-resolution structural methods will be used to understand the molecular determinants and mechanism of binding. Peptidomimetics will be prepared using automated solid-phase peptide synthesis and studied with structural biophysical methods to understand their conformational ensembles in the presence and absence of their target protein (using fluorescence anisotropy, surface plasmon resonance isothermal titration calorimetry and cutting edge 2D NMR experiments).

Supervisors: Professor Andy Wilson and Professor Teresa Carlomagno

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: PhD in an Integrated Intelligent Safe Environment (IISE) in the Nuclear Industry
jobs.description_html:
The nuclear industry is increasingly seeking to deploy robotic and autonomous systems were possible to reduce worker exposure to hazardous environments, improve productivity and enhance operational resilience. Whilst significant progress has been made in remote operations, a major barrier we currently still find is the ability for robots and operators to work collaboratively within the same safety envelope.

Current safety approaches generally require physical segregation, exclusion zones or reduced robot operating modes, with, in some cases, complete removal of personnel. This can limit the potential benefits we could realise with autonomy and prevents effective human-robot coexistence in complex nuclear operations.

The IISE project is aimed at developing technologies, methodologies and assurance frameworks to enable humans and robotic systems to operate safely, efficiently and collaboratively within a shared environment.

Vision

To create a nuclear working environment in which robotic systems and operators can safely coexist and collaborate within the same safety envelope, dynamically adapting to changing conditions whilst maintaining demonstrable safety and regulatory compliance.

Research Challenge

There are some fundamental challenges that need to be considered as part of this work:

• Human behaviour is unpredictable.
• Nuclear environments are dynamic.
• Safety regulations ensure our operators face minimal risk with predictable and repeatable operations.
• Autonomous systems need to be predictable and verifiable.
• Regulatory acceptance requires demonstrable evidence of safety performance.
• The complex design of our stores make wireless communications difficult.

Research Focus Area – Digital Twin enabled Human-Robot and Sensor Collaboration

This PhD centres around the creation and management of a detailed digital twin of an environment containing human-robot interaction.

The digital twin should be a like for like representation of the area and provide real-time insights into the condition of the area, including atmosphere and temperature readings.

The digital twin should be able to detect the position and orientation of both the robot and human within the environment, and distinguish between the two in the virtual display, it would be good to explore prediction of path mapping and analysis of common routes as well to establish traffic patterns.

The system should also be able to detect and visualise potential collision points and manage these appropriately to support operator health and safety.

The digital twin should be sophisticated enough to allow for jobs to be rehearsed prior to human entry into the environment, this should be detailed to allow for as much realism as possible.
Alongside this the digital twin should be able to display the health of the sensors located within the area, providing a real time RAG status and planned maintenance requirements to ensure that components can be replaced before failure, maintaining the reliability of the digital twin as a visual representation of the real world.

Funding notes:

This position is open to UK fee payers AND international students, and the funding will cover all tuition fees and also provide a stipend to cover living costs during the student’s studies.

The successful applicants should have a first degree classified at 1st (or equivalent) in Robotics and AI or a closely related subject. An MSc in robotics or a related area is also highly desirable.

If you are interested in this position, email Dr Steve Davis (s.davis.2@bham.ac.uk) including a CV and a brief (half page maximum) statement explaining how the position is related to your background and experience.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Understanding drug resistance in M. tuberculosis by applying machine learning to a national genomic census
jobs.description_html:
Tuberculosis (TB) kills more people globally than any other infectious disease, and progress towards its elimination is stagnating amid concerns about prevalence of drug resistance. Different lineages of M. tuberculosis differ in both their intrinsic drug susceptibility and their propensity to acquire antimicrobial resistance. Most studies of resistance use datasets enriched for drug-resistant isolates, creating an ascertainment bias that limits our understanding of how resistance evolves in the wider bacterial population. In this joint project between the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the University of Birmingham, we will analyse a national collection of M. tuberculosis genomes from England. The collection brings together drug-susceptible and drugresistant isolates with linked enhanced surveillance records and epidemiological data. We will use existing resistance catalogues to characterise drug resistance across lineages and apply genome-wide association methods to investigate genetic factors associated with resistance emergence, pathogenicity and heteroresistance. To address gaps in these catalogues, we will also examine whether advanced machine learning approaches such as genome and protein language models can improve resistance prediction for rare and novel genotypes. The student will develop skills in microbial genomics, bioinformatics and applied machine learning through investigating how emerging machine learning methods can support effective surveillance of TB and other pathogens.

Supervisors: Professor Nicholas Loman, Dr Esther Robinson and Dr Bede Constantinides.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Uncovering the impact of multiple anthropogenic stress factors on rhizosphere plant-microbe interactions
jobs.description_html:
Project ID: 3701

Supervisory team

Lead supervisors: Dr Harry Child (University of Plymouth) and Professor Iain Hartley (University of Exeter)

Other supervisors: Dr Richard Tennant (University of Exeter) and Dr Anne Plessis (University of Plymouth)

Registered Institution: University of Plymouth

Host Institutions: University of Exeter/University of Plymouth

Project description

Climate change and anthropogenic land use are known to impose stress factors (known as global change factors) on plants and soil microbial communities. These global change factors threaten the function, resilience and productivity of natural and agricultural ecosystems. Combined with increasing demand for agricultural productivity and declining soil health, improving the resilience of agricultural systems to these stress factors is vitally important. Simultaneous exposure to stress factors can have synergistic negative effects on plants and soil microbial communities, leading to the "multifactorial stress combination" (MFSC) principle that plant health and soil functions can decline sharply as stressors accumulate. However, multifactorial stress experiments have so far focused on soil microbial communities and plants separately.  This project would bridge these fields by investigating combinations of stressors (e.g. warming, drought, soil contaminants and pesticides) at the plant-soil interface. This will address whether the intimate interactions between microbes and plant roots in the rhizosphere can buffer-against or exacerbate the response of microbial community diversity and function to combined stressors.

This project will also reveal the influence of multifactorial stress on root traits and rhizosphere interactions to reveal how crops respond to stress combinations belowground, uncovering the consequences for crop health.  The project: you will combine interdisciplinary methods from microbial ecology, environmental genomics, soil biogeochemistry and plant science to investigate the impacts of multifactorial stress on rhizosphere plant-microbe interactions, root trait responses and soil health. You will carry out controlled plant growth experiments, using wheat as a study system, to understand the effect of combined stress factors on crop yield and physiology. You will investigate the outcomes for rhizosphere soil microbial communities using cutting-edge sequencing and bioinformatics methods. You will monitor soil function using soil biogeochemical methods to measure soil greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient cycling.

Through this work, you will learn how to use molecular biology, DNA sequencing and bioinformatics to understand complex microbial communities, while also gaining fundamental skills in experimental biology, soil science and plant science. As the project progresses, there is scope for you to direct the research questions depending on your interests, gaining experience of independent research design.  This project will improve our fundamental understanding how plant-soil interactions respond to multifactorial stress, with potential implications for how agricultural management can maintain productivity and improve resilience under the pressures of global change.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Can a picture predict strength? Learning how collagen architecture sets the mechanics of living tissue.
jobs.description_html:
Project ID: 3601

Supervisory team

Lead supervisors: Dr Daniela Oehring (University of Plymouth) and Dr Ben Sherlock (University of Exeter)

Other supervisors: Dr Ben Gardner (University of Exeter) and Dr Matt Jones (University of Plymouth)

Collaborators: Dr Craig Boote (Cardiff University) and Professor Ahmed Elsheikh (University of Liverpool)

Registered institution: University of Plymouth

Host Institutions: University of Exeter/University of Plymouth

Project description

Collagen makes connective tissue strong, and the direction its fibres run makes it stiff one way and compliant another, like grain in wood. What is unknown is whether an image of that structure predicts mechanical behaviour better than the two or three numbers we boil it down to: a mean fibre direction and how neatly the fibres line up. If the image wins, every model of soft tissue in use is leaving information behind. If not, a long-running argument closes. Either way it matters beyond the eye: such models borrow their material properties from other specimens. You will answer that in two tissues from the same eye. Cornea and sclera are continuous and built from the same collagen, arranged very differently: cornea in ordered lamellae of uniform fibrils, sclera interwoven and variable. Any difference in predictive performance comes from the arrangement. So there is a prediction you can be wrong about: the summary numbers should work on the ordered tissue and fail on the disordered one. At Exeter you will image collagen architecture in viable and freshly excised tissue by label-free, polarisation-resolved multiphoton microscopy.

At Plymouth, you will measure how the same specimens carry load. Generating that paired dataset, two architectures within one eye, is the project's first half. You will then learn the map from architecture to mechanics twice over: classically, fitting an established model to fibre orientation and dispersion, and with a neural network reading the whole image, constrained so thermodynamics holds by construction. Comparison on unseen specimens answers it. The last question is the most interesting. Living tissue rebuilds itself in response to load. Does tissue held under sustained load drift from what its architecture predicts? If so, mechanics depend on biological history in a way no current model captures.

You will finish able to image tissue microstructure, measure its mechanics, and build machine-learning models that respect physics and report uncertainty. Few people can do all three. Backgrounds in physics, engineering, mathematics, biology or biomedical science all fit; you need mathematical confidence and willingness to code, but no machine learning. You will belong to two groups, a biophotonics laboratory at Exeter and an eye and vision group at Plymouth, time split equally and worked in blocks, with no weekly commuting, alongside a doctoral cohort across the South West. Cardiff contributes an X-ray scattering archive of corneal and scleral collagen.

For Eligibility, Funding and to Apply, please click on the Apply button.

jobs.description_html:
This pathway will leverage excellent provision and research in sociological methods training at Swansea, to build capacity and realize a networked all-Wales strategy for doctoral training in Sociology and STS, drawing upon FtF, hybrid and blended approaches. Pathway strengths include centres and other UKRI investments, ADR Wales, Centre for Ageing and Dementia Research. 

Sociology/STS is an emerging disciplinary strength at Swansea University that currently sits within UoA20, with pockets of excellence that speak to WGSSS crosscutting themes. This is a merger of two DTP2 pathways, that are adjacent in disciplinary terms, with an extension to include Bangor and Swansea, as well as Cardiff.

Research Environment

Training: The pathway offers advanced training in: Quantitative and Qualitative Methods (all HEIs); Ethnography; Interaction Analysis (Audio, Video and Multimodal Approaches); Advanced Approaches to Science and Technology Studies; Theorising Contemporary Social Change and Transformation; Advanced Statistics; and the PGR Summer School on Statistics, from 2024 (Swansea). Students will also be able to participate in training provided by WISERD, which is closely aligned with the pathway, benefitting from its partnership with the ESRC National Centre for Research Methods (NCRM) (2019-2024), a centre for the delivery of innovative training and capacity-building activities. In addition to pooling these resources where possible, we will also use WGSSS training support to develop and package a suite of short on-line methods training courses, as well as create and deliver a pathway/cluster summer school (hosted on a rotating basis as a ‘signal’ event), also open to other pathways and DTPs, where feasible.

Community engagement includes presentations at the National Eisteddfod and Hay Festival and collaborative research with, e.g. National Adoption Service, Care Inspectorate Wales, Welsh Council for Voluntary Action (a formal partner in WGSSS), Shelter Cymru, and Senghenydd Youth and Community Centre (South Wales).

Cohort Building

We will open up HEI-focused research groups to all pathway and cluster students. This networked approach will fold these activities into a series of hybrid activities that will be open across the pathway, optimizing opportunities for cohort building and participation. Rotating the summer school acts as an annual cohort signal event.

Funding Details

More specifically, it examines the built and social environment and the impact that these have on multiple health and/or social outcomes. For example, a project may characterise the housing or school travel environment, and investigate the impact on injuries, mental health and educational outcomes; or shifting ageing and family-size demographics in relation to the epidemiology of chronic health conditions to address the pressing issue of the ‘care -gap’. jobs.title: LISS DTP Fully-Funded Social Science PhD Studentships
jobs.description_html:
Applications are now open for the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)- funded London Interdisciplinary Social Science Doctoral Training Partnership (LISS DTP) Open Competition Studentships for October 2027 Entry.

These fully funded studentships support student-led research projects, giving applicants the opportunity to develop and propose their own research ideas in collaboration with an academic supervisor.

Led by King’s College London, in partnership with Imperial College London and Queen Mary University of London, the LISS DTP provides a dynamic and supportive environment for interdisciplinary social science research.

For more information on LISS DTP vision please visit the LISS DTP webpage.

LISS DTP offer the following studentship options:

  • 1+3.5 studentships: one year of Master's study followed by a 3.5-year PhD.
  • +3.5 studentships: a 3.5-year PhD for applicants who already have the required training and preparation.
  • Part-time studentships are also available.
  • Current postgraduate research (PGR) students in their first year of full-time study, or first or second year of part-time study, may apply for funding for the remainder of their PhD.

Research Areas

We welcome applications across six interdisciplinary research areas:

  • RA1: Global Health Innovation
  • RA2: Business Analytics, Management, and Applied Economics
  • RA3: Language, Culture, and Education
  • RA4: Environment and Sustainability
  • RA5: Global Order and Security
  • RA6: Public Policy and Governance  

LISS DTP particularly encourage proposals that use advanced data skills, quantitative methods, and interdisciplinary approaches. Dedicated steered awards are available in these areas.

Inclusive Funding

We are committed to recruiting outstanding and diverse candidates from across the UK and internationally, including the EU.

We offer nine ringfenced studentships for Home students who face barriers to postgraduate study and are currently underrepresented within the LISS DTP.

Funding Eligibility

LISS DTP welcomes applications from both Home and International students.

Nationality and residency requirements for both Home and International students can be found in EU and international eligibility for UKRI studentships from 2021 – UKRI. Please read this document to determine whether you will be classed as a Home or International student and what this means for the funding available to you.

You can find out more on our Funding Eligibility webpage.

Academic Eligibility

Due to the limited number of studentships available, successful applicants are likely to have:

  • a very good first degree (BA or BSc Honours or equivalent) at 1st class standard or upper 2nd with average of 65% or above,
  • for +3.5 awards, an appropriate Masters degree (at distinction or at least high merit level) is expected,
  • other qualifications relevant to the proposed area of study, such as professional or work-related expertise, will also be considered.

The following are NOT eligible:

  • Students who will have less than 50% of their study time (usually 3.5 years for a full-time PhD) remaining when they start their LISS-funded studentship.
  • Students enrolled on OR applying for distance learning programmes.
  • Applicants who have already been awarded a PhD or equivalent degree.

Studentship Funding

Each studentship includes:

  • UKRI Home fees for Master’s and/or PhD study
  • Annual tax-free stipend of approximately £23,805 (2026/27 rate)
  • Additional funding for training, fieldwork, placements and more.

International students may be eligible for institutional fee waiver/ support to cover the fee difference. 

All funded students must undertake a 3-month placement, integrating research with practical experience.

All funded students must submit their PhD thesis within their funded period.

How to Apply

Candidates must complete their application for LISS DTP for their chosen studentship (1+3.5 or +3.5) and apply for admission to their chosen Masters’ or PhD programme at one of LISS DTP’s partner institutions.

The application deadline is 20 January 2027, 17:00 GMT.

The Department of Health and Physical Education (HPE) at the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) encompasses researchers in physical education, sports science, nutrition, and health, with an overarching focus on physical fitness and holistic health across the lifespan and generating knowledge that can be broadly applied in physical/health education and intervention. 

Three research cluster groups have been established to enhance the quantity and quality of research output through developing strategic research themes, identifying potential research areas/directions, and producing solid outcomes to maintain and even uphold the research performance. The groups are: 

  1. Physical Activity & Sport Education
  2. Biomechanic, Nutrition & Health Performance
  3. Applied Physiology & Technology 

PhD Opportunities 

The HPE welcomes high-achieving international candidates interested in pursuing a PhD in the areas of physical literacy, sport pedagogy, adapted physical activity, high-performance physiology, digital physical education, sports nutrition, and preventative health. For other potential areas of research supervision, please browse our academic staff profiles. 

Applicants should hold a strong academic record in relevant fields (e.g., sport science, psychology, PE, or health), ideally with a Master’s degree and publication experience. This opportunity is open to candidates of all nationalities. Strong academic training and a demonstrated capacity for research will be essential for progression to the next stage. 

Applicants with a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree from a university where the programme was not taught and assessed in English are required to attach their TOEFL or IELTS score results with their PhD applications. The TOEFL and IELTS scores are considered valid for two years from the test date and must be valid at the time of application submission to the EdUHK. 

For further details of the PhD application, please visit here. 

Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme (HKPFS)

The Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme (HKPFS), established by the Research Grants Council (RGC) of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government, aims to attract the best and brightest students in the world to pursue their PhD studies in Hong Kong's universities. 

The Fellowship provides an annual stipend of HK$344,400 (approximately US$44,150) and a conference and research-related travel allowance of HK$14,400 (approximately US$1,840) per year for each awardee for a period up to three years. 

For details on the HKPFS, please visit here.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From Variants to Placental Function: Using Cell-free DNA to Dissect the Functional Genomics of Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes
jobs.description_html:
Background: Adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs) like preeclampsia, foetal growth restriction, and pre-term delivery affect up to 30% of pregnancies, significantly impacting quality of life. These complications are difficult to detect before the appearance of clinical symptoms, and their biology is poorly understood. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified dozens of genetic loci associated with these conditions, as well as with perinatal traits like placental weight and birthweight. However, the functional consequences of these variants are not currently understood.

Previous research suggests that placental development plays a key role in perinatal health, and that genetic variants associated with APOs may disrupt placental function. However, accessing placental tissue is impractical due to the associated risk of miscarriage, which limits placental monitoring. This severely hinders our ability to functionally interpret APO-associated variants.

During pregnancy a large proportion of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in the parental bloodstream comes from the placenta. This makes cfDNA a unique, minimally invasive biomarker which could be used to monitor placental health. Thus, we propose a project that leverages cfDNA sequencing to track gene activity in the placenta throughout pregnancy. We aim to use these observations to dissect the role of genetic variants associated with perinatal traits and APOs.

Research questions:

1) Can cfDNA information be used to estimate gene activity in the placenta in real time?

2) Do genetic variants associated with APOs modulate gene activity in the placenta?

3) Can cfDNA be used as a minimally invasive biomarker of APOs?

Project design: With guidance from their supervisors, the student will leverage single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to identify cell type-specific markers of key placental cell types, which they will use to interpret publicly available cfDNA sequencing data from healthy pregnancies and APO cases. They will do this by mapping nucleosomal footprints from cfDNA, which they will integrate with single-cell markers to infer placental gene activity. The student will lead on the design and development of computational tools to predict gene activity from nucleosomal footprints, extending previous work published by KECG. The student will next integrate cfDNA-derived gene activity metrics with GWAS associations for perinatal traits and APOs using statistical genetics approaches like heritability partitioning and SNP enrichment. Where appropriate, the student may supplement these analyses with new data generation from plasma samples from pregnancies available via the Genetic Beta Cell Research Bank (GBCRB).

A key strength of our research environment is that, through their supervisory team, the student will have access to key data sets uniquely suited to answering these research questions. These include: 1) a collection of publicly available sequencing data sets of cfDNA from pregnancy cohorts, currently being curated by KECG and comprising both APOs and healthy pregnancies; 2) GWAS summary statistics for perinatal traits generated by RF, including associations with placental weight and birthweight; 3) a longitudinal data set of gene expression across pregnancy generated by ED within the Pregnancy Outcome Prediction Study 2 (POPS2); and 4) a scRNA-seq atlas of the placenta generated by the Vento-Tormo group at the Wellcome Sanger Institute. ED’s close links with this group will enable the student to access key knowledge and expertise, fostering collaborations and enhancing the value of this project.

jobs.title: PhD in Late Antique, Medieval and Early Modern Studies
jobs.description_html:
Up to 5 studentships

Historical Studies at CEU is recognized for its conscious interdisciplinarity and the wide geographical range of our faculty and students’ interests. We have particular strengths in the history of Central Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, whilst also researching and publishing on diverse topics from the US through to central and eastern Asia. Chronologically, our research covers late antiquity to the present day, with students encouraged to follow their individual interests rather than working on faculty-led projects.

The PhD in Late Antique, Medieval and Early Modern Studies is a four-year program accredited in Austria and the US. It emphasizes the importance of working with original sources, for which we provide instruction in a variety of languages, including Latin, Ancient Greek and Syriac. For the first year of the program, students are based in Vienna where they will attend courses in historiography, methodology, and any languages they need for their proposed research, and choose from a wide range of elective classes. The second and third years of the doctorate might be spent on archival research, field trips and conference participation. During this time, students will also complete a mandatory TA-ship, and have opportunities to further develop their teaching skills and organize conferences and workshops. The fourth year is spent writing the dissertation, supported by our faculty and PhD community.

For the academic year 2027/28, we are offering up to 5 funded PhD places, awarded on the basis of academic merit. We offer:

  • A full tuition waiver
  • A monthly stipend
  • A research allowance, currently 5,200 EUR, for the duration of the program
  • Dedicated PhD office space
  • Regular events with prestigious external speakers
  • Close ties to the Viennese academic community, including the universities, libraries and archives
  • A proven record of external grants and international collaborations with universities and research institutes

To apply, please submit two letters of recommendation, your research proposal and a writing sample in English through the CEU application portal by January 15, 2027 (click Apply button above to access). We strongly encourage prospective students to contact members of our faculty to discuss their proposed projects. For any questions, please email our PhD coordinator, Dr. Margaretha Boockmann, at boockmannm@ceu.edu.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Assessing Establishment and Efficacy of Rust Fungus Control of Himalayan Balsam
jobs.description_html:
Award summary

100% fees covered, and a minimum tax-free annual living allowance of £21,805 (2026/27 UKRI rate) plus additional research funds

Overview

Himalayan balsam (I. glandulifera), is an invasive plant which is notoriously problematic on riverbanks, forming monospecific stands which ultimately results in extirpation of native vegetation and can lead to bank erosion. In 2014, a biological control agent, rust fungus Puccinia komarovii, was approved for release in the EU and is being used across heavily invaded sites in the UK.

Over the 10 years since the initial inoculations the success of establishment and spread of the biocontrol has been variable between sites. The aim of this PhD project is to assess the impact of environmental conditions on rust fungus infection success of I.glandulifera. Working with CABI, Tweed Forum and Tees Rivers Trusts the student will collate existing monitoring and will undertake full site assessments, mapping key topographical features of the invaded riparian sites and catalogue flora present at the site using botanical survey methodology. The project requires a student wishing to develop skills in fieldwork, data collation and ecological modelling with an interest in spatial ecology and monitoring methods. Modelling and mapping of the spatial spread and control efforts, will be used to determine the natural dispersal efficacy of the rust fungus to other invaded sites and allow the student to produce evidence based guidance on suitable release sites and a revision of monitoring requirements.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: One read, one cell: Decoding cell identity with long-read sequencing
jobs.description_html:
Background

What if we could resolve the epigenome of individual cell types from complex human tissues without ever having to physically separate the cells?

The majority of disease-associated genetic variants exert their effects by modulating gene expression, driving considerable interest in profiling epigenomic variation at scale. Epigenomic patterns, chemical modifications to DNA and chromatin that controls which genes are active, are highly cell-type specific. When studying epigenetics, the tissue choice strongly influences the findings. A critical limitation of existing studies is that bulk tissues (such as whole blood) comprise a mixture of cell types, potentially masking true biological signals.

Historically, resolving this has required the physical isolation of individual cell populations, costly, low-throughput and impractical for population-level studies. Long-read sequencing changes this paradigm by detecting epigenetic modifications alongside genetic sequencing, and by capturing continuous stretches of a single DNA molecule so that each read provides a snapshot of its cell type of origin. We have developed a framework that classifies cell type for individual reads by comparing methylation patterns to reference profiles for different cell types. This enables the generation of cell type-specific epigenetic profiles directly from long-read sequencing data, bypassing the need for experimental cell separation. The project will exploit ~50,000 Oxford Nanopore long-read genomes available in UK Biobank, providing a unique opportunity to resolve cell-type-specific epigenetic variation at population scale.

Objectives

  1. Evaluate the predictive accuracy and optimal conditions for computational cell-type-of-origin prediction from long-read sequencing data.
  1. Curate a comprehensive atlas of reference cell-type methylomes to generalise the approach across multiple tissues.
  1. Apply the framework to large population biobank datasets to generate cellular composition estimates and cell-type-specific epigenetic profiles at scale.
  1. Leverage these cell-type-resolved profiles to conduct epigenome-wide association studies in large cohorts, identifying epigenetic effects linked to disease in specific cell types.

Methodology

The student will apply our suite of computational tools to blood-based long-read sequencing datasets, benchmarking cell-type-of-origin predictions against reference purified datasets to determine optimal conditions for the approach. This phase will include systematic fine-tuning of the prediction framework. The validated tools will then be applied to large biobank cohorts to generate cell composition predictions and cell-type-specific epigenetic profiles at population scale. Finally, these profiles will be used to perform a cell-type-specific epigenome-wide association study, identifying methylation changes associated with phenotypes of health and disease such as smoking and age, that are resolved to individual cell types.

Interdisciplinarity, Facilities and Resources

The supervisory team work at the intersection of functional genomics, mathematics and computer science, with expertise in large complex genomic datasets, method development, and advanced data science and AI methodologies. The student will work across two world-leading research groups, the Complex Disease Epigenetics Group at Exeter and the Birney Group at EBI. They will need strong mathematical and programming skills, a genuine interest in cutting-edge biotechnologies such as long-read sequencing, and willingness to engage with cell biology to interpret their findings. While predominantly a data-science project, long-read sequencing facilities are available to generate reference datasets where appropriate, and computational work will be supported by local (ISCA) and regional (ISAMBARD 3) HPC clusters. The student will benefit from training through Exeter's Coding for Reproducible Research programme and EBI's suite of resources.

Funded by: MRC Medical Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Next-generation machine learning for genetic interaction prediction with lab-in the-loop validation in pancreatic cancer
jobs.description_html:
Background

Cancer cells often depend on specific genes to survive, making those genes attractive drug targets. CRISPR screens knock out genes to measure their importance for cancer cell survival, and large efforts such as DepMap and Project Score have mapped individual single‑gene dependencies across many cancer models. However, single‑gene studies miss vulnerabilities that only appear when two genes are disrupted together. These genetic interactions (GIs), including synthetic lethality, are a rich but under‑explored source of oncology targets.

As testing ~400 million gene pairs is infeasible, computational prediction is essential. Current GI prediction methods combine limited pairwise screens with larger single‑gene screens but rely on low‑dimensional readouts and generalise poorly across disease contexts(1).

By contrast, a proof‑of‑concept study showed that perturb‑seq, which couples CRISPR editing with single‑cell transcriptomics, can support GI prediction using recommender‑system approaches(2). Near genome‑wide perturb‑seq datasets are now available(3, 4), providing transcriptome‑wide readouts that could enable scalable, accurate prediction models.

Objectives

  1. Build next‑generation GI prediction models using large‑scale perturb‑seq data. Initial model development will use publicly available perturb‑seq datasets, including large‑scale data from a leukaemia cell line and induced pluripotent stem cells(3, 4). You will evaluate graph neural networks, autoencoders, and other architectures capable of learning joint gene embeddings from perturb‑seq profiles. You will assess scalability to genome‑wide prediction, handling of sparsity and batch effects, and generalisation across cancer types.
  2. Insights into genetic interaction in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest cancers, with average survival at diagnosis under six months. The AstraZeneca and Cancer Research Horizons Functional Genomics Centre (FGC) will generate perturb-seq data and GI screens in pancreatic cancer models. These experiments will support a "lab in-the-loop" cycle, where new measurements fine-tune the computational model in the pancreatic cancer context. Note that researchers at the FGC will contribute the experimental data and "wet-lab" work, while the student project is purely computational.

Expected outcomes

  • A validated computational framework for GI prediction, released as open source software.
  • Experimentally validated high confidence genetic interactions in a pancreatic cancer cell line.
  • Insight into how GI predictions transfer across biological contexts.
  • A reproducible and rigorous workflow integrating computation and experiment in a “lab‑in‑the‑loop” cycle, while controlling bias and false discovery rates.

You will gain

  • Expertise with modern machine learning methods applied to genomics.
  • Expertise in single cell and CRISPR genomics.
  • High performance computing skills.
  • Industry aligned experience through FGC involvement, including exposure to data quality standards, model evaluation, and target prioritisation.

An interdisciplinary project

The main supervisor is an expert in statistical and machine‑learning methods for genome editing; the co‑supervisor specialises in statistics, reproducible coding and model evaluation. FGC supervisors (Dr Kalinka, Dr Ross‑Thriepland, Dr Walter) will provide additional expertise in genome editing, genomics, cancer biology and bioinformatics.

Facilities and Resources

The University of Exeter will provide high performance computing for model development and training. The FGC will provide world-leading CRISPR and single cell screening facilities and technical expertise.

Funded by: MRC Medical Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Mapping and functional interrogation of mitochondrial DNA modifications in Parkinson’s disease
jobs.description_html:
There is increasing evidence that the mitochondrial genome may be regulated by DNA modifications, but their extent, identity and functional importance remain unclear. This uncertainty partly reflects technical limitations, as conventional approaches for measuring DNA methylation can generate artefacts when applied to mtDNA. Long-read sequencing technologies now provide an opportunity to directly investigate multiple DNA modifications in native mtDNA. This is particularly relevant to Parkinson’s disease (PD), where mitochondrial dysfunction is strongly implicated in disease pathogenesis. We hypothesise that mtDNA contains reproducible patterns of DNA modification that influence mitochondrial genome regulation and are altered in PD.

We will address this through 3 objectives.

(1) To develop and validate Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) approaches to accurately characterise mtDNA modifications. ONT sequencing will be performed on native enriched mtDNA, enabling genetic variation and DNA modifications to be measured on individual molecules. We will generate artificial mtDNA molecules containing known levels of specific modifications and use these to establish the sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility of current modification-calling approaches. This will allow us to look at a range of DNA modifications (e.g. 5mC, 5hmC, 6mA).

(2) To define the landscape of mtDNA modifications in PD brain. We will apply the validated approach to an existing, well-characterised PD case-control cohort to determine the distribution and abundance of modifications across the mitochondrial genome and identify differences associated with disease. The single-molecule nature of ONT sequencing will also enable DNA modifications to be considered alongside mtDNA sequence variation and heteroplasmy, providing an integrated view of mitochondrial genetic and epigenetic variation. Analyses will encompass the entire mitochondrial genome while specifically testing the hypothesis that modification of regulatory regions, including the D-loop, is important in PD.

(3) To determine the functional relevance of mtDNA modifications by integrating them with molecular phenotypes in the same brains. We will initially test whether variation in mtDNA modifications, particularly within regulatory regions, is associated with mitochondrial transcription and mtDNA abundance. We will then integrate modification profiles with existing bulk and snRNA seq, small RNA-seq, nuclear DNA methylation and genetic data to determine how mtDNA modification states relate to cellular pathways and PD-associated molecular changes. This will prioritise candidate regulatory modifications for future causal investigation using emerging mitochondrial epigenome-editing approaches.

The project will establish a validated experimental and computational framework for studying mtDNA modifications, and determine their relationship with mitochondrial genome activity and wider cellular phenotypes in PD brain. It is highly interdisciplinary, combining long-read sequencing, mitochondrial genetics, epigenetics, bioinformatics and multiomic data integration. The project will exploit existing PD brain samples and extensive matched genomic and transcriptomic datasets, substantially reducing the requirement for costly new data generation.

The supervisory team brings complementary skills that directly reflects the project: Prof Lunnon has extensive expertise in neurodegenerative disease epigenetics and has led research investigating the mitochondrial epigenome in human brain; Prof Chinnery is an international leader in mitochondrial genetics, including the application of long-read and multiomic technologies; Dr Kouhsar brings expertise in bioinformatics, long-read sequencing analysis and multiomic data integration, whilst Dr Smith has experience in developing novel ONT approaches. Together, these existing samples, datasets, expertise and sequencing and computational infrastructure provide a strong PhD environment.

Funded by: MRC Medical Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: AI-Enabled Smart Spectroscopy Pixels: Revealing Microbial Responses to Antibiotics
jobs.description_html:
Spectroscopy has long offered a powerful window into nature, revealing the hidden structure and dynamics of matter through its interaction with light. Extending this window to individual microorganisms could transform understanding of how antibiotics act on living cells. Within apparently uniform populations, bacteria can respond very differently to treatment, with survival strategies concealed by measurements averaged across thousands of cells. Revealing this individuality requires new instruments that combine cellular precision, informative optical measurements and compact design.

The aim of this PhD is to develop intelligent spectroscopy pixels for investigating microbial responses to antibiotics, uniting physics, materials engineering, computer science and bioscience. Recent research demonstrated that a quantum device such as a single two dimensional perovskite photodetector can encode wavelength and light intensity in its nonlinear electrical response, with a compact neural network recovering this information.

This project will extend that principle towards biological sensing, combining advanced photodetectors with established microfluidic platforms that trap individual microorganisms, control antibiotic exposure and follow cellular behaviour over time.

The research will develop sensor quantum materials, optical and electronic interfaces, and learning algorithms to extract biological information from complex signals. Beginning with calibrated optical measurements and progressing towards individual-cell studies, it will investigate whether changes in transmitted or scattered light reveal antibiotic-induced changes in cellular state. Comparison with microscopy, growth, viability and recovery measurements will establish the biological meaning and reliability of these optical fingerprints.

The ambition is to uncover microbial responses early and without added labels, laying foundations for compact tools for future phenotypic antimicrobial-susceptibility assessment. The project offers a distinctive combination of training in quantum technologies, optical instrumentation, bacterial culturing, single-cell microfluidics, neural-network development and rigorous experimental validation. The balance between creating bespoke sensors, interfacing them with living systems and developing algorithms will be shaped by the doctoral researcher’s interests and strengths. This ability to connect quantum devices, instruments, computation and biology will prepare the researcher to contribute at the forefront of computational spectroscopy, AI-enabled biosensing, single-cell biotechnology and intelligent scientific instrumentation. Joint Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award supervision will support a coherent research programme and the development of skills relevant to both academic and industrial research.

References

  1. K. J. Riisnaes et al., “Compact Variational Neural Networks for Spectral Inference from a Single Nonlinear 2D Perovskite Photodetector”, arXiv preprint arXiv:2608.27977 (2026).
  2. U. Łapińska et al., “Fast bacterial growth reduces antibiotic accumulation and efficacy”, eLife 11, e74062 (2022).
  3. Y. Zhang et al., “Single Cell Killing Kinetics Differentiate Phenotypic Bacterial Responses to Different Antibacterial Classes”, Microbiology Spectrum 11, e03667-22 (2023).

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Modelling coevolution in aquatic environments shaped by flow
jobs.description_html:
Coevolution is the process of species evolving together and influencing each other’s evolutionary path. For a system of microbes and viruses, this entails an ongoing dynamic of the host microbe evading infection and the virus overcoming this protection. However, when fluid flow drives these partners apart, several questions arise: How will past coevolution affect the interactions with new partners?

How long do signatures of past coevolution persist? What happens when descendants re-encounter after stretches of isolated evolution, again through fluid flow? Understanding these questions is essential for understanding evolution in the ever-changing world of aqueous ecosystems. You will address these questions with physical modelling, simulations, machine learning and analytical calculations with a strong focus on parameters describing oceanic ecosystems. Following a bottom-up approach, you will first develop agent-based simulations in a prototypical flow field to test biological hypotheses on the effect of flow fields on coevolution, supplemented by analytical calculations and machine learning. In a second step, you will translate and test these findings to larger systems with more complex flow fields mimicking the situation in the ocean.

To achieve this goal, you will develop a hybrid modelling approach incorporating the efficiency of concentration-based and the stochasticity of agent-based modelling. You will join a supervisory team that is dedicated to research at the interface of physics and biology with significant research experience in model building and simulations: Wolfram Moebius (Exeter), a physicist with research experience and interest in evolution of bacterial viruses, and Daniel Kattnig (Exeter), a physicist and expert in large-scale simulations. We will collaborate with Adam Monier (Exeter) on the application to the marine environment and with Kit Yates (Bath) on the development of a hybrid simulation scheme. The research will take place in the Department of Physics and Astronomy and the Living Systems Institute, providing a stimulating atmosphere and plenty of opportunities for cross-disciplinary interactions, input, and advice.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: In Silico Directed Evolution of Biological Qubits: Rational Design of Nanoscale Quantum Transducers
jobs.description_html:
Engineered flavoproteins, LOV domains, and fluorescent proteins have recently demonstrated that radical pair mechanisms (RPM) can serve as biological qubits with optical readouts, achieving magnetic field responses up to a 50% fluorescence change in living cells. However, reaching such a large magnetic sensitivity involved empiric and slow laboratory exploration, including directed evolution, and the (optimized) function is strictly that of a passive quantum observers. The scientific frontier of this project lies in the transition from passive quantum observers (fluorescence-based readouts) to active quantum transducers, i.e., genetically encoded systems that actuate a downstream biological response directly governed by quantum spin dynamics. Concurrently, rapid breakthroughs in generative AI and de novo protein design enable the systematic exploration of sequence and backbone space beyond natural scaffolds.

By unifying open quantum system spin dynamics simulations with deep-learning protein generation, this project will establish an in silico directed evolution pipeline to engineer biological qubits that transduce spin-dependent events into functional, biological effector signals.

Project Aims and Objectives

➢ Aim 1: Mapping Optimal Spin Dynamics to Structural Targets. Translate theoretically optimal spin Hamiltonians (maximizing magnetic field sensitivity via tuned hyperfine couplings, exchange interactions, and recombination kinetics) into concrete physical constraints, such as inter-cofactor geometries and local environments.

➢ Aim 2: In Silico Generative Protein Design. Develop a de novo design workflow leveraging deep-learning inverse-folding algorithms and electronic structure estimations to generate novel protein scaffolds and sidechain packings optimized for radical pair generation and (coherent) lifetime.
