➢ Aim 3: Pipeline Calibration & Benchmarking. Calibrate the computational pipeline by reverse engineering existing laboratory directed-evolution constructs (such as MagLOV variants).

➢ Aim 4: Engineering Biological Transduction. Design allosteric coupling pathways wherein spin-selective chemical yields or radical lifetimes trigger structural shifts, converting the quantum sensor into a biological affector (e.g., modulating protein-protein interactions or enzymatic activity). Prospective predictions will be considered for experimental validation via Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award collaborating facilities at the Living Systems Institute (LSI) and National Physical Laboratory (NPL).

Methodology

The candidate will implement a multiscale computational framework combining open quantum spin dynamics (utilizing stochastic Liouville solvers and accounting for parametric uncertainty using a Bayesian approach) with generative AI protein design tools (e.g., ColabDesign, ProteinMPNN), molecular dynamics free-energy calculations, and ab initio prediction of spin Hamiltonian parameters and electron transfer rates (DFT based). The project is co-supervised by Prof. Alex Jones at NPL in support of the Laboratory’s strategic initiative in nanoscale quantum sensors for intracellular measurement and will leverage protein design methodology of start-up Orion Life Gmbh.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Functional interpretation of human NF1 genetic variation using precision genome editing and in vivo phenotyping
jobs.description_html:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a genetic disorder that causes a range of symptoms and affects approximately 1 in 3,000 people. These include abnormalities in skin pigmentation, problems with the heart and circulatory system, and nerve tumours that cause chronic pain and movement problems. This multisystem genetic disorder is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene, which encodes the neurofibromin protein. Neurofibromin contains seven functional domains and each domain interacts with different signalling pathways. Although mutations throughout the entire NF1 gene can cause disease, it remains unclear how genetic variants in different domains are associated with distinct clinical phenotypes.

This PhD project addresses the gap between genetic variants in humans, molecular functions, and organismal phenotypes in NF1. The project will be delivered by combining data science and in vitro and in vivo analyses to address three objectives; 1) Identification and prioritisation of human NF1 variants, 2) Assessment of their effects on NF1-dependent signalling, and 3) Validation of the genetic variants in zebrafish model. The student will screen and prioritise NF1 pathogenic variants using population data focusing on genotype–phenotype association. In addition, AI-based approaches such as biological foundation models will be used to predict their functional effects and select variants representing different NF1 domains. Next, effects of selected variants on the signalling pathways downstream of neurofibromin will be investigated using human cell culture systems.

The student will quantitatively measure cellular phenotypes and investigate the rescue by drug treatment with the existing chemical compounds such as MEK inhibitors targeting the oncogenic Ras pathway regulated by neurofibromin. To connect molecular function to organismal phenotype, the student will establish a novel humanised zebrafish platform during the project. Zebrafish possess two paralogs of the human NF1 gene, referred to as nf1a and nf1b, both of which show comparable levels of conservation across DNA sequences and protein domain structures. Interestingly, nf1a/b mutant zebrafish reproduce many of the common NF1 phenotypes, such as the loss of pigmentation and abnormal patterning of the central nervous system.

To generate a precise disease model, the protein-coding sequence of the zebrafish nf1 is excised and replaced with the human NF1 sequence using CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing technologies. By using the humanised zebrafish, the student will create a multidimensional functional map of NF1 which links the genetic variants, signalling activities, and organismal phenotypes. The selected variants will be introduced into the replaced human NF1 gene using precise genome editing technologies such as prime editing and donor DNA-based knock-in. Functional effects of the variants on tissue patterning and pharmacological responses will be assessed by imaging transgenic reporter zebrafish lines that label oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, or endothelial cells in blood vessels.

This integrated functional genomics project which combines data science and cell and developmental biology will lead to a deeper mechanistic understanding of neurofibromin function and the contributions of individual genetic variants to organismal phenotypes relevant to symptoms observed in NF1 patients. By connecting individual variants to quantitative in vivo phenotypes and signalling outputs, this platform will provide a scalable strategy for variant interpretation, understanding of disease mechanisms, and improved therapies.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Functional genomics of health and unhealthy fat distribution
jobs.description_html:
Where fat is stored in our bodies is a major determinant of health. Storing fat safely under the skin (subcutaneous fat) protects against metabolic disease like heart failure and type 2 diabetes, while storing fat centrally around the organs (visceral fat or "lipodystrophy") drastically increases disease risk. Although human genetics has identified some protein-coding genes that substantially affect fat distribution, the vast majority of disease-associated variation is hidden in non-coding regulatory regions that have been difficult to access and interpret at scale. Now, with increasing availability of whole-genome sequencing from millions of individuals; fat-specific genetic regulatory maps; AI variant interpretation tools, and advances in functional models of fat cells, we are in prime position to effectively interrogate these regions. This will allow us to determine which variants and genes affect fat distribution.

Key Question and Objectives:

Which genetic regulatory switches and genes drive human visceral versus subcutaneous adipocyte identity, and what are the biological mechanisms?

The student will:

1) Identify coding and non-coding variants associated with fat distribution using whole genome sequencing data across massive multi-ancestry cohorts.

2) Integrate genetic signals with multi-omic epigenetic maps, including AlphaGenome AI predictions, to prioritise and interrogate causal regulatory elements.

3) Establish human iPSC-derived adipocyte models patterned toward visceral and subcutaneous adipocytes.

4) Quantify the functional impact of prioritized genes and regulatory variants on adipocyte phenotypes using CRISPR-based perturbations.

Interdisciplinarity: This project is interdisciplinary, bridging data science with experimental biology. The studentship will comprise world-leading computational genomics and population genetics at the University of Exeter, alongside cutting-edge stem-cell biology and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing at the University of Cambridge. The supervisors also include leading senior clinical academics with expertise in lipodystrophy providing important clinical insight for the student.

Methodology:

1) At Exeter, you will harness established population-genetic association pipelines to analyse WGS and fat measurements from highly diverse cohorts. You will integrate these genetic signals with adipose-specific regulatory information (including gene expression, chromatin accessibility, enhancer gene relationships) and AI-based tools such as AlphaGenome to prioritise and test a set of candidate variants, regulatory elements and target genes.

2) At Cambridge, you will develop iPSCs patterned towards visceral and subcutaneous adipocyte identity, guided by developmental cues. A stable Cas9-expressing iPSC line will establish a reproducible perturbation pipeline, benchmarked using established adiposity genes like ALK7/ACVR1C and PLIN1. You will use high-content imaging and biochemical assays will quantify adipogenesis, lipid storage, and lipolysis. Your validated functional framework will then run a primary CRISPR knockout screen of genetically prioritised candidates.

Expected Outcomes:

The studentship will deliver a validated platform of human iPSC-adipocytes and uncover the biological mechanisms behind non-coding variants controlling human fat distribution. This will identify new therapeutic drug targets for cardiometabolic disease that focus on safe fat storage rather than just overall weight loss.

Facilities and Resources:

At Exeter, you will use large-scale computational platforms and Cloud Trusted Research Environments (DNANexus) to analyse over 1 million genomes. At Cambridge, you will be embedded in world-leading metabolic science facilities with comprehensive access to advanced iPSC infrastructure, high-content imaging, and flow cytometry.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Rare variant functional genomics for better understanding, prevention and treatment of musculoskeletal disorders
jobs.description_html:
Background: Musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis and Dupuytren’s contracture are severely disabling disorders that affect millions of people in the UK. Genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of common genetic variants that increase risk of musculoskeletal disorders. Translating these associations into biological insight has, however, been limited because identifying the causal variants is very challenging. Rare variant associations are much simpler to interpret because they have large effect sizes and limited correlation with other genetic variants. In this studentship, the student will analyse millions of individuals across diverse ancestries with whole genome sequencing and medical record data to identify rare genetic variants causing musculoskeletal conditions. They will functionally characterise these variants in relevant tissues to gain mechanistic insights crucial for developing novel, targeted treatments for these disabling disorders.

Key questions and objectives: What are the biological mechanisms that drive the development of musculoskeletal disorders? We will:

1. Identify causal rare genetic variants associated with musculoskeletal disorders using whole genome sequencing from millions of individuals from UK Biobank, All of Us and Our Future Health biobanks

2. Establish the functional consequences of these prioritised variants in disease-relevant, primary human cell and tissue models.

3. Determine the molecular pathways connecting genotype to disease, identifying potential therapeutic targets.

Interdisciplinarity: The student will bridge two leading research environments: health data science and statistical genomics at the University of Exeter, and molecular genetics and cellular modelling at the University of Oxford. This cross-disciplinary approach ensures the student develops a highly sought-after, dual skill set in both computational analysis and experimental validation.

Methodology: The PhD will be divided into two integrated phases.

Phase 1 (Exeter - computational): The student will use large-scale genomic datasets to conduct cutting-edge WGS association testing. Firstly, the student will synthesise information from complex sources, including medical records and assessment data, to define MSK disease phenotypes in UK Biobank, Our Future Health, and All of Us. This will facilitate analysing associated rare variants, structural variants, and integrating multi-omic data (e.g., eQTLs, pQTLs) using advanced bioinformatic pipelines and statistical modelling to prioritise candidate genes and regulatory regions.

Phase 2 (Oxford - laboratory): The student will then functionally validate the top-prioritised candidates. Developed as part of the UKRI HFGI MSK Cluster, the student will interrogate human tissue models of increasing complexity: primary human cells, ex-vivo tissue and humanoid robotic bioreactors. They will employ cutting-edge functional genomics tools - including CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, transcriptomics, and cellular phenotyping - to define how these variants alter cellular function and cause disease.

Expected outcomes: The project will deliver novel insights into the genetic architecture and molecular drivers of musculoskeletal conditions. Outputs will include the identification of validated causal genes, a deeper understanding of disease pathways, and the potential discovery of new targets for drug repurposing.

Facilities and resources: At Exeter, the student will have access to resources such as UK Biobank, All of Us and Our Future Health as well as high-performance computing infrastructure, and the extensive data science expertise of the supervisors who lead the MSc Health Data Science at Exeter. At Oxford, the student will leverage state-of-the-art molecular biology laboratories, established disease model pipelines, and direct access to well-phenotyped patient tissue biobanks within the Musculoskeletal Cluster.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Functional genomic characterisation of genetic risk for diabetic neuropathy using human stem cell models
jobs.description_html:
Around half of all people with diabetes develop peripheral neuropathy, its commonest complication worldwide. It begins with the loss of the smallest sensory nerve fibres, causing pain, numbness and, in severe cases, ulceration and amputation. No treatment halts or reverses it. Yet severity varies widely between people with similar glucose control, pointing to inherited differences in how nerves withstand metabolic stress.

Genetic studies nominate risk genes but cannot say where they act. The pain sensory system is a two-cell partnership: the sensory neuron, and the Schwann cell that ensheathes and metabolically supports it. Which partner carries the risk determines what a treatment must target.

This project focuses on apolipoprotein E (APOE). Best known for Alzheimer's risk, APOE is also made by the non-myelinating Schwann cells supporting the small pain-sensing fibres lost earliest in diabetic neuropathy (10.1006/exnr.1998.6872). Clinical studies have repeatedly, but inconsistently, linked the APOE e4 variant to neuropathy severity (10.5114/aoms.2012.30279), a discrepancy cohort studies cannot resolve, because they cannot separate effects within the nerve from effects on whole-body metabolism.

Key question:

does APOE genotype determine how human sensory neurons and Schwann cells withstand high glucose, and does it act through the neuron, the glial cell, or their partnership?

Objective 1. Establish a sensory neuron and Schwann cell co-culture from stem cells carrying APOE e2/e2, e3/e3 or e4/e4 on one genetic background. Both cell types carry the same genotype, as they do in a person. The student will determine how genotype affects cell survival, nerve fibre integrity, glial ensheathment and network activity under high glucose or cytokine challenge. Comparing all three variants will reveal whether risk changes stepwise with genotype; a strong test of causality. Because the disease involves network degeneration and abnormal excitability, nerve function will be measured by microelectrode arrays (MEAs) across networks and patch clamp electrophysiology in single neurons. Potential cell death will be measured using apoptosis assays.

Objective 2. Determine which cell carries the risk, by assembling mixed co-cultures in which only the neurons, or only the Schwann cells, carry e4, the partner carrying e3 (the “healthy” allele). Phenotypes will be assessed as above.

Objective 3. Identify the pathways responsible using long-read RNA sequencing, which resolves full length transcripts, revealing not only which genes change but how they are spliced, including isoform switching. Neurons and Schwann cells will also be profiled in monoculture, giving reference profiles against which co-culture changes can be assigned to a cellular source. The project will then functionally test candidate genes, asking whether perturbing each rescues the phenotype with the student leading selection and our industrial partner advising on druggability.

Training is interdisciplinary throughout, spanning stem cell biology, genome editing, electrophysiology, transcriptomics and statistical modelling across three institutions and industry. Isogenic APOE lines come through an established collaboration, and we have a working protocol for generating sensory neurons, with a manuscript in preparation. Facilities include high-content imaging, super-resolution microscopy to resolve ensheathment of individual fibres, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing at Exeter. Experiments are tiered, so cheaper assays across all three genotypes focus the costlier sequencing.

Expected outcomes:

A human isogenic model of the neuron-glia unit that degenerates in diabetic neuropathy, an answer to which cell type APOE acts in, and prioritised targets for protecting nerve cells.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Dissecting Metabolic Heterogeneity in Severe Mental Illness Through Genetic Clustering and Single-Cell Functional Genomics
jobs.description_html:
This PhD aims to understand why genetic liability to severe mental illness (SMI), particularly schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, is associated with different patterns of adiposity and metabolic health. Although obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are more common in people with SMI, substantial heterogeneity exists, with many individuals remaining metabolically healthy despite a high burden of SMI risk.

We hypothesise distinct components of psychiatric genetic liability influence metabolic health through different biological pathways, with some increasing susceptibility to obesity and T2D while others have little metabolic consequence. The PhD builds on recent work led by supervisor Tyrrell demonstrating that genetic liability to major depressive disorder comprises biologically distinct clusters of variants with contrasting effects on T2D.

Building on this, the student will apply genetic clustering approaches to SMI traits to identify biologically distinct components of psychiatric risk that differentially influence obesity and T2D. By integrating statistical genetics, causal inference approaches and functional genomics, the PhD will move beyond psychiatric diagnoses as single entities to identify the biological mechanisms underlying metabolic heterogeneity.

First, the PhD will identify genetically distinct clusters of psychiatric risk variants using large-scale genome-wide association study data and characterise their associations with obesity and T2D. The biological and clinical consequences of these clusters will be explored across population biobanks. The PhD will then investigate the cellular mechanisms underlying these genetic pathways using unique single-cell multiomic datasets generated in Exeter. By integrating genetic association data with cell-type-specific gene expression and chromatin accessibility data, the student will determine whether metabolically distinct psychiatric risk pathways act through different neuronal and glial cell populations and identify the genes and regulatory networks involved.

Selected regulatory elements and candidate genes emerging from these analyses will be prioritised for functional investigation using experimental approaches (e.g. CRISPR-based perturbation, neuronal cell models). This will provide mechanistic insight into how distinct components of SMI genetic liability influence both brain function and metabolic health. The PhD will provide multidisciplinary training in statistical genetics, genetic epidemiology, bioinformatics, single-cell genomics and functional genomics.

The student will gain experience in large-scale genomic datasets, causal inference and clustering methods, integrating transcriptomic data, and undertaking lab-based functional studies. Training in R, Python and high-performance computing will be complemented by experimental skills in molecular and cellular biology. While the PhD has clearly defined objectives, there will be considerable scope for the student to shape the direction of the PhD according to their interests and emerging findings.

Opportunities may include focusing on a specific SMI, ancestry-specific mechanisms, method development, particular neuronal cell populations, or in-depth functional characterisation of candidate genes. This flexibility will support the development of an independent research profile. This PhD will address a key question in psychiatric and metabolic disease biology: why do some individuals with a high SMI genetic liability develop obesity and metabolic complications whilst others remain metabolically healthy?

By identifying biologically distinct components of SMI risk and characterising the molecular mechanisms, the PhD has the potential to reveal new pathways linking brain function and metabolic regulation, improve understanding of disease heterogeneity, and identify novel targets. It will equip the student with a broad, highly transferable skills relevant to careers in academia, biotechnology and precision medicine.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Developing a variant effect predictor for multiple missense variants in the same protein molecule to aid clinical interpretation
jobs.description_html:
Context:

Genome sequencing is becoming increasingly widespread in both research and diagnostics, and over a million people have already had their genomes sequenced. However, interpreting the effect of genetic variants is challenging and frequently delays diagnosis in patients with rare genetic diseases. The number of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in clinical databases is growing exponentially, and >70% of them are missense variants, i.e. where one amino acid in a protein sequence is replaced with another. Numerous computational variant effect predictors (VEPs) have been developed to predict the effect of missense variants and are increasingly being used in genome sequencing analysis and diagnostic interpretation. However, despite every human having ~10,000 missense variants in their genome, and ~1000 genes on average with more than one missense, genetic variant interpretation still largely considers these variants individually. Although some computational models can predict the effects of multiple amino acid changes, these have mainly been developed for protein-engineering purposes.

Key question:

The aim of this PhD project is to develop and validate a new VEP designed to predict the effect of multiple amino acid changes in the same protein to aid clinical interpretation.

Interdisciplinarity:

This is a highly interdisciplinary project that involves in silico 3D protein structure modelling and machine learning methods, working with genetic (e.g. clinical, population), biochemical (e.g. AlphaFold) and functional (e.g. MAVEs) datasets. We have therefore assembled a team of supervisors with experience in genetics, bioinformatics and protein structure, who provide complementary expertise:

- Exeter (Wright, Leslie): applying and assessing VEPs for clinical diagnosis and gene-disease discovery in rare disease

- Edinburgh (Marsh): comparing and validating VEPs against different datasets

- Imperial (David): designing and developing VEPs using 3D protein structure

Methodology:

  1. Review and benchmark existing approaches for predicting multiple missense variants, including evolutionary, protein language and 3D structure-based models.
  2. Develop existing methodology to predict the effect of one missense variant in the presence of another:a. Within the same structured protein domain; b. Within the same protein but in different domains; c. Within the same protein but including unstructured/interdomain regions; d. In different proteins within the same complex. Predictions will use information about 3D proximity, interactions between the amino acids, substrate binding, post-translational modifications, contribution to domain stability, and standard metrics of conservation, constraint, etc.
  3. Test whether predictions capture interactions beyond the individual variant effects using existing data, e.g. MAVEs with double mutants, known examples of pathogenic alleles in cis, genome sequencing data in population cohorts (with statistical or read-based haplotyping), etc.
  4. Possible extension: further development of the VEP to include prediction of three or more missense variants in the same molecule. Expected outcomes: The main outcome will be a new “multiVEP” for multiple missense variants in the same molecule that is validated against experimental and clinical data and available for use by the community.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Uncovering the mechanism of minor spliceosome autoimmune diabetes
jobs.description_html:
Context/background

Before the instructions in a gene can be used, non-coding parts called introns must be cut out in a process called splicing. Most introns are spliced out by the major spliceosome. However, around 700 human genes contain a rare type of intron (U12 introns) that can only be removed by a separate minor spliceosome.

We recently discovered that inherited changes in two core minor spliceosome components, RNU4ATAC and RNU6ATAC, cause a single-gene (monogenic) form of autoimmune diabetes. In this condition, the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. This is a puzzle, as the minor splicing machinery is used by every cell in the body, yet when it goes wrong it results in a highly specific immune attack on the pancreatic beta cells. We do not yet know which of the 700 affected genes drive disease, or in which cells, though preliminary data suggests a major role for T cells, B cells and beta cells. Answering this could reveal new biology relevant to type 1 diabetes and to autoimmunity more broadly, uncovering new drug targets for autoimmune diseases.

Key question

Which incorrectly spliced U12-intron genes drive the immune system to attack beta cells and how?

Objectives

  • Develop a computational framework to rank U12-intron genes by how likely they are to cause disease. This will combine single-cell gene expression atlases, genetic studies of type 1 diabetes and autoimmunity, and annotation to predict how sensitive each intron is to minor spliceosome failure
  • Confirm that the top-ranked genes are misspliced in patient cells
  • Switch off a small shortlist of genes in B cell, T cell and/or beta cell models. Test the effect on key processes such as immune activation, tolerance, antigen presentation, cell stress and survival.

Methodology

  • Year 1 - prioritise candidate genes by analysis of publicly available data including single-cell RNA sequencing data from immune and pancreas cells, alongside existing patient RNAseq and immune data
  • Year 2 - measure intron retention of key genes in patient-derived cells using our established droplet digital PCR assay and establish the cell models
  • Years 2–3 - knockdown/knockout (e.g. CRISPR or siRNA) of 3–5 highest priority genes. Readouts will include flow cytometry, cytokine measurement and RNA sequencing
  • Final year - integrate findings, publish data, write and submit thesis

Interdisciplinary aspects of the project

The project spans data science, human genetics, immunology and cell biology. The student will be trained in computational analysis (R/Python, single-cell and public genomic data) and in laboratory methods (cell culture, CRISPR gene editing, digital PCR, flow cytometry).

We welcome applicants from biological, biomedical, computational, mathematical or data science backgrounds. Full training will be provided in unfamiliar areas.

Expected outcomes

  • An empirically defined set of U12-intron genes implicated in autoimmune diabetes
  • New understanding of how U12-intron containing genes shape immune and beta cell behaviour
  • New biomarkers and/or drug targets for type 1 diabetes and other common autoimmune conditions
  • Publications, conference presentations and a versatile skill set spanning dry (computational) and wet laboratory research

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Decoding the rules of human gene interaction networks using combinatorial functional genomics
jobs.description_html:
Large-scale sequencing initiatives have identified thousands of genetic variants associated with human traits and disease. However, understanding how these variants influence biology remains a major challenge because genes do not act independently but within interconnected networks. Existing approaches, including CRISPR screens, have transformed gene discovery but remain poorly suited to measuring dose-dependent and higher-order genetic interactions. This limits our ability to understand how gene networks generate cellular phenotypes and how genetic variation contributes to disease.

This project addresses a fundamental question in functional genomics: how do combinations of genes interact to determine cell behaviour? The student will develop and apply innovative technologies to map genetic interactions in human cells, generating new insights into how gene networks influence health and disease. The project builds on our recently developed multiplexed Variable Dose Analysis (mVDA) technology, supported by preliminary data demonstrating robust detection of genetic interactions and integration with single-cell sequencing in Drosophila cells. mVDA enables simultaneous perturbation of multiple genes across a range of knockdown efficiencies, providing greater sensitivity and higher throughput than conventional screening approaches.

Adapting mVDA for human cells represents a significant technical advance with the potential to transform genetic interaction mapping.

The project has three objectives. First, the student will adapt and optimise mVDA in human cells, using established control interactions. Second, they will integrate this approach with either live-cell microscopy or single-cell sequencing, depending on interest. Live imaging provides sensitive phenotypic measurements, while single-cell sequencing offers scalability for large screens. Third, the student will apply the platform as a proof-of-concept to investigate genetic interactions involving the tumour suppressor NF1. As NF1-associated tumours have proven difficult to treat with single agents, they provide an ideal test case for a screening platform designed to identify interacting genes and potential combination therapies.

The project is highly interdisciplinary, integrating functional genomics, molecular genetics, imaging, bioinformatics, statistics and data science. Training will include genetic perturbation technologies, advanced microscopy, single-cell genomics, computational analysis, statistical modelling and reproducible research practices. The project is intentionally flexible, allowing the student to shape its direction as their interests and expertise develop. For example, there are opportunities to focus on technology development, computational methods, network analysis or biological applications depending on their interests and expertise.

The student will join a collaborative research environment with access to state-of-the-art facilities for high-throughput screening, live-cell imaging, single-cell sequencing and computational methods. The project will be supported by expertise within the Functional Genomics Screening Laboratory and the Exeter Living Systems Institute, providing opportunities to work across disciplines and engage with national functional genomics networks.

Expected outcomes include validation of mVDA for genetic interaction mapping in human cells, development of analytical approaches for interpreting combinatorial perturbation data, and new understanding of NF1-associated gene networks. The project will help overcome a major barrier in functional genomics by enabling systematic exploration of how gene interactions generate cellular phenotypes. The student will develop a unique combination of experimental, computational and transferable skills highly relevant to careers in academia and industry. Responsible research practices, including reproducibility, FAIR data stewardship and research integrity will underpin all aspects of the project.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Editing the Alzheimer’s Epigenome: From Human Brain Variation to Functional Mechanisms
jobs.description_html:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterised by distinctive molecular changes across multiple cell types in the human brain. Epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified widespread alterations in epigenetic modifications associated with AD pathology, but a major challenge remains: which of these changes have functional consequences for gene regulation and disease biology. This question is particularly important in the brain, where different cell types have highly distinct regulatory landscapes. Using fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting (FANS), we have generated cell-type-specific epigenomic datasets from human post-mortem brain, including DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac), a marker of active regulatory elements (Ref. 1).

These unique datasets provide an opportunity to move beyond association and identify disease-associated epigenetic changes occurring within functional regulatory elements in specific brain cell types. The central question of this PhD is to identify AD-associated regions with regulatory potential, and to functionally characterise how they influence gene regulation and cellular phenotype. The project will address this through three complementary objectives. First, the student will integrate cell-type-specific DNA methylation, ATAC-seq and H3K27ac data to identify and prioritise candidate regulatory loci from our AD EWAS (Exeter).

These data will be combined with available gene expression, genetic association, and regulatory annotations to identify disease-associated epigenetic changes occurring within active promoters and enhancers and establish their likely target genes. This multi-omic approach will move beyond conventional annotation of EWAS signals based simply on proximity to the nearest gene and instead prioritise loci with strong evidence for a functional regulatory role. Second, selected regulatory loci will be functionally interrogated using targeted CRISPR epigenome editing. Catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9) fused to DNA methylation, demethylation, or chromatin remodelling enzymes will be used to induce or reverse disease-associated epigenetic states in relevant cell lines and human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neural cells (cortical neurons/microglia).

These novel methods are currently being optimised by the supervisory team funded by an FGx innovation and collaboration fund award (PI Bello, Milner Institute). Initial studies will focus on microglia, where we have identified prominent AD-associated DNA methylation differences and the possess relevant expertise (Washer), but still allowing the student to investigate neuronal or other glial mechanisms emerging from the computational analyses. Third, the student will determine the molecular and cellular consequences of these perturbations. Targeted assays will confirm epigenetic editing (e.g. bisulfite pyrosequencing), followed by analysis of gene expression and relevant cellular phenotypes.

For the strongest candidates, transcriptomic, methylomic and/or chromatin-accessibility profiling will establish how perturbation alters regulatory networks and cellular states. This interdisciplinary project combines human disease epigenomics, computational biology, stem-cell models and CRISPR-based functional genomics. The student will develop expertise spanning multi omic data integration, reproducible bioinformatics, experimental epigenomics, cell culture, epigenome editing and functional assays. Importantly, the initial analyses will allow the student to shape which loci, cell types and biological pathways are pursued experimentally.

The project is supported by extensive existing cell-type-specific datasets, established FANS and epigenomic pipelines (Dempster & Mill, Exeter), access to hiPSC-derived models of neurodegeneration (Washer (Oxford) & Bello (Cambridge)), omics (Dempster & Mill, Exeter), and expertise in targeted DNA methylation editing (Exeter, Oxford and Cambridge)

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Decoding cellular diversity in the brain: functional annotation of neuronal subtypes across development and disease
jobs.description_html:
The human brain contains an extraordinary diversity of cell types, each with distinct functions, molecular programmes and roles in disease. Even within neurons, numerous excitatory and inhibitory subtypes differ across brain regions and change across development and ageing. Understanding this diversity is essential for determining how the brain functions and why particular neuronal populations are selectively vulnerable in different brain diseases. Single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed our understanding of neuronal transcriptional diversity, but the regulatory mechanisms that establish and maintain these identities remain much less well characterised, particularly for rarer neuronal populations. We have developed methods for isolating defined cell populations from human post-mortem brain and generated multi-omic regulatory maps of major cell classes.

This PhD will extend these approaches to resolve the functional genomics of specific neuronal subtypes. The central objective is to isolate distinct neuronal populations, including excitatory and inhibitory subtypes and regionally specialised populations such as motor neurons, and determine how their regulatory landscapes vary across brain regions, development and ageing. The student will use existing single-cell and multiomic datasets to identify nuclear markers that distinguish neuronal populations, then develop fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting strategies to isolate them from human brain tissue. Samples will span cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, hypothalamus and other disease-relevant regions, with opportunities to examine development and ageing.

The project will use functional genomic technologies to characterise gene regulation within these populations. Approaches will include Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing to map DNA modifications, ATAC-seq to identify accessible regulatory elements, and CUT&Tag profiling of H3K27ac to identify active enhancers and promoters.

A particular focus will be direct measurement of DNA hydroxymethylation, an abundant neuronal DNA modification likely to have important regulatory functions. Long-read RNA sequencing will define full-length transcripts and cell-specific isoform usage, with opportunities to explore direct RNA sequencing and the neuronal epitranscriptome. Together these datasets will provide a functional annotation of neuronal diversity, identifying regulatory elements, transcripts and epigenetic features that distinguish populations across regions and stages of life.

They will also be used to interpret human genetic studies of neurological and psychiatric disease, including whole-genome sequencing and association datasets from large national cohorts. A further objective will be to use these high-resolution reference maps to develop computational methods for estimating the proportions and molecular states of specific neuronal populations in bulk brain datasets. These deconvolution approaches can then be applied to extensive in-house DNA methylation datasets from disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, enabling disease-associated molecular changes to be assigned to specific neuronal populations.

This is a highly interdisciplinary project spanning epigenomics, genomics, molecular biology, neuroscience and computational biology. The student will be based in Exeter (Mill, Dempster, Bamford) with collaborators at Imperial (Nott), KCL (Marzi), Cambridge (Ryten) and EBI-EMBL (Birney). The project is supported by exceptional resources, including existing multiomic human brain datasets, post-mortem tissue (multiple brain regions and developmental stages), cell-sorting platforms, state of-the-art sequencing facilities, and extensive high-performance computing. The resulting datasets and computational tools will provide a framework for understanding neuronal function and identifying the cell populations and regulatory mechanisms through which genetic and epigenetic variation contributes to brain disease.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Allele-resolved genetics and epigenetics in type 2 diabetes
jobs.description_html:
Type 2 diabetes (T2D) affects over 800 million people worldwide. It is a complex disorder and an individual’s genetics influences disease risk. Understanding how DNA differences drive this risk can enable disease prediction and personalised approaches to diagnosis and treatment, addressing the shortfall between genetic discovery and patient benefit.  Large scale genetic studies have identified hundreds of DNA regions linked to increased T2D risk. Most lie in regulatory regions, areas of DNA outside the genes that control when and where a gene is turned on. Changes here impact how islets – clusters of pancreatic cells that produce hormones including insulin – regulate blood glucose.  Interpreting these DNA changes is complicated because we inherit two parental copies of our genome, and the disease-causing changes generally reside on only one. Standard technologies merge data from both copies, making it challenging to resolve which DNA changes contribute to disease. 

This project will use chromatin stencilling (known as Fiber-seq), a cutting-edge technology, to address this problem.  This long-read sequencing technology simultaneously measures regulatory activity, epigenetic state, and genotype and allows us to distinguish the two parental copies of the genome.  Key question How do genetic variants associated with T2D alter regulatory activity on each inherited copy of our genome in pancreatic islets?

This will be achieved by:

  1. Generating unprecedented chromatin stencilling maps of DNA regulatory activity from healthy pancreatic islet donors.
  2. Targeting specific disease loci in islets from genetically selected type 2 diabetes donors to pinpoint failing regulation.
  3. Decoding how genetic changes affect DNA regulation, enabling the interpretation of diabetes associated genetics in large studies like the UK Biobank. Interdisciplinary Approach This project brings together laboratory genetics, epigenetics, long-read sequencing and extensive data science. The student will join the Gene Regulatory Defects in Disease Group at the University of Exeter, an interdisciplinary team of laboratory and computer scientists. The project will allow the student to shape the research direction, and they will receive expert supervision, training, and collaboration with international leaders.

The student will develop translatable skills in experimental design, DNA sequencing, bioinformatics and interpreting complex biological data.  Methodology Healthy and T2D islets will be selected using genetic, clinical, and existing molecular data. The islets will undergo our chromatin stencilling protocol, and the DNA will be sequenced using Oxford Nanopore. These long reads allow us to map activity to each inherited DNA copy and assess copy specific regulation.  Targeted sequencing will also provide deep coverage at selected disease regions. 

Computational analyses will then identify differences in DNA accessibility and methylation, resolving cell-type specific regulation and annotating regulatory protein binding sites. This will be combined with large-scale genetic (e.g. UK Biobank) to improve interpretation of variants in T2D.  Outcomes This project will generate the most detailed maps to date of gene regulation in healthy and T2D pancreatic islets, improving our understanding of the genetic basis for T2D. The resulting openly shared annotations and datasets will be a resource for the community. Student training will also be a significant output, they will gain cross-discipline expertise in long-read sequencing, epigenetics, computational biology, and statistical genetics.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Functional genomic approaches to convergent mechanisms in chromatinopathies
jobs.description_html:
Background

Chromatinopathies is a group of more than 180 rare genetic disorders caused by variants in genes encoding chromatin remodelling factors . Collectively, these disorders are amongst the most prevalent genetic conditions and are often characterised by neurodevelopmental features including developmental delay, intellectual disability and autism. Currently, no treatments exist for most chromatinopathies. Developing a personalised, targeted treatment for each of chromatinopathy represents a major, if not an impossible task. We hypothesised that the mechanisms of some chromatinopathies converge on overlapping pathways raising the possibility that the same drugs could potentially treat several chromatinopathies. Indeed, our initial studies have shown that the same class of drugs can rescue neurodevelopmental phenotypes in relevant mouse models. This opens an exciting opportunity to use functional genomics to investigate the fundamental biology of this important group of disorders and fulfil a major unmet medical need by discovering new treatments.

Key question and objectives

We have prioritised three related chromatinopathies to study in this project. The key question of this project is “What are the transcriptomic and epigenomic changes in the brain that characterise these chromatinopathies and how do they respond to treatment?”

Specific objectives are:

  1. To identify the cell types, genes and chromatin changes that characterise each of these chromatinopathies and identify convergent pathways in relevant mouse models.
  2. To test how treatment modifies the transcriptomic and epigenomic landscape in the brains of these mouse models.
  3. To test is the treatment can rescue behavioural phenotypes in the mouse models.

Methodology

The student will work closely with an expert post-doctoral scientist in the lab and will use a range of next generation sequencing based approaches to investigate the effects of these treatments on the epigenome and transcriptome and mouse behavioural assessments. The sequencing data for some of these experiments have already been collected and can be analysed straight away.

Parse snRNAseq will be used to compare gene expression differences in cell types of the mouse frontal cortex in mice, bulk RNA-seq to detect global transcriptional changes and CUT&Tag-seq to compare effects on the hypothesised convergent chromatin alterations.

Mouse behavioural tests will be employed to determine if key neurodevelopmental phenotypes in defined mouse models can be rescued by drug treatment. Tests for anxiety, activity, repetitive behaviours, social behaviours, motor function and learning and cognitive tests to assess learning and memory will be used.

Equivalent samples from mouse frontal cortex treated with drug will be analysed in parallel to identify the convergent molecular targets of drug treatment. Data from human neurons, from patient-derived and control induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) treated with the same drug is also available and can be compared directly with the data from the mouse models.

Expected outcomes

We expect to show that a single drug can rescue behavioural phenotypes in mouse models of several chromatinopathies and identify convergent epigenetic mechanisms that respond to the same drug to normalise aberrant gene expression in the frontal cortex.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Cut and project schemes in hyperbolic space with applications to acoustic metamaterials
jobs.description_html:
Alternative splicing enables a single gene to produce multiple mRNA isoforms, and potentially proteins with distinct functions. It is especially important in the brain, where transcript diversity supports development and ageing. Studies have implicated disrupted RNA splicing in neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Yet detecting a novel mRNA isoform does not prove that it is translated into a stable, functional protein. Establishing which transcripts reach the proteome is a major challenge in functional genomics. Long-read sequencing allows complete RNA molecules to be characterised, and studies have uncovered extensive unannotated transcript diversity in the human brain.

If transcripts are predicted to have coding potential, then these novel transcripts contain uncharacterised coding sequences (CDS). Our research has identified over 20,000 novel transcripts in the brain with CDS. These are a result of alternative splicing events such as exon skipping, alternative transcriptional start/end sites and fusion transcripts. Preliminary analyses suggest that genetic variation affecting these sequences is associated with neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions. The key question is ‘which novel brain mRNA isoforms are translated into proteins, and what are their functional and disease-relevant consequences?’

Objective 1 is to identify and prioritise novel CDS predicted to generate new protein isoforms, alter known proteins, or change the balance between functionally distinct isoforms. The initial focus will be on genes involved in brain development, ageing and disorders.

Objective 2 is to determine whether prioritised transcripts are translated. The student will integrate transcriptomic and proteomic data and validate selected candidates using mass spectrometry and Quantum-Si single-molecule protein sequencing. These approaches will also investigate protein isoforms and post-translational modifications.

Objective 3 is to establish how selected isoforms affect protein expression, localisation, interactions, and function using cell models. This interdisciplinary project combines bioinformatics, transcriptomics, proteomics and molecular biology. It is a combined bioinformatics and wet laboratory project. The focus will be on brain and blood, not any neuropsychiatric disease or disorder – this is open for the student to take a lead on genes of interest (candidate genes are available). This project can be steered towards where the student’s talent meets interest. The project involves bioinformatic analysis - prioritising the best targets to take forward for proteomics and then functional validation.

The student will analyse long-read datasets and can incorporate single-nucleus, spatial transcriptomic and public data to select candidates for experimental validation. Full computational and laboratory training will be provided, with opportunities to work with international collaborators developing methods for long-read transcriptome–proteome analysis and integration. The student will prepare proteomics samples from postmortem human brain for mass spectrometry and Quantum-si single protein molecule sequencing. Key splicing events will be investigated in cell models using protein extraction, co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting to determine whether the resulting proteins have distinct biological effects. The expected outcome will be a comprehensive analysis and validation of predicted novel CDS in the brain, with a better understanding of the functional consequences of these downstream and their involvement in neuropsychiatric disease and disorder.

The student will join an internationally recognised environment in brain genomics, long-read sequencing and functional genomics, with extensive datasets, advanced bioinformatics and high performance computing. The student will have access to all necessary laboratory facilities and equipment to support the project.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Cut and project schemes in hyperbolic space with applications to acoustic metamaterials
jobs.description_html:
The discovery of quasicrystals – honoured with the 2011 Chemistry Nobel prize – has generated and continues to stimulate a tremendous amount of research in the international mathematics and physics communities. Questions concerning the characterisation of order versus disorder, diffraction and spectral theory are extensively studied. Mathematical methods involved range from number theory and geometry, to ergodic theory and harmonic analysis, over to noncommutative geometry. Central to understanding properties of physical quasicrystals and acoustic metamaterials (deliberately engineered composites with bespoke wave-control properties that arise from their structure) is the careful analysis of point sets arising from, for instance, cut and project schemes.

Here, loosely speaking, one takes a straight-line cutting through a square lattice, projects a given window of lattice points onto the straight-line, and considers the resulting point set. This method has recently been adapted by examining what happens when instead of a straight-line one takes a quadratic curve. Using this new construction, Davies, Chaplain, Starkey and Craster, built new acoustic metamaterials with large spectral gaps, yielding high performing sound insulators. This work raised the open question: Can developing new cut and project models, where the lattice is not square or the curve is non-linear, generate better performing graded metamaterials?

Drawing on the rich body of results in the mathematical study of aperiodic order, ergodic theory and hyperbolic geometry, in its first part, this project aims to answer the theoretical aspects of this question, by enhancing the mathematical theory of cut and project schemes in hyperbolic space, and by extracting spectral information of diffraction measures and associated Schrödinger operators arising from the resulting point sets. Building on this, the focus of the second part is to initiate investigations on building and testing new metamaterials based on the mathematical theory developed in the first part of this project.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Virtual brain networks to guide deep brain stimulation in childhood epilepsy
jobs.description_html:
Around a third of children with epilepsy continue to have seizures despite medication. For those who cannot be helped by conventional surgery, electrical stimulation delivered by an implanted device is one of the few remaining options. Its use is expanding quickly, yet responses vary widely between children, and there is still no principled way to decide where to stimulate, or with what settings, for an individual patient. These choices are currently made by careful trial and error over many months.

This project uses mathematical models of brain networks to help predict efficacy of stimulation. Seizures are increasingly understood as emergent properties of brain networks, which makes them well suited to the tools of nonlinear dynamics and network science. We use multimodal imaging to develop patient-specific, mathematical models of brain networks that can be used to quantify the dynamics of brain networks. These models can then be used to predict the effect of stimulation and to probe the location and timings that most effectively alleviate seizures.

You will develop methods for constructing these models from patient recordings, implement and simulate stimulation within them, and evaluate how far their predictions correspond to measured effects using clinical data. The project therefore combines many interesting problems in mathematics, statistics and computational neuroscience including development of physiological models of neurostimulation, understanding and quantifying the dynamics of networked systems, model and parameter inference, uncertainty quantification and efficient simulation of large dynamical systems. There is scope to shape the direction of the work according to your own interests.

You will join a supportive research group at Exeter with established expertise in the mathematics of brain dynamics, and will be co-supervised by clinicians working in paediatric neurosurgery. You therefore have the opportunity to gain unique insight and training in real world clinical uses of mathematics and statistics.  We welcome applicants from mathematics, physics, engineering, computer science, quantitative neuroscience or related disciplines. Prior experience of neuroscience or clinical research is not required, and training will be provided.

Informal enquiries are warmly encouraged.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Arithmetic Moments and Random Matrix Statistics over Function Fields
jobs.description_html:
The study of L-functions — their moments, zero statistics, and connections to random matrix theory — sits at the heart of modern analytic number theory. Function fields over finite fields 𝔽_q provide a setting where deep conjectures first posed for classical L-functions become rigorously provable, thanks to tools unavailable over the integers, including the Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields (Weil) and the equidistribution results of Katz and Sarnak. This project develops three interlinked strands of research at the interface of number theory, arithmetic statistics, and random matrix theory. Strand 1: Moments of L-functions at s = 1. For a family of quadratic Dirichlet characters χ_D associated to squarefree polynomials D ∈ 𝔽_q[T], the analytic class number formula relates the special value L(1,χ_D) directly to the class number h(D) of the corresponding function field. While moments of L(1/2,χ_D) at the central point are well studied, moments of the shape M_k(q) = Σ_{deg D = 2g+1} L(1,χ_D)^k remain comparatively unexplored.

This strand develops asymptotic formulae for M_k(q) as q or the degree of D grows, with direct consequences for the statistical distribution of class numbers h(D) and for related counting problems in arithmetic statistics. Analogous questions for other families of L-functions may also be pursued. Strand 2: Correlations of arithmetic function over 𝔽_q[T]. Building on algebraic approaches that encode divisor-type functions via the cycle structure of permutations associated to polynomials over 𝔽_q[T], this strand studies shifted correlation sums Σ_{deg f = n} d_k(f) d_k(f+a) for the k fold divisor function d_k and fixed shift a ∈ 𝔽_q[T], together with their connections to the moments in Strand 1 via multiplicative structure and to conjectural analogues of the classical divisor-correlation (Ingham/Titchmarsh-type) problems. Other problems concerning the distribution of arithmetic functions over function fields may also be investigated. Strand 3: Moments of moments of characteristic polynomials. For a random matrix A drawn from the unitary, symplectic, or orthogonal groups with characteristic polynomial Λ_A(θ), the moments of moments M_N(k,β) = 𝔼[ ( (1/2π) ∫₀^{2π} |Λ_A(θ)|^{2β} dθ )^k ] encode fine statistical information connecting random matrix theory to Painlevé equations and partition functions in mathematical physics.

Extending recent results on joint moments of derivatives of Λ_A across matrix ensembles, this strand develops new formulae for M_N(k,β) in previously untreated Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award regimes of k and β, strengthening the emerging dictionary between these statistics and moments of L-functions established in Strand 1. Across all three strands, the project offers scope to explore AI-assisted methods — symbolic computation and machine-learning-based pattern detection — as a complementary tool for conjecture generation and numerical verification alongside classical analytic and algebraic techniques, providing interdisciplinary experience at the interface of pure mathematics and computation. Scope and flexibility. The three strands above are intended as guidance for the general direction of the research rather than a fixed programme. Other projects, problems and topics within analytic number theory, function-field arithmetic and random matrix theory may be selected by the supervisors and pursued instead, depending on the background and interests of the successful candidate and in agreement with the supervisors. The successful candidate will be trained in at least one of the following: analytic number theory, function-field arithmetic, and random matrix theory.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Understanding osteogenic potential using musculoskeletal and finite element modelling
jobs.description_html:
Osteoporosis is a bone-wasting disease that makes bones thin, weak and more likely to break. Breaking bones in the hip and spine is painful and life-changing. It affects more women (1 in 2) than men (1 in 5) because women have smaller bones, lose bone-protecting hormones after the menopause and typically experience less impact activity earlier in life. Osteoporosis can be prevented or delayed by stimulating bone via load bearing exercise earlier in life. However, despite some generic advice being available (for example 50 impacts a day), there is limited advice on how to make up an appropriate exercise regimen for bone health and frailty prevention. With very limited advice on exercise selection, frequency, duration and intensity.

Many studies have investigated the effects of different exercise modalities on bone health however, these studies vary in exercise selection, intervention length, frequency and intensity giving a heterogeneous body of literature and ultimately leading to poor understanding of the features of exercise that maximise osteogenic growth that could be easily integrated into daily living. A key driver of osteogenic growth and remodelling is the peak intensity of stress a bone experiences during a bout of exercise. This is difficult to measure in vivo, as it requires highly invasive surgery to implant bone strain gauges.

Alternatively, modelling is a valuable non-invasive method by which individual responses of bones to exercise can be estimated, allowing both highly subject and site-specific responses to exercises to be estimated, but also allowing “what if” questions to be investigated. Previous work by our group has developed an initial bone stress modelling data pipeline that can estimate bone stress in the femoral neck during activities. This project aims to build on this work by investigating the effects of different exercise interventions on bone stress, investigating individual responses to exercise (e.g. the effect of the size and shape of individuals bone on the estimated stress) and correlating a simple to use metric (e.g. data from an inertial measurement unit or accelerometer) with estimated stresses in order to allow an easy to use metric to be presented to the public to engage with their bone health in a meaningful way.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Digital Movement Biomarkers of Mood and Fatigue in Older Adults: Using Computer Vision, Artificial Intelligence and Functional Movement Analysis to Detect Anxiety, Depression and Fatigue in People With and Without Multiple longterm conditions
jobs.description_html:
Digital Movement Biomarkers of Mood and Fatigue in Older Adults: Using Computer Vision, Artificial Intelligence and Functional Movement Analysis to Detect Anxiety, Depression and Fatigue in People with and without Multiple Long-Term Conditions (MLTCs) Depression, anxiety and fatigue are among the most common and disabling symptoms experienced by older adults living with multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs), including stroke, Parkinson's disease, frailty, arthritis and mild cognitive impairment. These symptoms are associated with reduced mobility, poorer rehabilitation outcomes, loss of independence, increased healthcare utilisation and lower quality of life.

However, detecting changes in mood and fatigue within these populations remains challenging. Symptoms often overlap with physical impairments, cognitive changes and disease-related functional limitations, making accurate identification difficult and delaying intervention. As the prevalence of MLTCs continues to rise, improving the objective detection and monitoring of mood-related symptoms has become a major healthcare and research priority. Current assessment approaches rely primarily on self-report questionnaires and clinical interviews conducted during infrequent healthcare encounters. These methods are subjective, vulnerable to reporting bias and often fail to capture subtle fluctuations that occur between appointments. There is therefore a critical need for innovative and scalable technologies capable of objectively assessing psychological wellbeing.

Emerging evidence suggests that depression, anxiety and fatigue influence movement behaviour, affecting posture, balance, movement variability, transfers and overall functional performance. Advances in computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI) now provide a unique opportunity to quantify these movement signatures using standard 2D video recordings. Markerless pose estimation methods can extract detailed skeletal movement information from low-cost RGB cameras without wearable sensors or specialist laboratory equipment, creating opportunities for large-scale deployment across healthcare, community and home settings.

This PhD aims to develop and validate digital movement biomarkers capable of detecting depression, anxiety and fatigue from functional movement recordings in older adults with and without MLTCs. A major strength of the project is the availability of an existing, richly characterised dataset that has already been collected. The dataset comprises more than 1,000 functional movement assessments from adults aged 60 years and older, including healthy individuals and people living with stroke, Parkinson's disease, frailty, arthritis and mild cognitive impairment. Associated measures include demographics, clinical characteristics, functional outcomes, mood assessments and fatigue scales, providing a unique foundation for the development and validation of novel digital biomarkers. The project will first apply state-of-the-art computer vision approaches, including OpenPose, MediaPipe and MoveNet, to extract biomechanical and behavioural features from videos of posture, balance, transfers, walking and activities of daily living.

Extracted variables will include spatiotemporal characteristics, joint kinematics, movement smoothness, symmetry, postural alignment and inter-limb coordination. Traditional statistical techniques will establish interpretable baseline relationships between movement patterns and measures of depression, anxiety and fatigue. Nonlinear movement analyses, including entropy measures, fractal dynamics and recurrence based metrics, will then be used to identify subtle neurobehavioural signatures that may not be captured through conventional biomechanical approaches. Building on these features, the research will develop a hierarchical AI framework for digital biomarker discovery. Explainable machine learning models, including Random Forests, XGBoost and LightGBM.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Development of New Generation Corrosion-resistant Aluminium Alloys
jobs.description_html:
This 3.5-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive a tax-free annual stipend at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27, subject to annual uplift), with tuition fees fully covered. The stipend is expected to increase each year. The start date is October 2027.

We strongly encourage early applications, as the advert may close before the stated deadline.

Applications are invited for a full time PhD Studentship in research on new generation corrosion resistant aluminium alloys at the Department of Materials, The University of Manchester. The successful applicant will receive an annual stipend (bursary) plus payment of their full time Home tuition fees for 4 years.

Advanced aluminium alloys have a key role in the aerospace and automotive industries for structural components. However, the increasing global demand for aluminium alloys will only be met in the near term by the circulation of secondary metals, which inevitably introduces impurities to alloys. Increased additions of impurities like iron or deliberate additions like copper and nickel can be detrimentalto corrosion resistance particularly in the accelerated tests used for qualification with automotive OEMs. This means that there is a strong research incentive to improve the corrosion performance of wrought high strength aluminium alloys in response to this demand and to formulate these alloys from end-of life recycled aluminium to reduce embedded carbon level to below 2 tonnes CO2e/tonne of aluminium as a supplied component and eventually to Net Zero carbon.

This project is concerned with development of high strength aluminium alloys designed to provide better performance compared with existing alloys. The properties of this alloy depend on careful control of the microstructure, in particular the second phase particles and recrystallization. The project aims to understand the complex interactions between alloy chemistry, processing, microstructure and performance. The alloy microstructure will be characterised by using advanced high resolution electron microscopy. The relationship between the fabrication process parameters and the microstructure of the alloys will be investigated. The assessment of performance will be based on correlative accelerated laboratory testing and electrochemical measurements. The newly developed X-ray and electron-based nanotomography will also be employed to spatially determine the microstructure features that are responsible for the initiation and propagation of alloy degradation.

This project provides a unique opportunity to combine pioneering academic research with industrial experience. In addition to the access to state-of-the-art facilities, the student also has the opportunity to develop interdisciplinary skills and to work in a team environment involving over 8 PhD students and researchers, leading academics and industrial experts. The group runs regular seminars and social events. The industrial collaborators will work closely with the student during the project and opportunities exist for gaining exposure to the industrial manufacturing environment in Europe.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

To apply please contact the main supervisor; Prof Xiaorong Zhou. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Computer vision to predict falls from everyday movement in older adults
jobs.description_html:
Falls are the most common cause of injury-related hospital admission and death among older adults, yet fall prevention has made little measurable progress for two decades. Around a third of people aged 65 and over fall each year, and falls result in around 210,000 emergency hospital admissions a year in England. Current risk assessment relies on brief clinical tests, carried out once, in a clinic. These tests reveal little about how a person moves through an ordinary day, which is when most falls happen. Our recent research on real world falls recorded with wearable sensors has shown what goes wrong. Most falls happen indoors, during everyday actions such as standing up, sitting down, walking and turning, and 82% involve interaction with furniture or other objects.

We recently identified the common movements most often present before a fall, yet people rarely report them. In addition, in people with neurological conditions, movement becomes measurably abnormal in the minutes before a fall. We then recreated these high-risk situations in the STEPPING OUT Home Scene, a simulated home at the University's VSimulators facility, within Professor Sallie Lamb's ERC-funded programme. Older adults stand up, sit down, turn, move around furniture, open doors, change surfaces and respond to slips and trips while multi camera video, motion capture and wearable sensors record every movement. Participants' clinical and falls histories are known, fallers with non-fallers.

Data collection is ongoing, and by the start of the studentship, data from around 225 participants will have been collected. This PhD asks whether a simple camera can see what an experienced clinician sees. The aims are to: (1) derive measures of stability and movement quality from markerless pose estimation, validated against motion capture; (2) find the movement patterns and markers of instability that distinguish people who fall from those who do not, including near-falls and the moments before a loss of balance; (3) test how well these measures predict falls and how early change can be detected; and (4) make the methods work on low-cost devices in homes, care homes and hospitals, with processing on the device. 

The student will use pose estimation, deep learning for movement sequences and self supervised learning, with interpretability as a priority so that clinicians can understand and act on the results. Deliverables include a validated pipeline, open benchmarks for stability assessment from video, evidence on how well falls can be predicted from ordinary video, and a tested low-cost prototype. The studentship offers training across computer vision, data science, biomechanics and clinical falls research, with a supportive supervisory team spanning all of these areas.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Living materials in nature: active matter, behaviour and bee nests
jobs.description_html:
Self-organised systems in animals, such as the nests of social insects, have evolved to offer advantages that support survival across diverse habitats and climates. These nests represent ideal systems to study materials and their role in dynamic physical and biological processes. This PhD project explores how active bumblebee nests maintain efficient thermoregulation, combining perspectives from multiple disciplines to uncover the mechanisms that enable this remarkable feat. The level of complexity and self-regulation in bumblebee nests raises interesting, unsolved questions that are of a general nature and apply more broadly to a wide range of species that live collectively, from bees to humans. For instance, are the adopted structures a form of biometamaterial, designed to manipulate heat?

How are efficiency, equilibrium and resilience maintained through social information, self-organisation of behaviour and space use? In social insect colonies, individual efforts are joined and balanced across a range of behavioural tasks resulting in elaborate shelters for the colony and its offspring, fine-tuned control of the nest's internal conditions, effective nest maintenance and defence. This is all achieved without a need for centralised control. Individual insects make decisions based on information gathered through interactions with nest mates and from their surroundings, including nest structures, materials and climatic conditions. Bumblebee nests are particularly suited to explore such questions and combine empirical and modelling approaches.

There is opportunity in this project to develop those and combine them where suitable. The successful candidate will join a collaborative team of supervisors with complementary interdisciplinary and methodological expertise and address innovative research questions at the interface of physics, material engineering and behavioural science. This work will make a significant contribution to the nascent field of active matter and biometamaterials where emergent material properties are governed by movement and energy exchange between components. These new types of material form an exciting and promising branch of metamaterials (an area where the University of Exeter plays a major research and leadership role in the UK) with uses across a whole range of applications, including thermal management. Adaptability of nests to changes in environments and climate determine the resilience of bee population and pollination services.

By exploring how structures and materials can meet the thermoregulatory demands of these pollinators, this project endeavours to make a meaningful contribution across materials science, ecology and environmental monitoring. We look for a candidate with a background in natural sciences, life sciences, physics or engineering, with an interest in modelling and/or experimental approaches that are motivated by the application of physics-based solutions to environmental and biological problems. The successful candidate will benefit from working within lively and interdisciplinary research environments and have access to sophisticated experimental facilities and equipment.

The work will be based on the UoE's Streatham campus; in the Exeter Bee Lab of the Centre for Research in Animal Behaviour (CRAB, https://psychology.exeter.ac.uk/research/centres/crab/), supervised by Professor Natalie Hempel de Ibarra, and in the Centre for Metamaterial Research and Innovation, spending time in the lab of the second supervisor Dr David Horsell (https://www.exeter.ac.uk/research/metamaterials) as well as interacting with the other co supervisors in the departments of Physics and Engineering.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The emotional basis of behaviour
jobs.description_html:
Emotions and mood states are notoriously difficult to study in non-human animals, but recent years have seen important progress in inferring these states and their links to behaviour and welfare. For example, the use of judgment-bias tasks has shown that differences in housing conditions for captive animals can generate ‘optimistic’ or ‘pessimistic’ attitudes towards ambiguous stimuli. The fundamental question that has not yet been addressed, however, is why evolution would favour a decision-making system guided by emotions, rather than a ‘cold’, unemotional, rational mapping directly from stimuli to behaviour.

One important idea is that emotions act as a physiological memory of past experiences, and thus provide a valuable information source for making adaptive decisions in real-world environments. In previous theoretical work (Higginson et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2017.2411), we have shown that in an environment characterised by temporal autocorrelation, a simple rule for foraging behaviour based purely on current hunger performs almost as well as an optimal strategy that uses Bayesian learning to integrate information from all previous experiences.
