More generally, across a wide variety of contexts, past experiences might be efficiently summarised by internal state variables (like hunger) that can be used to guide future decisions, without the need for cognitively demanding Bayesian computations.

This points to the intriguing possibility that such internal state variables are the physiological basis and evolutionary precursor of emotions and mood states. In this PhD project you will use evolutionary modelling and artificial neural networks to identify adaptive emotion-based systems for decision-making in specified real-world scenarios (e.g. finding food in a dangerous environment; finding mates in a competitive environment). You will then compare the performance (in terms of biological fitness) of the emotional decision-making system to that of an unemotional, Bayesian system that explicitly computes the optimal decision based on current information. This comparison will reveal the conditions under which emotions are favoured by evolutionary pressures. This is an innovative, interdisciplinary project that will shed light on the fundamental evolutionary basis of emotions, and potentially explain some empirically observed cases of irrational or maladaptive behaviour.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Sensing the Ocean Through Surfing: A New Wave in Ocean Observation
jobs.description_html:
Understanding how the ocean is changing requires observations that are increasingly extensive in both space and time. However, conventional oceanographic observations rely on relatively expensive and specialised instruments deployed from research vessels, autonomous platforms or fixed observing stations. These approaches provide high quality measurements, but their cost and logistical requirements limit the spatial coverage of observations, particularly in dynamic coastal environments. At the same time, millions of people interact with the ocean every year through recreational activities such as surfing, creating a largely untapped opportunity for environmental observation. Using surfers and surfboards as a trial group, this project will investigate whether recreational platforms can be transformed into low-cost platforms for ocean observation. It builds directly on previous research developing low-cost environmental sensing technologies and will combine expertise in biological and physical oceanography, engineering and environmental sensing.

The project will develop and integrate miniaturised sensors capable of measuring key environmental properties while a surfboard is being used, and investigate how these observations can be collected, quality controlled and combined to produce useful environmental datasets. The research will address four key challenges. First, how can low-cost environmental sensors be robustly integrated into recreational platforms like surfboards without affecting their normal use? Second, how accurately can these sensors measure environmental properties under the challenging and highly variable conditions experienced during recreational activities? Third, how can observations collected opportunistically by multiple recreational users be integrated to provide meaningful information about spatial and temporal variability in coastal environments? Fourthly, what are the key motivators recreational water users have to participate in data collection. The student will work across sensor development, experimental testing, field observations, data analysis, and social citizen science, supported by expertise within the University of Exeter and University of North Carolina Wilmington, and through collaboration with a UK surfboard manufacturer and open-hardware company.

Engineering expertise will support sensor Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award integration and platform design, while marine science expertise will underpin the interpretation and validation of the observations. The project will also explore approaches for combining these new observations with existing satellite, autonomous and conventional oceanographic datasets. The research has the potential to establish a new model for distributed and accessible ocean observation, complementing existing observing systems rather than replacing them.

Success in this project will show how a whole range of recreational platforms could provide observations in locations and at frequencies that are difficult or expensive to achieve using conventional approaches, while simultaneously engaging ocean users in environmental monitoring. The project will provide the foundation for a longer-term research programme exploring how emerging technologies and everyday platforms can be harnessed to increase our ability to observe the ocean. Ultimately, it aims to demonstrate that the people who use the ocean can also help us observe it, creating new opportunities to understand and monitor rapidly changing coastal environments.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Digital twinning for post-mining environmental transitions
jobs.description_html:
Mining is a cornerstone industry that utilises natural capital. Downsizing or cessation of mining occurs when ore deposits become subeconomic or exhausted. The loss of a cornerstone industry, combined with limited economic diversification and negative environmental legacies, are key challenges for resilience in post-mining communities. The PhD project mission is to build sustainability on the natural capital and infrastructure foundations left behind by end-of-life extractive industries. 

The research has strategic importance because escalating resource consumption will drive a greater number of mine sites into transition, for reopening of legacy sites, care and maintenance of marginally economic mines, or closure of mines in exhausted ore bodies. Existing strategies for decision-making about reuse of mined landscapes are not adequate. This project builds the UK-based knowledge economy for responsible mining life cycles. The ultimate goal of the project is a decision-making strategy to support mine transition, from the outset of the industrial planning stage and through mine development. Identification of opportunities for economic diversification (and thereby community resilience) must be sensitive to the physical landscape and environmental protections, to minimize industrial pressure on ecosystems. 

The approaches must be robust enough to apply to multiple geological and geographic contexts because there is an ever-wider range of ore deposits being exploited. The primary case studies are overland (S Wales) and underland (Isle of Portland) mine spaces that are ready for reutilisation. A digital twin is a virtual replica that will be created for each of the two primary case study landscapes. The virtual replicas will be used to model possible reuse scenario and test alternative futures without costly mistakes and socioenvironmental missteps. Input data will be required on the alternative future landscape uses and how they are selected. The project will therefore consist of a three-step approach: (1) understand how mine sites can be reused; (2) test the suitability of alternative futures using the digital twin models for the main case studies; (3) determine how twinning tools and policy can steer decision-making towards optimized positive outcomes.

Scalability will be interrogated using wider comparisons, e.g. with SW England and the Peak District). 

Methodology:  This work will be supported by Deep Digital Cornwall (DDC) lab facility at Camborne School of Mines (CSM). Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award

The student will: 

1. Desk-survey and consult on the ways that old mine/quarry/tip sites are internationally remined for: resources, environmental restoration, tourism or cultural heritage projects, alternative and innovative manufacturing and research industries,   

2. Field-survey using remote sensing and laser scanning, for data to replicate the primary UK post-extractive underground and overground landscape case studies, 

3. Digitally twin the landscapes using the DDC lab and test how they can be reconfigured for alternative uses, 

4. Analyse the sustainability potential for the alternative options using appropriate criteria and local consultation, to optimize solutions,  

5. Develop the technical approach as an optimization tool kit that is adaptable to multiple scenario, and  

6. Determine how the approach can be used to create impact by transforming decision making for management of industrial extraction and post-extractive resilience.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Advancing Multi-Mission Satellite Radar for Monitoring Permafrost Degradation and Erosion in a Changing Arctic
jobs.description_html:
The Arctic is warming rapidly, causing widespread permafrost thaw and associated ground deformation, instability and erosion. Monitoring these changes across vast and remote Arctic regions is challenging, yet understanding how the ground responds to permafrost degradation is increasingly important for assessing environmental change and risks to infrastructure and communities. Satellite radar interferometry (InSAR) provides a powerful means of measuring ground deformation from space. However, individual satellite missions have important limitations.

Sentinel-1 operates at C-band and can lose measurement coherence over vegetated and rapidly changing surfaces, while the newly available NISAR mission provides L-band observations that can maintain greater coherence over many natural surfaces and have different sensitivity to vegetation and surface properties. The missions also have different acquisition geometries, temporal sampling and measurement uncertainties. Rather than treating these observations independently, this PhD will investigate how their complementary information can be combined to produce more complete and reliable measurements of ground deformation. The project will develop a new multi-mission InSAR framework integrating Sentinel-1 C-band and NISAR L-band observations.

Research will investigate the effects of wavelength-dependent scattering, differences in spatial and temporal sampling, viewing geometry and measurement uncertainty on the integration of observations from the two missions. Importantly, the complementary viewing geometries of the two missions, with Sentinel-1 operating in a right looking configuration and NISAR providing left-looking observations, offer an opportunity to better constrain the north–south deformation component, which is poorly resolved by either mission independently due to their near-polar orbits. New joint inversion approaches will therefore be developed to exploit these complementary geometries alongside the heterogeneous multi-frequency observations to improve estimates of temporally evolving three dimensional ground deformation. Arctic permafrost environments will provide a demanding real-world testbed for developing and evaluating these methods.

Satellite-derived deformation will be investigated in relation to active-layer thickness, permafrost degradation and progressive ground instability, including riverbank and coastal erosion. Through collaboration with Montana State University, the project will benefit from complementary geotechnical expertise and access to extensive in Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award situ active-layer-thickness observations for validation and interpretation.

The project will also offer the opportunity for a research visit to Montana State University, providing experience within an international, interdisciplinary research environment. The student will work with large Earth observation datasets and high-performance computing, including the COMET-LiCSAR processing framework and JASMIN, the UK’s data analysis facility for environmental science. The project will provide advanced training in satellite radar remote sensing, InSAR, inverse methods, scientific programming and environmental data analysis. Although demonstrated in the Arctic, the resulting multi-mission methodology will have wider potential for monitoring landslides, subsidence, volcanic deformation and other geohazards.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Engineering Ceramic Powder Feedstocks for Additive Manufacturing of Components for Extreme Environments
jobs.description_html:
Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and presents a significant socioeconomic burden from direct treatment costs, and indirect costs due to losses in productivity. An ageing population, combined with increases in inactivity and obesity is expected to further increase this burden. Low back pain is initially treated conservatively, but approximately 20% of patients will require surgery. However, spinal surgery is expensive, clinical outcomes are relatively poor, and reoperation rates are relatively high (~20% within 10 years). Spinal surgery often uses pedicle screws and rods to provide stabilisation.

However, screw loosening and pull-out are major complications, particularly in patients with poor bone quality (e.g., osteoporosis), which can result in pain and instability, ultimately requiring expensive revision surgery. The design of screws has been adapted to mitigate loosening, including larger or longer screws, altered thread geometry, expandable screws, and bone cement augmentation. Non-biodegradable sleeves (e.g. Ogmend) have been used to distribute screw loading to increase pull-out force. However, clinical evidence of these mitigation strategies is inconsistent, or limited, and many devices are evaluated pre-clinically using insertion torque, uniaxial pull-out tests, or simplified cyclic loading, which do not replicate the complex multi-axis loading experienced in vivo. Furthermore, they do not actively regenerate the screw–bone interface or progressively transfer load to newly formed bone.

The aim of this project is to develop a new generation of bioresorbable, regenerative scaffolds that engineer the screw-bone interface to improve primary and secondary fixation. By controlling scaffold architecture, mechanical properties, bioactivity and degradation, the scaffold will enhance immediate fixation whilst promoting osseointegration and progressive load transfer to newly formed bone. The project will combine biomaterials and tissue engineering with advanced pre-clinical evaluation using Exeter’s six-axis bioreactor. COSA Ltd will provide expertise in medical imaging, anatomical modelling, and multi-material 3D printing to develop reproducible bone-mimicking models for in vitro mechanical testing, whilst clinical guidance will help ensure that scaffold development is aligned with surgical practice.

The project will:

Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award

1. Develop and evaluate functionally graded and anisotropic scaffold architectures using additive manufacturing that are designed to distribute interfacial stresses, reduce damaging micromotion, and improve resistance to screw loosening and pull-out.
2. Engineer material compositions to promote bone formation and tissue integration. Bioactive and mechanically responsive material strategies will also be explored to determine whether physiological loading can be harnessed to stimulate regeneration at the screw–bone interface (e.g., piezoelectric biomaterials).
3. Integrate scaffold development with physiologically relevant six-axis mechanical bioreactor testing. Candidate designs will be evaluated under complex loading that better reflects activities of daily living than conventional tests. This will reveal how scaffold architecture influences load transfer, micromotion, and biological response, directly informing iterative design and optimisation.

The project will therefore establish a design–manufacture–test process for engineering mechanically adaptive screw–bone interfaces. Although pedicle screw fixation will provide the primary clinical application, the underlying principles could ultimately be translated to other orthopaedic fixation devices where poor bone quality and implant loosening remain major challenges. In order to achieve these goals, the project will be supported by an interdisciplinary supervisory team consisting of academics, clinicians, and industry with expertise in biomaterials, tissue engineering, additive manufacturing, and mechanobiology.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Engineering Catalyst-Layer Microenvironments for Selective and Durable Acidic CO₂ Electrolysis
jobs.description_html:
Electrochemical conversion of carbon dioxide offers a route to manufacture valuable chemicals using renewable electricity. However, most high-rate CO₂ electrolysers operate under alkaline conditions, where substantial carbon can be lost through carbonate formation. Acidic CO₂ electrolysis could overcome this problem, but introduces a different challenge: intense competition from hydrogen evolution and strong sensitivity to the local
environment inside the catalyst layer. This PhD will investigate how the catalyst-layer microenvironment can be engineered to improve the selectivity and durability of acidic CO₂ electrolysis at technologically relevant reaction rates.

The central hypothesis is that local transport, ionomer chemistry, water availability and ion distributions govern the competition between CO₂ reduction and hydrogen evolution. The student will fabricate gas-diffusion electrodes using well-defined Cu-based reference catalysts,
systematically varying ionomer chemistry, wettability and porous architecture while controlling catalyst composition. Their performance will be evaluated using high-rate acidic CO₂ electrolysis, quantitative product analysis and electrochemical diagnostics. Advanced characterisation will then be used to understand how interfacial transport and local reaction conditions influence multicarbon selectivity and electrode degradation. The aim is to establish transferable microenvironment design principles rather than optimise individual catalyst compositions.

Through collaboration with Professor Ifan Stephens at Imperial College London and the Henry Royce Institute, the project will provide opportunities for specialist mechanistic characterisation and research visits. The project will be embedded within the five-year Royal Academy of Engineering Research Fellowship led by Dr Mengnan Wang on scalable acidic CO₂ electrolysers, providing a strong long-term research platform and links to industrial
collaborators including Johnson Matthey. The successful candidate is expected to join a growing cohort of three to four PhD researchers working on complementary projects, benefiting from peer support, shared expertise and collaborative research opportunities. The outcome will be new understanding and practical design rules for controlling catalyst-layer environments in acidic CO₂ electrolysis, supporting more efficient and durable low-carbon chemical manufacturing.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Using data to predict risk of hospital-acquired acute kidney injury (HA-AKI)
jobs.description_html:
Background

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is where kidneys suddenly stop working properly. It can range from minor loss of kidney function to complete kidney failure. Without quick treatment, abnormal levels of salts and chemicals can build up in the body, which affects the ability of other organs to work properly. According to UK renal registry, the overall AKI episode rate was over 12,000 per million population. Among the AKI events, 30-33% are hospital-acquired acute kidney injury (HA-AKI). The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence reported that the estimated annual cost of HA-AKI ranges from £430 million to over £1 billion to the NHS. In the US, the EPIC risk of HA-AKI model is a machine learning tool developed within the EPIC systems to predict the risk of HA AKI in hospitalised patients.

However, the model was trained on US populations, and may not be directly applicable to the UK context due to differences in patient demographics, clinical practice, and data infrastructure. Recent external validation of the EPIC HA-AKI model reported moderate predictive performance, and it predicts more accurately low risk but less so in high risk patients. These limitations highlight the need for a HA-AKI risk prediction model trained on UK population. This project aims to develop and validate a HA-AKI prediction model tailored to the UK population using modern statistical and machine learning approaches.

Objectives and methodology

  1. Data curation from electronic health records. We will curate large-scale, analysis-ready datasets from NHS electronic health records. HA-AKI outcomes will be defined using validated medicine code lists. Candidate predictors will include demographics, pre-existing comorbidities, treatment history, laboratory biomarkers, and prescribed medications. We will develop preprocessing pipelines to ensure data quality, reproducibility, and clinical relevance.
  2. Model development. We will build prediction models using information available at the time of hospital admission. A range of statistical and machine learning methods will be explored, including logistic regression and penalised regression models, tree-based methods, random forests, and gradient boosting. Feature selection strategies will be applied to reduce dimensionality and enhance clinical interpretability.
  3. Model validation. Internal validation will be conducted using cross-validation and bootstrapping. External validation will be performed across different NHS sites to assess Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award generalisability. Model performance will be evaluated in terms of discrimination (ability to classify patients into outcome categories) and calibration (agreement between predicted and observed risk). We will conduct decision curve analysis to further assess clinical utility.
  4. Model implementation and accessibility. Based on the results of the developed and validated models, we will create an accessible tool using open-source software, to estimate individual risk for HA-AKI. We will conduct stakeholder engagement activities to guide usability within clinical workflows. Open science and impact. All analyses will adhere to TRIPOD guidelines for prediction model research, with reproducible pipelines and open-source software. The project will develop a HA AKI risk prediction model tailored to the UK population, with the potential to improve early detection and patient outcomes.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: AI and Image Processing for Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) Smart Cameras
jobs.description_html:
Background:

Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of blindness in working aged people. All people with diabetes aged over 12 need annual retina screening by attending ophthalmology clinic. This produces over a billion retina images every year. However, about 50% of diabetic adults do not receive this recommended annual screening, and lower middle income countries, have below 10% screening rate. Factors contributing to low screening rates include shortages of trained expert ophthalmologists, lack of facilities in rural areas and inability of patients to attend clinics in person.

Aims:

The project aims to develop and evaluate AI methods for medical image analysis to detect diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, cataract and age-related macular degeneration (AMD). As well as retinal fundus images, we will explore analysis of new eye image datasets including OCTA and CCM images for diagnosis of diabetic neuropathy. Machine Learning: We will develop artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL) and Data science methods for medical image analysis, to autonomously grade the fundus images from large datasets. This will be supported by Professor Neil Vaughan and Professor Xujiong Ye with input from members of our medical image analysis labs. This will enable the assessment of ML approaches for image grading and application to grade retinopathy severity levels 0-4 (None, Mild, Moderate, Severe, Proliferative).

We will also focus on optimising training for explainable, to ensure the reasons for diagnosis are understandable for clinicians and patients. The ML will use 500,000 fundus images from open source and customised retinopathy datasets. We will compare retinopathy grading accuracy by NHS clinician vs ML algorithm. This will build on Exeter’s reviews of DL retinopathy image analysis which found that ML & DL retinopathy grading systems have potential to be more sensitive than human graders, and will develop evidence that this approach could be safe to use in clinical practice.

Datasets Available:

We have gained unique access to a large number of datasets of fundus images that will be used. EyePACS Dataset. This has over 5 million retinal images from diverse populations with various degrees of diabetic retinopathy. UK BioBank fundus Dataset. The UK Biobank has collected 175,824 fundus images from 85,848 participants. INSIGHT Data. From two NHS Trusts: University Hospitals Birmingham (UHB) and Moorfields Eye Hospital. They include over 35 million retinal images including OCT scans and fundus retinal photographs. HVDROPDB dataset. We have international collaboration with leading institutes in India who are collecting retinal image data in rural India communities. North Devon and Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust Data. Our co-supervisor from RDUH NHS runs eye clinics within NHS and regularly screens patients.

Supervisory team:

Our established team consists of experts including academic medical image analysis, NHS ophthalmologist and external partners.

Benefits:

Automation of screening with ML can enable more regular eye screening for patients. This will reduce the undetected cases of retinopathy, enable retinal issues to be detected earlier. This will increase chances that irreversible damage may occur before retinopathy is detected. Reducing the costs for the NHS and reducing number of appointments.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Improving Artificial Intelligence through Neuroscience
jobs.description_html:
Neuroscience has been a major source of inspiration for modern Artificial Intelligence frameworks, such as Deep Networks, Reinforcement Learning, and Large Language Models. This project investigates how two more recent Neuroscience developments could help improve Deep Networks. The first development is the realisation in the last 20 years that a population of brain cells, astrocytes, have complex and coordinated responses to neural activity, and feed back onto neural activity.

What is the effect of these neuron-astrocyte interactions on brain computations? You will explore the hypothesis that astrocytes provide a source of regularisation to neural networks. That is, they provide constraints to the networks, making them simpler and thus better able to generalise learned concepts to data they have not yet seen. Concretely, you will add astrocyte-inspired regularisation rule to Deep Network training, and then test whether the resulting networks generalise better, are more resistant to injury, and are easier to explain than standard ones. The second development is the description of spontaneous, coordinated activity in developing networks. For instance, before eye opening there are spontaneous waves of activity on the retina, which drive synaptic plasticity in downstream brain structures.

So, before neural networks involved in visual processing "see" their first images, they have already been sculpted by spontaneous retinal waves. In other words, the connections between neurons are not set randomly. This could help with initialisation of Deep Networks. Initial connection weights determines whether the networks can learn effectively and how fast they learn. Learning also requires a large amount of data, because of the large number of connection weights that need to be optimised through training. Drawing on what is known about these waves and the plasticity they drive, you will apply the resulting synaptic plasticity rules to initialise Deep Networks, and then determine if this speeds up learning and if less data is required to train the networks. Answering these questions will lead to the development of better, more explainable, and more sustainable AI.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Integrating Machine Learning with One Health Frameworks to Quantify Disease Transmission Pathways between Wildlife and the Environment
jobs.description_html:
The behaviour of animals determines their responses to environmental change and ultimately shapes whether populations persist or decline. Tools to record and analyse the behaviour of individual animals under natural conditions are therefore vital not only for fundamental research to understand why animals behave in the ways they do, but also for applied work addressing urgent challenges in animal conservation and welfare.

However, existing technologies have mostly been developed for controlled laboratory settings and are often unsuitable for field conditions. For instance, cameras used to monitor nesting birds typically require mains power or are too bulky to fit in nests without disturbing occupants. Thermal imaging is emerging as a vital tool for non-invasive monitoring of stress, but thermal cameras are typically large, expensive and power-hungry. Similarly, animal-borne microphones can provide insights into vocal communication and responses to anthropogenic disturbance, but have limited battery life and are too heavy for most species. These limitations highlight the need for integrated sensing systems that are miniaturised, low-power, robust and capable of autonomous operation in challenging field environments. At the heart of this PhD is an engineering challenge: how can sensing hardware and intelligent data processing be designed together to obtain biologically meaningful information from wild animals while operating under constraints on device mass, size, power and environmental robustness?

Advances in AI will be crucial, for example by enabling individual recognition from visual and vocal characteristics and automated quantification of behavioural and physiological responses. Rather than treating hardware and AI as separate components, they will be co-designed to acquire only the information needed to answer biologically meaningful questions, at appropriate spatial and temporal resolution, thereby reducing energy, storage and processing demands. Candidate systems will first be quantitatively benchmarked under controlled conditions before deployment and validation with established wild-animal study populations. The project brings together complementary expertise in behavioural field biology (Dr Alex Thornton), passive monitoring and ecological applications of AI (Dr Kim Hockings), and electronic engineering and sensing (Prof Monica Craciun). Thornton will provide expertise in behavioural ecology, field experimentation and biological validation; Hockings will contribute Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award expertise in passive acoustic and visual monitoring and AI for ecological applications; and Craciun will provide expertise in sensor and electronic-system design, including miniaturisation and low-power sensing.

The project is particularly suited to an interdisciplinary candidate interested in applying engineering, computer science and/or AI to real-world biological problems. The Cornish Jackdaw Project – Thornton’s long-term wild jackdaw study population – provides the ideal setting to test and validate methods before applying them to field sites in more remote locations, including Hockings’ study sites in West Africa. The student will gain experience and transferable skills spanning ecological research, engineering and data science, alongside opportunities for technology translation, stakeholder engagement and commercialisation. Given the urgent need for robust, affordable tools to evaluate behavioural responses to environmental change, the resulting technologies could have applications well beyond the focal study systems, including conservation, wildlife management, animal welfare and environmental monitoring.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The call of the wild: innovative technology to record and understand wild animal behaviour
jobs.description_html:
Emerging infectious diseases pose substantial threats to the health of wildlife, livestock, humans and ecosystems. Wildlife serve as important reservoirs and vectors for a diverse range of microorganisms, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. However, pathogen transmission dynamics within wildlife populations and between wildlife and their environments remain poorly understood because transmission pathways are complex, and vary in both space and time. Metagenomic sequencing allows us to generate huge volumes of data on the composition and dynamics of host and environment-associated microbiomes, including the profiling of pathogens but the sheer complexity of these data make identifying causal pathways and ecological mechanisms shaping disease transmission difficult.

This interdisciplinary PhD project aims to integrate environmental and host-associated metagenomic data with state-of-the-art machine learning approaches to identify patterns of pathogen transmission in wildlife populations, including migratory birds and badgers. By combining genomic, ecological, and environmental datasets, the project will develop predictive models capable of detecting transmission hotspots, identifying key environmental reservoirs, and forecasting pathogen spread under changing environmental conditions.

Research Objectives

The project will address three primary objectives:

  1. Characterise microbial and pathogen diversity in model wildlife populations and associated environmental samples, including water, soil, sediment, and foraging habitats, using high throughput metagenomic sequencing.
  2. Identify transmission pathways and ecological drivers by linking microbial community composition to host traits, movement behaviour, habitat use, seasonality, and environmental conditions.
  3. Develop machine learning pipelines that include appropriate preprocessing of the various datasets, feature engineering and (predictive) model / feature selection. We will use this pipeline to infer likely transmission networks and predict pathogen occurrence, persistence, and spread across landscapes. We will use metagenomic data to identify taxa, functional genes, and potential pathogens. We will then combine metagenomic & Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award environmental with supervised machine learning approaches (e.g. Random Forests, Gradient Boosting Machines, and Deep Neural Networks) to predict pathogen occurrence and transmission risk. We will also employ Multiomics Factor Analysis (MOFA) to identify covariance between metagenomic and environmental data, and network analysis to identify putative transmission pathways.

Expected Outcome and Impact:

The project will generate fundamental insights into how pathogens circulate within wildlife systems and the role of environmental reservoirs in maintaining disease transmission. By integrating machine learning with metagenomic surveillance, the research will provide novel analytical frameworks for identifying transmission pathways that are difficult to observe directly. The findings will contribute to wildlife disease ecology, conservation biology, and One Health research by improving understanding of the links between environmental change, biodiversity, and infectious disease dynamics. The predictive tools developed during the project could support disease surveillance programmes, inform targeted management interventions, and enhance preparedness for emerging pathogens affecting wildlife, livestock, and human populations.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Integrating sensing, modelling and data analytics to understand forest microclimate dynamics under fire, degradation and climate change in Amazonia
jobs.description_html:
This project combines environmental sensing, computational modelling and data analytics to understand how climate change, wildfire and land use are reshaping tropical forest microclimates. Tropical forests are warming and drying from the inside. Wildfire, degradation, land-use change and climate extremes open the canopy and alter the microclimate beneath it, increasing tree mortality and making forests more flammable. Predicting these changes requires measurements and models that work at the fine scales where trees live and die, yet both remain poorly tested in the tropics. Low-cost sensors drift, fail and vary with design and placement; physics-based microclimate models are rarely validated against dense field data; and scaling point measurements up to landscapes introduces uncertainty that is seldom quantified. This PhD will develop and test an integrated sensing and modelling framework for predicting fine-scale climate in complex, data-sparse environments, using Amazonian forests as a demanding test case. It has four linked objectives:

  1. Sensor performance and uncertainty: quantify how sensor design, placement, drift and data gaps affect microclimate measurements, by testing established dataloggers against custom-built and industry-partner prototype devices.
  2. Model validation and improvement: test physics-based models of energy, heat and water exchange between atmosphere, canopy and soil against measured vertical profiles, from soil to canopy, across intact, burned and degraded forest.
  3. Data fusion and machine learning: combine in-situ sensor data with airborne and spaceborne Lidar (e.g. GEDI) and optical satellite data, using machine learning to calibrate low cost sensors and correct systematic model errors.
  4. Upscaling with quantified uncertainty: propagate uncertainty from the sensor to landscape-scale predictions, and apply the framework to forecast where warmer, drier conditions put trees under heat and drought stress and raise fire risk, including during ENSO related droughts. The project builds on the large environmental sensor network and datasets of the UKRI-funded Amazon PyroCarbon Project, which records soil temperature, soil moisture and near-surface air temperature across forests with contrasting fire and land-use histories. These are complemented by open remote sensing and land-use data, and by the open-source microclimate models developed by Prof Maclean's group, already validated across tropical forest sites worldwide.

An industry sensor partner will support testing of prototype devices, offering a possible route to a placement. The doctoral researcher will take a leading role in shaping the project, and can emphasise sensor development, modelling or data science according to their interests. Training will cover sensor design and calibration, physics-based and statistical modelling, machine learning, geospatial analysis and high-performance computing in R and Python, and reproducible research practice. Fieldwork in Brazil is possible (subject to research permits); alternatively, the project can be completed as a desk-based study using existing data and ongoing data collection by partners across Amazonia.

The successful candidate will join an international UK–Brazil research team at Exeter, with links to the University's strengths in weather and climate science and data science. The methods developed will transfer well beyond the tropics, to environmental monitoring in agriculture, cities, conservation and wildfire management.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Physics-Informed AI and Experimental Modelling of Ocean Mixing: From Fracture Zones to Ocean Ventilation
jobs.description_html:
Ocean mixing plays a fundamental role in regulating Earth's climate by controlling how heat, carbon and nutrients are transported through the deep ocean. Small scale turbulent mixing drives the buoyancy gain of dense abyssal waters and enables the return flow of the global Meridional Overturning Circulation (MOC), yet the pathways linking localized mixing processes to basin-scale circulation remain poorly resolved. Recent results from a unique 22-year tracer-release experiment in the Brazil Basin have provided the first large-scale observational evidence connecting abyssal water transformation to overturning pathways and revealed an unexpected 2000 m upwelling of abyssal waters through the Rio de Janeiro Fracture Zone, a deep passage linking the Brazil and Angola Basins.

These observations highlight the important role that fracture zones may play in controlling water-mass transformation and the return of abyssal waters toward the ocean interior, and suggest that these processes are not adequately represented in existing ocean and climate models. This project will investigate the physical mechanisms within fracture zones that drive ocean mixing, water-mass transformation, tracer horizontal and vertical transport, and exchange between overturning circulation cells. The student will combine unique tracer observations, turbulence measurements, data-science methods, and numerical modelling to quantify the mixing-driven circulation through these deep passages.

The project will build on an established framework based on the MIT General Circulation Model (MITgcm), extending previous canyon simulations to represent an open fracture-zone geometry connecting the Brazil and Angola Basins. Numerical experiments will be used to investigate how topography, stratification, and mixing influence tracer dispersion and overturning circulation. A key objective is to use these observational and modelling insights to improve the representation of ocean mixing in large-scale ocean and climate models. Existing parameterisations are largely based on local turbulence measurements or idealised process studies and do not fully account for the integrated transport pathways revealed by the long-term tracer observations. By combining observations, simulations, and statistical analysis, the project will provide new constraints on the rates and pathways of abyssal upwelling and water mass transformation. The project will further explore the use of physics-informed artificial intelligence to accelerate environmental simulation and support the development of computationally efficient modelling tools.

Machine-learning surrogate models will be trained on ensembles of MITgcm simulations to learn the relationships between topography, mixing intensity, stratification, and large-scale tracer transport. These AI emulators will reproduce the essential dynamics of the numerical model at a low computational cost, enabling rapid exploration, uncertainty quantification, and testing of new mixing parameterisations.

The project will therefore contribute to the growing integration of physical modelling, data science, and AI in environmental prediction. The project combines observational oceanography, environmental fluid dynamics, numerical simulation, data science, and artificial intelligence to address a fundamental challenge in climate prediction while exploring next-generation computational approaches for Earth-system modelling.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Quantifying compounding and cascading physical climate risk to UK infrastructure
jobs.description_html:
Climate change is intensifying hazards, such as flooding, heat, drought, storms, that threaten the resilience of UK infrastructure. Most existing risk assessments treat these hazards in isolation and for single asset classes, missing two critical realities: hazards compound (e.g. heat and drought together) and cascade across interdependent systems (e.g. flooding disrupts power, which disrupts water treatment and transport).

This project will develop a UK infrastructure risk assessment that starts with rigorous hazard damage modelling for a single infrastructure sector, then extends this to quantify compounding and cascading risk pathways across interconnected infrastructure systems, and finally translates physical risk into economic loss estimates relevant to investors, insurers and policymakers. The student will use probabilistic UK climate projections (UKCP18) and infrastructure network data to develop this analysis from the ground up.

The project offers training in climate science, infrastructure risk engineering, network analysis and economic risk quantification, and the opportunity to engage with real-world users of climate risk assessments in finance, insurance and government.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: Fully funded AHRC Doctoral Landscape awards at Kent: Arts & Humanities Postgraduate Scholarships
jobs.description_html:
