jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Multiscale Scientific Machine Learning Digital Twins for High-Torque Electric Propulsion under Extreme Duty Cycles
jobs.description_html:
Electrifying heavy-duty maritime vessels, mining equipment and off-highway machinery is central to Net Zero and Clean Energy goals. Unlike conventional automotive traction systems, electric propulsion for these applications must often deliver sustained high torque at low rotational speed during demanding operations such as bollard pull, winching and heavy excavation. Under these extreme duty cycles, motor behaviour is governed by processes that evolve over very different timescales: fast electromagnetic dynamics determine torque response and saturation behaviour, electromechanical and load-history effects shape transient performance, and slow thermal dynamics govern the gradual build-up and dissipation of heat over extended operating periods.

These processes are strongly coupled, since changes in temperature alter electrical resistance, efficiency and torque capability, making the overall behaviour difficult to predict with physics-based models or conventional machine learning alone. Characterising these operating regimes experimentally is genuinely difficult. Testing high-power motors repeatedly to their thermal limits is energy-intensive, costly and potentially damaging, with risks including insulation degradation, excessive winding temperatures and permanent-magnet demagnetisation. Detailed physics-based simulations can be too slow to run for long, variable duty cycles, while conventional machine-learning models often generalise poorly beyond the conditions they were trained on, particularly for long-horizon thermal behaviour. This project will develop a multiscale Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) digital-twin framework predicting thermal trajectories, torque capability and efficiency variation in low speed, high-torque propulsion systems, investigating physics-informed hybrid architectures spanning fast, intermediate and slow system dynamics: Deep Neural Networks for nonlinear electromagnetic relationships and saturation effects, recurrent or neural state-space models for transient behaviour and load-history dependence, and Neural Ordinary Differential Equations for continuous-time thermal accumulation over multi-hour horizons.

The student will design safety-constrained dynamometer experiments at the University's Centre for Future Clean Mobility (CFCM), acquiring high-frequency electrical, mechanical and thermal measurements to train and validate the digital twin. Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award A central research challenge is determining how reliable operating-envelope predictions can be obtained from a small number of carefully chosen, non-destructive experiments rather than exhaustive testing to physical limits, requiring data-efficient experimental design, physics based constraints, and uncertainty quantification to assess confidence when the motor operates under conditions it hasn't directly been tested on. The resulting digital twin will provide fast, uncertainty-aware predictions of thermal loading, torque capability and efficiency over time, supporting safe evaluation of severe operating profiles that are difficult or risky to reproduce repeatedly on a physical testbed, and providing evidence to guide motor sizing and duty-cycle decisions for next-generation zero-emission propulsion systems.

This is a collaborative studentship with Ecomar Innovations, a marine power-systems company. The student will spend time on-site with Ecomar's engineering team, testing the framework against real industrial hardware and supporting improved thermal-management strategies for their systems, giving direct exposure to industry-scale equipment and a route from research to real-world deployment, alongside supervision from a team with an established track record in maritime electrification and control systems. The project welcomes applicants from electrical/mechanical engineering, control systems, applied mathematics or computer science, and offers interdisciplinary training in electric machines, SciML, thermal modelling and digital-twin validation.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Bioinspired fluidic metamaterials for passive directional water transport
jobs.description_html:
Metamaterials use engineered structures to achieve functionality that the constituent materials alone cannot provide. This project explores novel bioinspired fluidic metamaterials which use hierarchical surface patterns inspired by carnivorous plants to control the speed and direction of water transport. Precision control of wetting and liquid flow on surfaces has the potential to transform medical care, save resources, mitigate the effects of climate change and optimise production processes. Engineered surfaces with defined fluid transport properties can revolutionise healthcare applications such as microfluidic point-of-care diagnostics, automated drug delivery, or more efficient wound drainage. Capturing and directing water is essential for fog water harvesting in arid regions.

Passive micro-irrigation systems save water and energy while increasing crop yields. Passive fluid transport surfaces can also improve the sustainability of manufacturing processes by optimising the supply of lubricants and extending the lifetime of moving parts. Insect-eating pitcher plants have hydrophilic trapping surfaces with extraordinary capacity to transport and direct water. The collar-shaped rim of their pitfall traps features ridges and grooves on two distinct length scales, with the microscale grooves further intersected by acute angled, overhanging arches. This is a natural metasurface: the anisotropic hierarchical microtopography makes water spread against gravity within milliseconds and form a thin film on which insects aquaplane to their death.

However, no study to-date has systematically investigated how the microtopographical features interact with each other and with the intrinsic hydrophilicity of the surface to determine wetting and fluid flow. Without this understanding, we are currently unable to unlock the full potential of bioinspired surface design for the microscale control of liquid flow.

This PhD takes a three-step approach:

  1. Characterize the diversity of natural plant surfaces and quantify their capacity to guide and transport water. Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award
  2. Fabricate synthetic surface replicas (PDMS casts) and systematically vary their hydrophilicity using oxygen plasma treatment to disentangle the contributions of surface chemistry and topography on wetting and water spreading.
  3. Utilise two-photon polymerisation, a nanoscale 3D-printing technology, to investigate the effects of individual topographical features (macro- and microscale grooves, overhanging arches) on wetting and water spreading in isolation. These experiments will provide a mechanistic understanding of the functional significance of each topographical feature. By varying feature shape, size and spacing within and beyond the natural parameter space, the student will identify the functional limits of water transport on pitcher plant-inspired metasurfaces.

The data generated from this PhD will provide the foundation for the development of computational models that can accurately predict fluid behaviour on hierarchically ridged surfaces, ultimately the first step towards evidence-based precision design of bioinspired metasurfaces with application-optimised fluid transport properties.

The student will join a culturally diverse, interdisciplinary lab with two decades of experience studying specialised plant surfaces and carnivorous plant traps, supported by two co supervisors with backgrounds in Physics (Calum Williams, Exeter Centre for Metamaterial Research and Innovation) and Engineering (Halim Kusumaatmaja, Institute for Multiscale Thermofluids, University of Edinburgh). They will develop a diverse skillset including surface design, microfabrication and characterisation, experimental design and execution, data analysis, modelling, communication and teamwork.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Using modelling and experiments to understand how, when and where viruses undergo recombination in plants
jobs.description_html:
Plant viruses pose a major challenge to global food production. Their ability to evolve, overcome crop defences, cross species barriers and emerge in more damaging forms threatens agricultural sustainability worldwide. Yet we still do not understand one of the key processes driving viral evolution within infected plants: when and where viral genomes recombine to generate new variants. Recombination occurs when two viruses exchange genetic material, creating novel hybrid viruses with potentially altered host ranges, virulence, or ability to overcome host resistance. Understanding the circumstances that promote recombination could reveal opportunities to limit viral evolution before new pathogenic variants emerge. In this project, you will combine computational and experimental approaches to investigate where and when recombination occurs within infected plants, addressing a fundamental question at the intersection of plant pathology, evolution and food security.

A central puzzle motivates this work. Recombination requires different viral strains to encounter one another within the host. However, infections by distinct strains typically form largely non-overlapping patches within plant tissues, limiting opportunities for interaction. How, then, do recombinant viruses arise? To address this question, you will begin by analysing a collection of fluorescence images of real viral infections that reveal how viruses spread through plants and where different strains come into contact. To that end, you will use both traditional image-analysis methods and modern machine-learning approaches.

The insights gained from this analysis will be used to develop a multiscale model of viral spread within the plant, linking processes occurring at the level of individual cells to patterns observed across tissues and the whole organism. You will then use simulations to work backwards from the experimental observations, uncovering the hidden biological processes that shape viral spread and estimating the parameters that govern infection dynamics. The resulting framework will allow you to predict when and where opportunities for recombination are most likely to occur within a plant.

In the second phase of the project, you will test these model predictions experimentally. Working with existing molecular resources, you will be introduced to plant pathology, molecular biology and microbial techniques, allowing you to connect theoretical predictions with real biological systems. You will develop a novel molecular tool to detect viral genome recombination events using engineered split and mutated fluorescent proteins. This system will provide a direct way to identify and quantify recombination within infected plants and to evaluate the predictions generated by the computational models.

This project offers a rare opportunity to combine quantitative image analysis with machine learning, mathematical modelling, simulation and experimental biology within a single research programme. You will be jointly supervised by Dr Mike Deeks, a cell biologist and plant pathologist, and Dr Wolfram Moebius, a physicist with a research programme centring around evolution. Supported by this interdisciplinary team, you will integrate computational and laboratory approaches to address a fundamental question in virus evolution while developing a highly transferable interdisciplinary skill set. The outcomes will advance our understanding of how new plant viruses emerge and could ultimately help inform strategies to reduce the evolutionary potential of viral pathogens threatening UK and global food security.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Raman Spectroscopy for Early On-Farm Diagnosis of Nephrocalcinosis (Kidney Stone Disease) - The #1 Issue of Concern for Salmon and Trout Aquaculture
jobs.description_html:
Rainbow trout and Atlantic salmon represent the gold standard for technologically advanced fish farming (aquaculture). The market is valued at $5.3 billion for trout globally (£59 million in the UK) and $18.9 billion for salmon globally (£1.13 billion in the UK). An emerging but quantitatively important disease problem in aquaculture is nephrocalcinosis (‘kidney stones’ formed by precipitation of calcium minerals). This is now the #1 issue of concern within trout producers for all 4 categories surveyed (‘mortality’, ‘reduced growth’, ‘reduced-welfare’ and ‘increasing problem’), and ranked 1st, 2nd or 3rd for these categories for salmon (1). Nephrocalcinosis in fish is associated with sub-optimal water chemistry in aquaculture.

The key variables are elevated dissolved CO2 associated with intensive production, but elevated calcium, salinity, phosphate, and alkalinity in the water also play a role. The digestive process, regardless of diet composition, induces major changes in blood acid-base chemistry in fish (2) that also translate into urine chemistry changes that can increase the likelihood of mineral precipitation within the kidney (3). Some diet ingredients can further exacerbate kidney stone formation in both fish and humans (4). A key limitation for improving fish welfare and aquaculture productivity with respect to this disease is the lack of early and cost-effective diagnosis of nephrocalcinosis.

However, coherent Raman scattering microscopy – including Stimulated Raman Scattering (SRS) and Broadband Coherent Anti-Stokes Raman Scattering (BCARS) – is proving its value for label-free, chemically-specific diagnosis of calcification related pathologies in humans, including calcification associated with breast cancer (5). Recent progress with this technology suggests strong opportunities for diagnosing and quantifying calcium-based mineral deposits in animal tissues WITHOUT fixation OR the need for tissue staining, generating hyperspectral image data that maps tissue chemistry at sub-micron resolution. This raises the potential for small hand-held or bench top devices for use at farm sites, eliminating delays and diagnostic difficulties associated with send-away lab samples that need fixing and staining. Machine learning will be central to converting these complex spectral image data into simple, actionable outputs for industry – for example automated classification Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award and quantification of mineral deposits – enabling rapid diagnosis of pathologies and health problems associated with nephrocalcinosis.

We have existing strong collaborative relationships with both trout and salmon producers in the UK (e.g. British Trout Association, Kames, MOWI, Cooke Aquaculture Scotland) and plan to use fish tissue samples obtained from their sites as part of this project. In addition, we will conduct in vivo experiments with fish at the Aquatic Resources Facility (Biosciences) at Exeter that mimic the conditions linked to nephrocalcinosis to generate kidney tissue samples from known origins. Together these samples will allow the PhD student to explore disease aetiology and test the efficacy of Raman spectroscopy as a rapid diagnostic tool for nephrocalcinosis, and explore options for cost-effective analysis on site at aquaculture sites.

References:

  1. Moldal et al (2024) Fish Health Report (www.vetinst.no)
  2. Cooper & Wilson (2008) J Experimental Biology, 211(15):2542-2550
  3. Emadi et al (2026) Aquaculture, 613: 743354
  4. Crivelli et al (2021) Nutrients, 13:62
  5. Bouzy et al (2023) Analytical Methods15(13):1620-1630

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: SCALE-Decode: Unlocking Growth Workflows in UK SMEs
jobs.description_html:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) underpin UK employment and innovation, yet many struggle to turn early success into sustainable growth. Rising demand can expose informal routines, disconnected systems, founder dependence and employee overload. Managers may see delayed delivery or lost sales without understanding how constraints travel across the firm. Research and policy treat issues separately, while generic AI lacks context. SCALE-Decode examines how responsible AI can reveal growth workflows, diagnose bottlenecks, and build an AI system to support managerial actions.

Work Package 1 (months 1-12) will map and explain SME scale-up workflows. Manager and employee interviews, walkthroughs, task diaries, process documents and privacy-preserving event logs, where suitable, will be integrated through qualitative analysis, Business Process Model and Notation and process mining. Cross-case comparison will distinguish symptoms, including delay and rework, from underlying causes such as centralised approvals, capability gaps and poor information transfer. Stakeholder validation will refine three deliverables: a Scale-up Workflow Framework, anonymised maps and a bottleneck taxonomy. Together, they will help firms and advisers trace local constraints across an organisation and strengthen workflow-centred scaling theory through credible evidence.

Work Package 2 (months 10-24) will build SCALE-Decode, a secure AI system to help SMEs scale by reconstructing workflows, diagnosing scaling bottlenecks and generating feasible action plans. A knowledge graph will connect activities, dependencies, organisational conditions, evidence and interventions. Four AI components will gather information, produce editable maps, diagnose constraints, and generate and critique actions. Each recommendation will identify its evidence, prerequisites, expected benefit, cost, effort, risk and uncertainty. Managers will correct maps and approve recommendations. Technical, adversarial, usability and unseen-case testing will assess fidelity, traceability, feasibility and unsupported claims. Deliverables comprise a validated prototype, documentation and responsible-use guidance.

Work Package 3 (months 22-36) will evaluate feasibility, usefulness and implementation in SMEs. A longitudinal field study will compare AI-assisted diagnosis with existing approaches and track workflow understanding, decision quality, action completion and selected operational indicators. Usage records, surveys and interviews will show why recommendations Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award are accepted, adapted or rejected and whether outcomes vary with workflow maturity, digital readiness or owner-manager dependence. Case studies will examine employee capability and wellbeing, recognising that gains must not depend on work intensification. Deliverables will include an evaluation dataset, comparative findings and implementation evidence, establishing where SCALE-Decode adds value, where human expertise remains essential and which conditions support responsible adoption.

Work Package 4 (months 36-42) will integrate findings and translate them for research and practice. Outputs will include academic papers, reusable workflow passports, sector templates, checklists, an adviser toolkit, policy brief and public-engagement materials. Practitioner workshops will refine resources and inform future development. This package will convert evidence into usable guidance for SMEs, advisers, growth hubs, policymakers and technology providers.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Beyond Pilots: De-Risking the Scale-Up of Artificial Intelligence in Digitally Enabled Circular Supply Chains
jobs.description_html:
Most organisations can demonstrate that AI works in a pilot; far fewer can sustain its value when it is embedded in complex, high-throughput operations. In supply chains, this matters not only commercially but environmentally. When AI-enabled forecasting, inventory and decision-support systems lose reliability or user trust, organisations may revert to inefficient practices, contributing to over-ordering, excess inventory, product waste and unnecessary resource use. This project investigates why AI scaling fails in operational settings and how this failure can be anticipated and mitigated. Its central proposition is that scaling failure is fundamentally a socio technical systems problem, rather than simply an algorithmic one. As AI moves from controlled pilots into live operations, validation gates, review checkpoints and governance workflows operate under continuous operational pressure. Rather than being deliberately removed, these controls may gradually degrade or be bypassed as throughput demands increase, allowing drift, unmonitored errors and declining resource-efficiency benefits to emerge.

Food and perishable goods supply chains provide a particularly valuable empirical setting. Forecasting accuracy, inventory decisions and operational controls have immediate consequences for spoilage, waste, resource consumption and carbon emissions. The South West's substantial agricultural and food economy therefore provides an important regional context in which to investigate how AI can support more productive, resilient and resource-efficient supply chains, while generating insights transferable to other time-critical sectors. The research will comprise three integrated phases. - First, a systematic review will map evidence on AI scaling, governance mechanisms and failure modes in operations and supply-chain contexts. - Second, a multi-case empirical study will examine organisations at different stages of AI deployment, combining interviews across strategic, operational and frontline roles with analysis of available deployment and operational data to identify where and under what conditions governance and validation controls degrade.

Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award - Third, an agent-based simulation will model control degradation under varying levels of operational load. The resulting scaling-readiness framework will then be validated through a survey of operations professionals. The project will deliver both theoretical and practical contributions: a socio-technical model explaining how AI governance and validation controls behave under operational pressure, and a diagnostic instrument to help organisations assess their readiness to scale AI while protecting the resource-efficiency gains that motivated adoption. The project also advances digitally enabled circularity. Circular systems depend on reliable information about material flows, product condition, demand and resource use. Maintaining trustworthy AI-enabled decision support is therefore an important enabler of effective circular operations and value retention.

The student will join a supervisory environment spanning sustainable operations, analytics, AI and computational modelling, with access to the ECCE, INDEX and the IDSAI. An extended industry placement will provide exposure to live operational challenges and knowledge exchange. Training will span computational simulation, mixed-methods research, AI governance and industry engagement. Applicants from engineering, computer science, data science, operations management, information systems and related disciplines are welcome, particularly those with experience of data-driven or AI-enabled operational environments or returning to academic study after industry.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Responsible innovation in metamaterials for circular economy and sustainability: building the evidence base for inclusive and sustainable applications
jobs.description_html:
Metamaterials are advanced materials with engineered structures that give them properties beyond those of their constituent materials. They are increasingly positioned by academics and policymakers as a critical addition to advanced materials product pipelines. Public and private investment in the field is accelerating significantly – UKRI alone have more than £58 million currently invested in active grants linked to metamaterials. The Advanced Manufacturing Sector Plan of the UK’s Modern Industrial Strategy (2025) highlights the £19.6 million investment by EPSRC and partners in the 3D Nanoscale Metamaterials Hub for a Sustainable Future (MetaHUB), led by the University of Exeter.

Potential applications of metamaterials span a huge range of sectors and challenges, including significantly reducing and/or replacing critical minerals, designing more efficient solar panels, reducing the radar interference of wind turbines, creating antimicrobial surfaces, or making invisibility cloaks. While metamaterials hold great promise for reducing dependence on finite resources, enabling more sustainable manufacturing, and improving access to renewable energy - among other socially, economically and environmentally beneficial outcomes - the evidence base for these benefits and impacts is underdeveloped.

Furthermore, metamaterials research and innovation to date has been predominantly driven by academic, industry and policy actors. This project addresses this gap by developing a responsible innovation approach to metamaterials for circular economy and sustainability. The project will investigate the promise and impacts of metamaterials applications by combining sustainability and circularity analysis such as Life Cycle Assessment with qualitative and mixed methods responsible innovation approaches to anticipate, reflect, engage and act on metamaterials and their potential futures.

This comes at a crucial time for metamaterials development where the main manufacturing and hence end of life options are being decided now. he MetaHUB’s manufacturing theme in particular is comparing scaled manufacturing methods over the next 4 years with key industry members ranging from STMicroelectronics to Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award PepsiCo.

This project will result in research findings, policy and practice recommendations towards more sustainable, inclusive and responsible metamaterials applications. More specifically, the project will:

  • Scope and analyse the range of applications, sectors and sociotechnical visions embedded in current metamaterials research, innovation and policy contexts, first broadly, and then with a particular focus on circular economy and sustainability-relevant research and applications (e.g. metamaterials for clean energy, bioinspired design, etc.).
  • Conduct in depth case studies of up to five metamaterials projects, devices, components or products to investigate how sustainability, circular economy and responsible innovation are currently conceptualised, measured, embedded and practiced.
  • Compare these metamaterial devices, components or products with their equivalents through LCA and related sustainability assessment.
  • Develop frameworks and practices for responsible innovation in metamaterials research, including stakeholder and public engagement, exploring the sociotechnical, sociomaterial, ethical, political, aesthetic, cultural, environmental and ecological dimensions of metamaterials.
  • Combine qualitative and quantitative methods to develop new systemic and situated understandings of metamaterials within their broader social, environmental and economic contexts, and to build the evidence base for their potential social, environmental and economic impacts.
  • Make recommendations for academic, industry, policy and civil society actors to enable responsible, inclusive, sustainable metamaterials research, innovation and deployment, including how value can be captured, distributed and shared. The project will draw on the extensive networks of the Centre for Metamaterial Research and Innovation, Exeter Centre for Circular Economy, and the Centre for Responsible Innovation.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Building the world's most advanced polarisation-resolved nonlinear microscope
jobs.description_html:
Structured light for full 3D vectorial control of the focal field — and the first true 3D readout of molecular organisation in tissue. During this project you will lead the design, build and programming an optical microscope that does something no existing instrument can: Shape the full 3D vector of a light field at the focus of an objective lens and use it to read out how biomolecules are organised in three dimensions. The microscopy technique you will begin working on is polarisation-resolved second-harmonic generation (pSHG): a fast, label-free nonlinear technique that is the gold standard for imaging collagen in living tissue. Conventional pSHG has a fundamental blind spot — its excitation field lies in the image plane, so it is insensitive to structure tilted out of that plane.  

Using a spatial light modulator to sculpt both the wavefront and the polarisation, you will engineer a longitudinal (z-polarised) field in a high-numerical-aperture focus and controllably drive SHG from out-of-plane collagen fibrils for the first time. This novel capability will allow you to study the organisation of the 3D collagen matrix in unprecedented detail.  What you'll do, and the skills you'll gain: Optical design and hands-on alignment of an ultrafast nonlinear microscope; SLM/DMD wavefront and polarisation shaping; vectorial focal-field modelling; the Jones, Stokes and Mueller formalisms; nonlinear optics; and Python for instrument control and image analysis — with scope for machine-learning approaches to the vectorial inverse problem.  

Why it matters: collagen's 3D architecture sets the mechanical behaviour of tissue — the same molecule, type I collagen, builds both the transparent corneal lattice and the load-bearing tendon. That architecture, and its breakdown in disease, has never been measurable in true 3D. An instrument that reads it directly is a new tool for biophysics, biomechanics and structural biology. You will be based in the Physics department at the University of Exeter. The supervision team includes Prof Dave Phillips (structured light) and Dr Ben Sherlock (polarisation-resolved nonlinear microscopy).

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Quantum Information with Mechanical Systems (QuIMS): Modelling Nonlinear Quantum Optomechanical Devices
jobs.description_html:
Quantum technologies require new approaches to overcoming limited coherence, control errors and connectivity between qubits. This 3.5-year PhD will investigate whether nanomechanical systems can provide an alternative platform for quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced sensing. The project focuses on suspended graphene resonators integrated with superconducting microwave cavities. Because graphene is extremely light, its mechanical motion is sensitive to very small electromagnetic forces.

The central objective is to model and control the nonlinear—or quadratic—optomechanical interaction required to prepare mechanical states that cannot be described classically. Such states could support enhanced force and mass sensing, long-lived quantum memories and mechanically encoded quantum information. The student will own a focused theoretical and computational research programme. They will develop analytical and numerical models of the device dynamics and determine how resonator geometry, phononic-crystal design, electrical control, mechanical and electrical quality factors, and linear and quadratic coupling strengths affect device performance.

The research will examine practical limitations including parasitic linear coupling, multimode interference, heating, dissipation and decoherence. These models will be used to identify experimentally achievable operating regimes and translate theoretical results into design rules and fabrication tolerances. The student will also investigate protocols for preparing, controlling and measuring non-classical mechanical states, with possible applications in quantum sensing and quantum information processing.

The project is embedded within the EPSRC-funded Quantum Information with Mechanical Systems programme. The student will work closely with quantum theorists, graphene-device researchers and low-temperature experimental physicists. Their predictions will inform device development at Exeter and, through the wider collaboration, be compared with fabrication, characterisation and cryogenic-measurement results. The student’s primary contribution will be computational; previous nanofabrication experience is not required. However, they will gain interdisciplinary understanding of graphene nanodevices, superconducting circuits and low-temperature quantum measurement. Expected outputs include documented research software, experimentally relevant device-design principles, conference presentations, peer-reviewed publications and a doctoral thesis.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Deterministic Recording via All-optical Magnetic Switching
jobs.description_html:
Our aim is to control the magnetic state of a material using only pulses of light. “Switching” the magnetization of a magnet means that its north and south poles are interchanged without mechanically inverting the magnet.  Magnets are normally opaque so that incident light only affects ten to one hundred layers of atoms closest to the surface.  Therefore, the magnet must be sufficiently thin if light is to influence all the atoms present. The magnetization derives from the “spin” angular momentum of electrons within the material. We can visualise each electron spinning about an axis through its centre, with the axes of all electrons aligned in the same direction.   

While light interacts strongly with the charge of an electron, the interaction with its spin is very weak.  Therefore, a different approach is required if light is to strongly influence the magnetization. Two principal strategies will be explored in multi-layered thin film structures in which electrons with aligned spins can be transferred between layers.  There will be no net transfer of charge, so that only spin current flows between layers.  In a first case, trilayers will be studied in which two ferromagnetic (FM) layers are separated by a non-magnetic metal (NMM) layer.  Excitation by a laser pulse with duration ~10-13 seconds will heat the FM layers, cause their magnetization to decrease, and drive a spin current into the NMM layer.   

The FM layers will be designed so that one (FM1) demagnetizes more strongly than the other (FM2) so that a net spin current flows between the two.  By controlling the intensity of the light, the spin current will be used to switch the magnetization of FM1 into a desired state.  In a second case, a FM layer will adjoin a NMM bilayer consisting of a light metal (small atomic number), such as Cu, and a heavy metal (large atomic number), such as Pt.  Light with circular polarization will induce a circular motion of electrons in the light metal.  The associated orbital angular momentum will then be converted into spin angular momentum in the heavy metal before passing into the FM to control the orientation of the magnetization. Robust optical control of magnetism would have enormous consequences for magnetic hard disk drive (HDD) technology.  

The magnetic disk coating is used to store “bits” of information, with the two orientations of the magnetization representing binary digits “0” and “1”.  In a conventional HDD a miniature electromagnet is used to switch the magnetization of the bits.  However, as HDD capacity has increased, the size of each bit has decreased, and the energy barrier between the two magnetic states has been increased so that the magnetization remains thermally stable.  The problem is that the “write” magnetic field required to switch the magnetization has increased beyond what any electromagnet can provide. The mechanisms developed within this project will be needed if the capacity of HDDs is to continue to grow.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Multi-symplectic methods for nonlinear wave interactions and ocean wave forecasting
jobs.description_html:
The motivation for this project is to develop the mathematical foundations for the next generation of ocean-wave forecasting models. Accurate and timely wave forecasts are essential for the safety of shipping, coastal communities, and offshore operations, including the construction and maintenance of offshore wind farms, wave-energy converter arrays, and other marine infrastructure. In particular, a principal objective of ocean-wave forecasting is to predict when and where extreme waves may occur, thereby helping to mitigate risks to lives, vessels, and offshore assets.  

Existing operational models (ECMWF’s ECWAM, NOAA’s WAVEWATCH III) are successful but are based on a weakly-nonlinear model for wave action conservation (kinetic equation). The mathematics now exists to take the theoretical and numerical underpinnings into the fully nonlinear regime. This project has two key aims: (a) develop a fully nonlinear kinetic equation using a multi-symplectic formulation, which will then serve as the backbone of the next generation ocean wave forecasting algorithm, and (b) develop new multi-symplectic numerical methods (structure-preserving algorithms in both space and time directions) for 2+1 Hamiltonian wave equations. These latter algorithms will then be used for both the forecasting model and an attendant fundamental study on nonlinear wave interactions and emergence of extremity and complexity in the theory of nonlinear waves and patterns. 

To choose one aspect that can be visualized: how is an extreme surface wave generated from nonlinear wave interactions? How does surface complexity arise from nonlinear water waves? This latter fundamental study will feed into the theory of forecasting.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Uncertainty quantification for healthcare models: a route to precision medicine
jobs.description_html:
Mathematical models are important tools for gaining insight into complex processes across biological systems and healthcare. To support high-stakes decisions in a clinical setting using these models, we need to ensure that their predictions are credible. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is one of the key principles of model credibility. Throughout this PhD project, the student will have an opportunity to work with a diverse suite of cardiovascular mathematical models to develop an efficient UQ pipeline. Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide, and patient-specific models are increasingly proposed to guide diagnosis, device selection and treatment planning.

The barrier to clinical adoption is not modelling capability but credibility: regulators and clinicians need to know how far a prediction can be trusted for an individual patient. This project addresses that gap directly, developing UQ methods that make model predictions and their uncertainties defensible. The project sits at the intersection of statistics, cardiovascular physiology, mathematical modelling and scientific computing. Its methodological core emulation, calibration and the treatment of model discrepancy - comes from the UQ field, but the driving questions come from mathematical modelling: which parameters are identifiable from clinical measurements, and what confidence is defensible in a clinical setting. The student will have an opportunity to closely engage with these communities to explore these questions.

 Within the project, there are two main UQ focusses:

  1. Emulation and surrogate modelling: to perform forward and inverse UQ, many runs of mathematical models are required. If we are dealing with a computationally expensive model, it is common to adopt a surrogate model to speed up the process. Cardiovascular models have a large number of unknown model parameters and generate multiple outputs at the same time. Training emulators in large input spaces and across multiple related outputs is non-trivial. The student will explore different existing methods, and develop novel, efficient emulation methodologies.
  2. Inverse UQ. To make mathematical models actionable and relevant in practice, it is crucial to calibrate them using real-world observations while accounting for their limitations. The student will explore various calibration methods to find ‘good’ settings of model inputs, whilst explicitly accounting for structural uncertainty (model discrepancy) in the model, which Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award comes from the notion that the model is not a perfect representation of the physical process of interest. The goal is to provide insight of where different models outperform others, identifying limitations of existing models and where further development is needed to provide accurate and timely decisions. Whilst the overall goal of the PhD is to apply and develop emulation and calibration methodologies for cardiovascular modelling specifically, these will likely be applicable across a wider range of problems, and the project may seek additional partners to apply and test developed methods across further important application areas.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Khintchine-Groshev Theorem: Beyond Removing Monotonicity
jobs.description_html:
This project is primarily in the field of Diophantine Approximation, which studies how well real numbers can be approximated by rational numbers and variations on this theme. Sets encountered in Diophantine Approximation are often fractal-like and it is natural to use notions from Fractal Geometry to study them. Diophantine Approximation and Fractal Geometry have found wide-ranging applications in areas such as medicine, materials science, geology, and wireless communications, and have attracted attention of several Fields Medallists. A classical theorem of Khintchine (1924) states that the set of real numbers which can be approximated at a given rate by rationals has zero or full Lebesgue measure depending on whether a certain sum converges/diverges.

This result relies on a monotonicity condition. Duffin and Schaeffer (1941) showed that this monotonicity assumption cannot be removed and conjectured the correct statement without monotonicity. Resolving the Duffin-Schaeffer Conjecture was one of the biggest unsolved problems in Diophantine Approximation until its resolution by Koukoulopoulos and 2022 Fields Medallist Maynard (2020). The Khintchine Groshev Theorem generalises Khintchine’s Theorem to higher dimensions and originally required monotonicity conditions. Beresnevich and Velani (2010) showed that monotonicity could be dropped from the homogeneous Khintchine-Groshev Theorem except when the result reduced to Khintchine’s Theorem. In a series of recent works ([Allen+Ramirez, 2023], [Hauke, 2025], [Kim, 2025], [Kim, 2026+], [Allen+Ramirez+Hauke-Treuer, 2026+]) it has been shown that in all except the classical one dimensional case (where monotonicity is known to be absolutely necessary), we can also remove monotonicity from the inhomogeneous Khintchine-Groshev Theorem.

The aim of this project will be to investigate questions related to the Khintchine-Groshev Theorem beyond that of removing monotonicity.

Possible directions for this project include:

  1. Applications of the “Independence Inheritance” phenomenon. In [Allen+Ramirez, 2023], we established an independence inheritance phenomenon, showing that independence of certain sets in dimension n implies k-fold more independence of related sets in n+k dimensions. Our initial motivation for proving this independence inheritance phenomenon was studying the question of whether we could remove monotonicity from the inhomogeneous Khintchine Groshev Theorem. However, this result is very general and one could investigate further applications of independence inheritance, both in Diophantine Approximation and beyond. Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award
  2. Khintchine-Groshev Theorem on Fractals. Recently, there has been groundbreaking work of Khalil and Luethi (2023), and Bénard, He, and Zhang (2025 and 2026+) proving analogues of Khintchine’s classical theorem in self-similar sets (a very natural class of fractals). It would be natural to investigate whether one can prove an analogue of the Khintchine-Groshev Theorem in Fractals.
  3. Multivariable Khintchine-Groshev Theorem and Matrix Approximation. In recent work, Zhang, Wang, and Li (2023) studied a problem on “Inhomogeneous multiplicative Diophantine Approximation on Matrix Approximation”. To prove their results, they use a mass transference principle for systems of linear forms [Allen+Beresnevich, 2018] and the Khintchine-Groshev Theorem. The aim would be to develop these results further by relaxing the monotonicity condition Zhang, Wang, and Li assume and studying a question they pose about extending their result from dealing with single variable approximation functions to multi-variable ones.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Modelling Relativistic Effects in Metamaterials With Quantum Graph Theory
jobs.description_html:
Quantum graph theory (QGT), defined as metric graphs endowed with differential operators, has a long history in mathematics, physics, and both theoretical chemistry and biology. The theory describes the wave properties of networks constructed from edges, endowed with the Schrödinger operator, connected by vertices that serve as scattering sites, given specific boundary conditions. A key advantage to this discrete scattering language is that the eigenvalue condition can be written in terms of a secular equation involving the determinant of a unitary matrix of dimension equal to twice the number of edges on the graph.

Quantum graph models have found a great number of applications including the study of spectral statistics, quantum chaos, modelling the vibrations of coupled plates, formulating quantum random walks, quantum search algorithms, nerve impulse transmission and model various proteins, and molecular structures. Indeed the model has been applied to both finite and infinite lattice systems. with natural applications in photonic and phononic crystals. Quantum Graph Theory has recently found utility in modelling metamaterial structures.

These materials are typically composed of subwavelength building blocks (meta-atoms), often periodically repeated in space, which can have exotic effective material properties in both space and time. Recently it has been shown that in such exotic metamaterials, analogies to black and white hole event horizons can occur, where wave energy is absorbed or created, mediated by an effective moving medium that can be described as a metamaterial with time-varying properties. This PhD proposal seeks to apply QGT to other avenues of relativistic effects, realising curved spacetimes with metamaterials through a discrete graph model.

The material properties of vacuous curved spacetime and of a certain fictitious material, known as the Tamm medium, in flat spacetime are known to be noncovariantly equivalent; various realisations of these nonhomogeneous media have been discussed in the context of metamaterials, often with regions of high anisotropy. Often the nature of these fictitious media can be accommodated by adopting a piecewise homogeneous approach, which is valid for appropriate wavelength regimes where the graph model finds strength.

This project will explore the effective materials properties of various curved-spacetime scenarios that may be impractical to explore by direct methods and provide a route to experimental realisation; QGT has found application in spectral analysis of metamaterial structures and has been experimentally verified in both acoustic and electromagnetic networks.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Sovereign Agentic AI: Distilling Small Language Model Agents for Local Deployment
jobs.description_html:
Agentic AI systems are language models that plan, call software tools, and complete multi-step tasks with little human input. They are moving from demonstrations into business operations such as customer support, procurement, invoice processing, and compliance checking. Most of these agents run on large models hosted by a few overseas cloud providers. For many UK businesses, this is a fragile position. Operational data leaves the organisation, cost grows with every request, and the capability depends on a supplier that the business does not control. The UK’s Sovereign AI programme, launched in 2026 with up to £500 million, and UKRI’s AI strategic framework, which names agentic AI and edge computing as areas where the UK should lead, both respond to this concern. Sovereign AI here means capability that a UK organisation owns, runs on hardware it controls, and keeps running without an external provider.

This project asks whether small language models, which run on a single workstation or an on-premises server, can become reliable agents for the bounded workflows that most businesses need. The idea is that business operations share much structure across organisations. For example, a procurement agent, an invoice reconciliation agent, or a first-line support agent works over a limited set of tools, document types, and decision rules. A general-purpose frontier model is more capable than such a task requires, and that surplus capability is what makes it expensive and hard to host locally. The project will distil agentic capability from large models into small models that keep the behaviour a task needs and drop the rest, along two complementary routes. The first route is harness optimisation.

The harness is everything around the model, including the prompts, the tool interfaces, the memory and retrieval components, the checks that verify an intermediate result, and the control flow that decides which step comes next. A well-designed harness lets a small model succeed where it would fail if asked to improvise. The student will develop methods that optimise the harness automatically for a given family of tasks under a fixed budget of local computation and latency. The second route is fine-tuning of small language models on traces of successful agent behaviour. The traces come from larger teacher models and from execution feedback that the tools return, such as whether a database query ran.

The student will study which parts of agent behaviour transfer to small models through fine-tuning, which parts are better placed in the harness, and Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award how the two should be optimised together. Throughout, the project will measure reliability, cost, latency, and data locality on realistic task suites, and will release open tooling that a UK small or medium-sized enterprise could adopt. The supervisors are Professor Shiqiang Wang (CORE-AIx Lab, IEEE Fellow, formerly IBM Research) and Dr. Tianjin Huang. The project is a collaboration with an industry research lab, whose enterprise clients face these deployment constraints. The student will join regular meetings with both supervisors and the industry collaborator, with possible visits to the industry research lab, and will publish at leading machine learning venues.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Structured and patterned food products for improved flavour, sensation, and nutrition
jobs.description_html:
Food texture and mouthfeel are not only critical for consumer liking and acceptance, but are also intrinsically linked to mastication, swallowing and digestion. In turn, this effects the nutritional and dietary characteristics of a product. The human perception of food texture is governed by the material properties of the food, breakdown during mastication, hydration with saliva, and interaction with oral surfaces and receptors. A combination of physical properties such as viscosity, density, particle size and aroma release can drive the perception of a singular textural attribute such as ‘creaminess’. During oral food processing, the mixture of saliva and masticated food is called a food bolus, a lubricated mass which is ready to be swallowed.  

Observing and quantifying the dynamic modifications of food during eating helps us to determine the mechanical properties significant in driving texture perception [1], whereas chemical and other analysis of the bolus can insight into the nutrient properties [2]. 

In this project we will apply emerging techniques from the field of metamaterials to design structured and patterned food products that allow control of the oral food processing and perception. Metamaterials are a new class of artificial materials that can be engineered to possess properties that do not exist in natural materials and, for example, can be used to control and manipulate fluid flow over a solid surface [3].  

We will start by investigating the microstructure of the food bolus, using optical microscopy to image a representative of a food bolus (for example, a crushed biscuit mixed with artificial saliva) while forces, mimicking those which the bolus would be exposed to in chewing, are applied. Initially 3D printing, an emerging approach in food manufacturing [4], will be used to create structured, patterned and multitexture food products.  

Analytical techniques, such as infrared spectroscopy and chromatography will be explored as means of determining the effect of patterning and structuring on the nutrient properties or flavour release of the food during breakdown. Models of mastication will be developed using a combination of finite element and analytical modelling. The student will have the opportunity to spend significant time at Mondelēz’s R&D site and Innovation Lab based on the University of Reading campus.  

This will be a unique opportunity to gain analytical skills using cutting-edge facilities as well as gaining invaluable insight into industrial led R&D.   

  1. M. Devezeaux de Lavergne et al., Bolus matters: the influence of food oral breakdown on dynamic texture perception, Food Funct. 8, 464 (2017).  
  2. P. Morell et al., Understanding the relevance of in mouth food processing. A review of in vitro techniques, Trends Food Sci. Technol. 35, 18 (2014).  
  3. F. Avallone et al., Metamaterials and Fluid Flows, Nat. Commun. 17, 4144 (2026).  
  4. Varghese et al., Influence of Selected Product and Process Parameters on Microstructure, Rheological, and Textural Properties of 3D Printed Cookies, Foods 9, 907 (2020).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: R2T2-Med: Resource-Aware AI for Scalable and Deployable Medical Image Analysis
jobs.description_html:
Medical imaging generates very large and rapidly growing volumes of data. Although AI can support automated image analysis, many current models require substantial computing power, memory and processing time. This limits population-scale research, increases deployment costs and restricts adoption in healthcare settings with limited hardware or connectivity. There is therefore a need for medical AI that is not only accurate, but also efficient, reliable and practical to deploy. Research aim and details: This project aims to develop a resource-aware AI framework for both 2D and 3D medical imaging. The framework will adapt its computational requirements to the complexity and uncertainty of each case, the clinical risk and the available hardware.

The project will investigate where unnecessary computation occurs within medical imaging models and how it can be reduced without losing clinically important information. It will then develop a flexible model family that can be trained once and configured for different resource budgets. Safety will be embedded Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award throughout the research by assessing whether efficiency measures affect particular anatomies, clinical sites or patient groups disproportionately. It will be validated in two complementary settings: population-scale abdominal MRI analysis using UK Biobank and near-patient dermatology imaging using public and established clinical data pathways.

The research will also examine whether improved efficiency can be achieved without reducing performance or disproportionately affecting particular clinical sites or patient groups. Expected outcomes: The project will deliver an adaptive and deployable medical imaging AI framework, reproducible efficiency benchmarks, reusable software and evidence from both large-scale and resource-constrained settings. It targets substantial reductions in processing time and memory while maintaining accuracy, reliability and subgroup safety. The resulting technology will reduce computational and hardware requirements, enabling more scalable, sustainable and equitable use of medical imaging AI across research, NHS and commercial healthcare environments.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Uncertainty-Aware Synchronisation for Sustainable Data Centre Digital Twins
jobs.description_html:
Digital Twins rely on synchronisation between physical and virtual entities to maintain sufficient fidelity with the systems they represent. However, determining when synchronisation is genuinely necessary remains a significant challenge, particularly under uncertainty emerging from forecast errors. As the future state of the physical system is often estimated rather than directly observed, forecast errors can accumulate over time and increase the discrepancy between the predicted and actual system states. This growing uncertainty can further exacerbate the synchronisation challenge by making it difficult to determine when the Digital Twin has deviated sufficiently from the physical system to warrant an update.  

Existing approaches based on fixed thresholds, periodic updates, or heuristic policies can lead either to excessive synchronisation and unnecessary resource consumption or to delayed updates that allow the Digital Twin to drift from the operational system.  Sustainable datacentres are one particular area where self-adaptive Digital Twins are increasingly being adopted to model and optimise renewable energy utilisation. In such environments, continuous synchronisation between the physical entities and their virtual counterparts remains a key challenge due to the involvement of multiple prediction modules, including renewable energy availability, datacentre and workload dynamics.  

Each of these modules introduces a degree of prediction uncertainty, where forecast errors can propagate through the Digital Twin, potentially increasing the discrepancy between the predicted and actual states of the physical system. Consequently, determining when synchronisation is necessary becomes particularly challenging, as the decision must account not only for the current state discrepancy but also for the uncertainty associated with future system states. This raises a central research question for this PhD project: How can a self-adaptive sustainable datacentre digital twin determine when synchronisation between an operational system and its Digital Twin is necessary, while accounting for physical drift, uncertainty, and stakeholder-defined operational and performance tolerances? This makes synchronisation fundamentally a decision-making problem rather than a simple update mechanism. Instead of asking whether the current drift exceeds a predefined threshold, the Digital Twin must decide whether the available evidence is sufficient to trigger synchronisation, whether the divergence remains acceptable, or whether additional information should be gathered before making a decision.     

Research Objectives  

  1. Develop an uncertainty-aware synchronisation framework for Digital Twins: Design a self-adaptive framework that models physical drift, forecasting uncertainty, and stakeholder-defined operational tolerances to enable intelligent synchronisation decisions between physical and virtual systems.  
  2. Develop and evaluate AI-based synchronisation strategies for sustainable data centres: Investigate AI techniques, such as reinforcement learning, probabilistic machine learning, and Bayesian inference, to learn adaptive synchronisation policies that improve Digital Twin fidelity while reducing unnecessary updates and supporting renewable energy optimisation.  

Expected Contributions  

  • A novel self-adaptive decision-making framework for uncertainty-aware synchronisation in self-adaptive Digital Twins.  
  • Adaptive AI-based synchronisation algorithms that combine predictive uncertainty with real-time operational context to support intelligent update decisions.  
  • A multi-objective synchronisation strategy that balances Digital Twin fidelity, computational and communication overhead, renewable energy utilisation, and stakeholder performance requirements.  
  • A comprehensive experimental evaluation and reproducible benchmark demonstrating the effectiveness of uncertainty-aware synchronisation for sustainable data centre Digital Twins. 

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Overcoming the Quantification Problem in Deep Raman Spectroscopy using Advanced Optical Metrology and 3D Phantoms
jobs.description_html:
Summary:

This PhD project will develop the next generation of hyper realistic animal free phantoms to overcome the "quantification problem" in deep Raman spectroscopy (DRS). This will enable quantitative analysis in future animal studies and varied healthcare applications. By combining time-domain diffuse optical spectroscopy (TDDOS), 3D-printed tissue models, and advanced computer simulations, the project will develop tools to measure light propagation and allow drug biodistribution to be quantified non-invasively.

Motivation: While Raman spectroscopy non-destructively reveals detailed chemical information and is being developed for a range innovative healthcare applications (e.g., theranostic nanomedicines and improved pathology), quantifying these signals in complex 3D samples remains a major barrier. Current methods struggle with inconsistent geometries and varying optical properties. By resolving this quantification problem, we can enable longitudinal biodistribution studies that require fewer animals, directly aligning with the 3Rs principles (replace, reduce, refine) for more ethical research.

Project Aims: The student will develop a pipeline to enable quantitative DRS by achieving three key milestones: Develop and validate a time domain diffuse optical spectroscopy device to precisely quantify optical properties—specifically absorption and reduced scattering within the 1st biological optical window. Utilize 3D printing to create highly realistic, animal-free 3D tissue phantoms that accurately replicate the optical properties of living tissues. Combine high resolution photogrammetry with Monte Carlo modelling to simulate light propagation through complex 3D geometries, moving beyond simplistic layered models.

jobs.title: PhD in Physics-Aware Graph Neural Networks for Robust Short-Term Visibility Forecasting
jobs.description_html:
Accurate short-term visibility forecasts are essential for safe and efficient transport operations, particularly aviation, where low visibility can reduce airport capacity and cause delays and cancellations. Yet visibility remains difficult to predict. Poor visibility is highly localised and governed by interactions between moisture, temperature, aerosols, surface conditions and atmospheric boundary-layer processes, many occurring at scales that numerical weather prediction (NWP) models cannot fully resolve. Current machine-learning approaches are also largely site-specific or used to post-process NWP, leaving both spatial relationships between observing locations and the physical information learned by ML models under-explored.  

This PhD will develop physics-aware spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs) for 0–6-hour visibility forecasting, initially focusing on low-visibility events (<1000 m) in southeast England. The central hypothesis is that ML can exploit distributed observations to capture local atmospheric processes inadequately represented by NWP, and that connecting learned ML representations with atmospheric physics can improve model understanding, reliability and forecasting skill.  

The project comprises six work packages.   

WP1 Atmospheric processes, data and benchmarks: characterise low-visibility events using observations and NWP, identify relevant boundary-layer and local processes, examine situations in which NWP struggles, and establish persistence, NWP and ML benchmarks.   

WP2 Graph-based forecasting: develop STGNNs that exploit spatial and temporal dependencies between observing sites for continuous visibility prediction, threshold classification, and prediction of event onset and cessation.   

WP3 Linking machine learning model representations with atmospheric physics: analyse latent states, learned spatio-temporal relationships and feature importance to determine whether internal model representations correspond to physically meaningful atmospheric regimes and processes, and investigate why forecasts succeed or fail.   

WP4 Physics-aware multi-source learning: combine observations and NWP fields, using insights from WP1–3 to investigate physically informed model inputs, graph structures and learning constraints, and quantify the value added by different information sources.   

WP5 Robustness and failure diagnosis: develop methods to maintain performance when observations are missing, delayed or degraded, and distinguish data-related failures from unusual or poorly represented meteorological conditions.   

WP6 Operational evaluation and translation: evaluate forecasting skill, reliability and failure modes with Met Office scientists using operationally relevant cases, and assess whether the framework can transfer to other local-scale weather phenomena.  

The project brings together a distinctive supervisory team. Dr Zhou Zhou will lead the machine-learning and spatio-temporal modelling research. Prof. Georgios Efstathiou will contribute expertise in boundary-layer meteorology, turbulence and high-resolution NWP. Prof. Cyril Morcrette will provide complementary expertise in atmospheric processes, sub-grid representation and parameterisation, strengthening the connection between machine learning and operational weather modelling. Steven Ramsdale (Met Office) will provide operational forecasting expertise, relevant data and guidance on practical forecasting requirements and failure modes.  

The student will work across Exeter's data-centric engineering and atmospheric-science communities and engage closely with Met Office scientists. Subject to availability, a Met Office placement or secondment will provide first-hand experience of translating AI research into operational forecasting practice. The project will therefore train the student at the interface of AI, atmospheric physics and operational meteorology.

jobs.title: PhD in 3D Printing Mechanically Adaptive Regenerative Interfaces for Improved Bone Screw Fixation
jobs.description_html:
Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and presents a significant socioeconomic burden from direct treatment costs, and indirect costs due to losses in productivity. An ageing population, combined with increases in inactivity and obesity is expected to further increase this burden. Low back pain is initially treated conservatively, but approximately 20% of patients will require surgery. However, spinal surgery is expensive, clinical outcomes are relatively poor, and reoperation rates are relatively high (~20% within 10 years).  Spinal surgery often uses pedicle screws and rods to provide stabilisation.  

However, screw loosening and pull-out are major complications, particularly in patients with poor bone quality (e.g., osteoporosis), which can result in pain and instability, ultimately requiring expensive revision surgery.  The design of screws has been adapted to mitigate loosening, including larger or longer screws, altered thread geometry, expandable screws, and bone cement augmentation. Non-biodegradable sleeves (e.g. Ogmend) have been used to distribute screw loading to increase pull-out force. However, clinical evidence of these mitigation strategies is inconsistent, or limited, and many devices are evaluated pre-clinically using insertion torque, uniaxial pull-out tests, or simplified cyclic loading, which do not replicate the complex multi-axis loading experienced in vivo. Furthermore, they do not actively regenerate the screw–bone interface or progressively transfer load to newly formed bone.   

The aim of this project is to develop a new generation of bioresorbable, regenerative scaffolds that engineer the screw-bone interface to improve primary and secondary fixation. By controlling scaffold architecture, mechanical properties, bioactivity and degradation, the scaffold will enhance immediate fixation whilst promoting osseointegration and progressive load transfer to newly formed bone. The project will combine biomaterials and tissue engineering with advanced pre-clinical evaluation using Exeter’s six-axis bioreactor. COSA Ltd will provide expertise in medical imaging, anatomical modelling, and multi-material 3D printing to develop reproducible bone-mimicking models for in vitro mechanical testing, whilst clinical guidance will help ensure that scaffold development is aligned with surgical practice.   

The project will:  

  1. Develop and evaluate functionally graded and anisotropic scaffold architectures using additive manufacturing that are designed to distribute interfacial stresses, reduce damaging micromotion, and improve resistance to screw loosening and pull-out. 
  2. Engineer material compositions to promote bone formation and tissue integration. Bioactive and mechanically responsive material strategies will also be explored to determine whether physiological loading can be harnessed to stimulate regeneration at the screw–bone interface (e.g., piezoelectric biomaterials). 
  3. Integrate scaffold development with physiologically relevant six-axis mechanical bioreactor testing. Candidate designs will be evaluated under complex loading that better reflects activities of daily living than conventional tests. This will reveal how scaffold architecture influences load transfer, micromotion, and biological response, directly informing iterative design and optimisation.   

The project will therefore establish a design–manufacture–test process for engineering mechanically adaptive screw–bone interfaces. Although pedicle screw fixation will provide the primary clinical application, the underlying principles could ultimately be translated to other orthopaedic fixation devices where poor bone quality and implant loosening remain major challenges.  In order to achieve these goals, the project will be supported by an interdisciplinary supervisory team consisting of academics, clinicians, and industry with expertise in biomaterials, tissue engineering, additive manufacturing, and  mechanobiology.

University of Exeter, Penryn Campus

jobs.title: PhD in Electrochemcial Lithium Extraction
jobs.description_html:
Lithium-ion batteries are essential to achieving net zero by 2050, supporting electric vehicles, energy storage and the continued expansion of renewable energy. Rapid growth in battery manufacturing is driving demand for lithium, with UK battery manufacturers alone potentially requiring approximately 15,000 tonnes of lithium annually by 2030. Securing a sustainable and resilient lithium supply is therefore critical to the UK's future battery industry and clean-energy transition. Commercial lithium production is currently dominated by high-grade ores and salt-lake brines, using processes including evaporation, precipitation, solvent extraction and adsorption/desorption. These approaches can be energy- and water-intensive, have environmental impacts, and are geographically constrained. Electrochemical lithium extraction offers an alternative route that could recover lithium from lower-concentration brines without relying on slow evaporation processes.  

Importantly, electrochemical systems can operate continuously and potentially be coupled directly with renewable electricity. This project will develop a lithium-selective membrane-based electrochemical extraction process for recovering lithium from complex brines. Unlike electrode-based lithium adsorption, where competing ions can cause slow kinetics and material degradation, lithium-ion-conducting ceramic membranes can selectively transport Li⁺ while blocking other cations through differences in crystal chemistry and ion transport. NASICON-type and perovskite-type lithium-ion conductors have demonstrated this principle; however, significant challenges remain in achieving high Li⁺ selectivity, rapid transport, long-term stability and high energy efficiency under realistic brine conditions.  

The PhD will address these challenges through three interconnected objectives:  

  1. Solid-state lithium-ion conductors, used as electrolyte of all-solid-state batteries, will be systematically investigated to identify the mechanisms controlling conductivity and ion selectivity. Establish the relationship between membrane composition, microstructure, defects and grain-boundary chemistry and the selective transport of Li⁺ in the presence of competing ions such as Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺.  
  2. Determine the mechanisms responsible for membrane degradation in aqueous and chemically complex brines and develop surface modification, coating and additive strategies to improve chemical stability without compromising lithium-ion transport. The effects of pH, ionic composition and operating conditions on membrane structure, transport and selectivity will be systematically established. 
  3. Demonstrate the optimised membrane in an electrochemical lithium-extraction system and evaluate Li⁺ transport, selectivity, extraction efficiency and stability under increasingly realistic brine conditions. The results will be used to establish materials design rules and performance limits for future scale-up and integration into sustainable lithium-recovery processes.Engagement with the emerging critical-minerals and geothermal sectors will help ensure that the research addresses practical resource and processing challenges.  

The PhD will generate new knowledge in electrochemical materials and lithium-selective membranes while developing a potentially scalable, low-carbon approach to critical-mineral recovery. It will provide the student with interdisciplinary expertise across materials science, electrochemistry, energy systems and sustainable resource recovery, supporting future academic and industrial innovation in the UK's critical-minerals and clean-energy sectors.

University of Exeter, Penryn Campus

jobs.title: PhD in Explainable AI for Early Dementia Detection and Deployment
jobs.description_html:
The aim of the project is to develop explainable and trustworthy machine-learning models for the early detection of cognitive decline and dementia. By integrating multimodal data (cognitive assessments, neuroimaging, genetics, lifestyle factors and comorbidities) from diversified information sources like partner cohorts (e.g., PROTECT and evergreen life), and ADNI. we will develop AI tools that predict individuals’ risk trajectories with high accuracy, transparency and fairness, so clinicians can identify high-risk patients earlier and have confidence in recommendations.   

We formulate the task as a longitudinal prediction modelling problem to forecast cognitive decline and dementia progression. For early detection of cognitive decline and dementia, there exists a significant semantic gap among multi-source heterogeneous modalities, including neuroimaging (e.g. MRI or PET scans), and discrete textual data (e.g. cognitive assessment scores and clinical notes), polygenic risk scores and blood biomarkers, and the rich concept entities in biomedical Knowledge Graphs (KGs, as in Chen et al., 2023). To address this challenge, we propose an unsupervised, neural-based and latent knowledge-enhanced approach. The approach learns latent representations (e.g., neural entity embeddings) to elicit and align with entities across multimodal data and knowledge to ensure high explainability.    

We will leverage an explainable agentic framework for early diagnosis with the developed modelling tools, where an example of an agentic framework is in the work (Li et al., 2025). Vision language models in the agentic framework will be leveraged to form natural language explanations from the visual-concept rationales (Zhao et al., 2024). The explanations will be evaluated by clinicians, with criteria including trustworthiness and bias. Bias will be measured through counterfactual data, e.g. perturbed patients’ demographical data, with clinical expert validation, from diverse populations. Bias will also be revealed through visual-concept rationales. The visual-concept rationales will be evaluated through two fairness metrics, comprehensiveness and sufficiency in NLP (DeYoung et al., 2020), with extension to the vision-language domain.    

Uncertainty quantification in the agentic framework will be achieved through a novel, post-hoc calibration model based on the sub latent graph, the extracted rationales with quantified scores (e.g. attention or mutual information scores), and probabilistic prediction outcomes. The proposed approach will be validated through an integrated longitudinal multimodal prediction and explanation system. The outcomes and explanations will be presented to clinicians and patients during PPIE.  

References: 

  1. Chen, H. Dong et al., ‘Knowledge Graphs for the Life Sciences: Recent Developments, Challenges and Opportunities’, 33 pages, 2023, doi: 10.4230/TGDK.1.1.5. 
  2. Li, X. Wang, D. Berlowitz, J. Mez, H. Lin, and H. Yu, ‘CARE-AD: a multi-agent large language model framework for Alzheimer’s disease prediction using longitudinal clinical notes’, npj Digit. Med., vol. 8, no. 1, p. 541, Aug. 2025, doi: 10.1038/s41746-025-01940-4. 
  3. Zhao et al., ‘Explainability for Large Language Models: A Survey’, ACM Trans. Intell. Syst. Technol., vol. 15, no. 2, p. 20:1-20:38, Feb. 2024, doi: 10.1145/3639372. 
  4. DeYoung et al., ‘ERASER: A Benchmark to Evaluate Rationalized NLP Models’, in Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, D. Jurafsky, J. Chai, N. Schluter, and J. Tetreault, Eds, Online: Association for Computational Linguistics, Jul. 2020, pp. 4443–4458. doi: 10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.408.

jobs.title: PhD in End-to-End Verification of Security Protocols in Isabelle
jobs.description_html:
Modern security systems often rely on complex software that translates programs into forms that can be checked automatically. To trust such systems, it is not enough to verify the underlying security protocol: we must also know that the checked representation faithfully captures the intended program. This PhD project will investigate how theorem proving can be used to establish such end-to-end guarantees.

The work will focus on verified translations between programs and the representations used by security protocols, using Isabelle/HOL as the main formalisation environment. Zero-knowledge proof systems, including STARK-style protocols, will provide one important application area. The central research question is how to connect programs, compilation and cryptographic protocols so that correctness and security guarantees can be composed and reused.

The project spans formal methods, programming languages, cybersecurity and cryptography, with scope to shape its direction according to the student's interests. The student will develop and verify semantic models and compilation techniques in Isabelle/HOL, showing that generated representations faithfully capture source-program behaviour. The longer-term goal is to connect these results with mechanised security arguments for the underlying verification protocol.

The supervisory team brings expertise in Isabelle, formal methods, smart-contract verification and security-protocol verification. The project is suitable for candidates interested in formal verification, programming languages, cybersecurity, cryptography, compilers or theorem proving. Prior experience with Isabelle or zero-knowledge proofs is useful but not essential.
